title: Jewish Dem defections threaten El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race decided by razor-thin margins
summary: Some Jewish voters in Michigan say they may cross party lines to support Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate election due to concerns over antisemitism and Israel.
story: Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., reflects on the legacy of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., and the influence of democratic socialists on the Democratic Party on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’

Jewish voters could provide the decisive margin in Michigan’s November Senate election, particularly as some lifelong Democrats say they are prepared to cross party lines and vote for Republican Mike Rogers against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

Analysts point to Michigan’s last U.S. Senate race decided by just 19,006 votes. With estimates placing the state’s Jewish population between approximately 105,000 and 130,000 adults, those votes could tip the scales in favor of Rogers.

"Republicans made real gains in the most Jewish areas in 2024, and Michigan was no exception," Matthew Knee, a Republican pollster and consultant who serves as chief data officer of Pulse Decision Science, told Fox News Digital.

"Stevens massively outperformed in many Jewish precincts as well," Knee said, commenting on the primary. "Rogers and El-Sayed are both the kinds of candidates that will accelerate this trend. There are only 130,000 Jewish voters in Michigan, but in 2024, Rogers only lost by 19,006 votes, so that can make the difference in that kind of razor-thin environment."
DEM ATTORNEY BACKS GOP HOPEFUL IN MICHIGAN RACE AGAINST EL-SAYED, 'JUMPING SHIP' FROM HIS PARTY'S 'LUNATICS'

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, talks poolside with streamer Hasan Piker at a party for content creators supporting his campaign Aug. 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)
For generations, voting for the Democratic Party has been part of the identity of many Jewish families across the state, but since El-Sayed’s victory, some are moving toward the Republican Party.

In interviews with Fox News Digital, several Jewish Michigan voters said El-Sayed’s positions regarding Israel and Zionism have forced them to choose between the liberal values they have supported throughout their lives and what they view as the safety of their children and community.
For many, that prospective vote would not represent a wholesale rejection of the Democratic Party. It would be a break in this single race, a split-ticket vote they once considered unthinkable.
Steve Cohen, a lifelong Michigan resident and self-described "notorious ticket splitter," said the current political climate has made the Senate race especially consequential.

"We’ve had attacks on our synagogues and our school buildings where our kids go," Cohen said. "There’s a torrent of activity pushing anti-Israel and anti-Jewish things on our campuses, and that includes every part of the state of Michigan. So, right now, it’s a little bit scary to be a Jew here."
LEFT-WING ACTIVISTS HECKLE PRO-ISRAEL DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS AT MICHIGAN CONVENTION
Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters at an election night rally at the Majestic Theatre Aug. 4, 2026, in Detroit. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

"I now feel forced to choose between those liberal values and the safety of my children," said Benji, a lifelong Michigan resident and self-identified liberal whose last name Fox News Digital is withholding for security reasons.

"As a lifelong Jewish liberal, I have advocated for liberal values, including commonsense gun laws, LGBT rights, women’s reproductive healthcare, healthcare reform and Black Lives Matter," Benji said.

"El-Sayed may claim to love Jews and the Jewish people, but requiring Jews to be anti-Zionist is a racist purity test and makes his claim ring hollow," he added. "I believe in changing the system from within, but it is no longer safe inside that system for me or for my children."

Stacy, who also asked to withhold her last name, comes from a fifth-generation Democratic Jewish family and has lived in Michigan for 13 years. She has also never voted Republican. Her alienation from the Democratic Party intensified at its state convention in April, where she said she felt hostility toward anyone who openly supported Israel.

"I felt the hatred and hostility in the room toward me if I dared to be supportive of Israel," Stacy said. She recalled watching Stevens being booed and harassed and said she "could see the writing on the wall."
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers waits to go onstage at his election watch party with the MIGOP Nov. 5, 2024 in Novi, Mich.  (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)
"I take no joy in feeling like my party has abandoned me, but I need to vote this way for self-preservation," she said.
Stacy also pointed to Rogers’ experience, calling him the more qualified candidate "if you look at it just on paper."
Mike Rogers is a former Army officer, FBI special agent, congressman and chairman of the House Intelligence Committee.

Jewish voters make up approximately 1.4% of Michigan’s electorate, representing an estimated 105,000 people statewide, according to the American Jewish Population Project at Brandeis University. Much of the community is concentrated in the politically significant Detroit suburbs.

"We hear constantly about the Muslim vote in Michigan, particularly in Dearborn, as a crucial political bloc. But the truth is that Jews in the Great Lakes State are a comparably sized religious minority and historically a much more important constituency for the Democratic Party," said Jesse Arm, Manhattan Institute vice president and pollster.
BIDEN-WORLD VETERAN ISSUES STARK WARNING ABOUT ABDUL EL-SAYED AS HE CROSSES PARTY LINES
Caution tape near the front entrance of Temple Israel a day after an active shooter incident March 13, 2026, in West Bloomfield, Mich. (Emily Elconin/Getty Images)

Arm said Jewish voters turn out at high rates and have long provided Democratic candidates with votes and financial support. He said Jewish organizers and political fundraisers described "an unprecedented level of opposition to El-Sayed among Jewish Democrats."
"Some intend simply to withhold their votes and contributions," Arm said. "But many prominent Jewish Democratic families and donors are prepared to go further and directly support Mike Rogers."
Sam Markstein, national political director and spokesman for the Republican Jewish Coalition, told Fox News Digital those voters could provide the decisive margin in November.

Markstein said the RJC analyzed primary results in Oak Park, Bloomfield Township, West Bloomfield and Southfield, four Oakland County communities with sizable Jewish populations. According to the organization’s analysis, Stevens received approximately 37,000 votes across those communities, compared with about 20,000 for El-Sayed.
Her combined 17,000-vote advantage was greater than the statewide margin by which Rogers lost his 2024 Senate campaign to Democrat Elissa Slotkin.

Anti-Israel supporters march during a rally marking the 75th anniversary of Nakba, or the "catastrophe" of the creation of Israel, in Dearborn, Mich., May 13, 2023. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)
"That’s a really big delta there that shows that Jewish voters do not like Abdul El-Sayed," Markstein said.
He called Michigan’s Jewish voters "not just a rounding error" and said Republicans have an opportunity to move more of them into their column in November.

Markstein also criticized El-Sayed’s response to the March terrorist attack at Temple Israel in West Bloomfield. An armed attacker rammed a vehicle into the synagogue, where approximately 140 children were present, before opening fire. No children, congregants or staff members were physically harmed.
FBI NABS 7 FOR ALLEGED 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE' TO PRESSURE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN, BUSINESSES OVER ISRAEL TIES

El-Sayed initially condemned the attack as "heinous" but later faced criticism after discussing violence in the Middle East while reflecting on the attacker’s actions and saying "hurt people do hurt people."
El-Sayed has maintained that he condemns antisemitism and is committed to protecting Michigan’s Jewish community.
Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed’s campaign regarding the concerns raised by the Jewish voters who were interviewed but did not receive a response.

However, in a previous statement on concerns over antisemitism, El-Sayed stated in May, "I understand what it’s like to be discriminated against for how I pray. This is why I will always stand against antisemitism and stand with my Jewish brothers and sisters and their right to practice their faith safely, freely and unabashedly."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus for comment but did not receive a response. In a statement issued after the primary, however, the caucus congratulated El-Sayed on his victory while acknowledging "frustration, anxiety and deep disappointment" among Jewish Democrats and calling on the nominee to engage directly with Michigan’s Jewish community.
A heavy police presence at Temple Israel, a synagogue in West Bloomfield Township, Mich., after reports of an active shooter March 12, 2026.  (Fox 2)

The caucus said El-Sayed must "address the harm caused during this campaign," arguing his repeated focus on organized Jewish political participation had "crossed an alarming line." At the same time, it urged concerned Jewish Democrats not to abandon the party, saying their place in the Democratic coalition remains "indispensable."
Arm cautioned that Rogers should not take the voting bloc for granted.

"Rogers shouldn’t assume he has it in the bag," Arm said. "El-Sayed is telegenic, disciplined and politically crafty, and he’ll spend the months between now and November looking for ways to present himself as more heterodox and less radical than the record suggests."

The Jewish Federation of Detroit directed Fox News Digital to a statement it released after the primary election result, while noting that, as a 501(c)(3), it "cannot and does not endorse or oppose candidates."
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

"As an organization, we will continue to engage across the political spectrum to advocate for issues essential to our future, including standing against antisemitism, violence and bigotry, ensuring the safety and security of the Jewish community and houses of worship, and championing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state," the statement said.
Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in suburban Detroit said the concerns extend beyond any single candidate.
The Jewish religious symbol of the Star of David inside a synagogue.  (iStock)
"American Jews have long rejected extremism, particularly within our political parties," Starr told Fox News Digital. "We reject extremism on the right, and we reject extremism on the left.

"Right now, however, it feels as though extremism on the left is not only becoming louder, but increasingly normalized. That has created a frightening moment for American Jews and certainly for the Jewish community here in Michigan."

For Benji and Stacy, the possibility of voting Republican does not mean they have stopped believing in the causes they have supported for decades. It means that, for the first time, they believe their Democratic values and their safety as Jews have been placed in conflict.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Voting for a Republican was once unthinkable. Following El-Sayed’s nomination, they say it now feels unavoidable.

Ariella Noveck is a journalist specializing in antisemitism and Middle East affairs, with extensive experience covering Jewish communities worldwide. She can be followed on X and Instagram @AriellaNoveck

title: Marine veteran Robert Gilman returns to US soil as Trump admin fulfills request: 'No American left behind'
summary: Photos show Robert Gilman arriving on U.S. soil, where he was met by Steve Witkoff and Sebastian Gorka after the Trump administration secured his release.
story: Wrongful detentions of American citizens overseas decline as President Donald Trump secures the release of a Marine veteran from a Russian prison. Former hostage negotiator Dan O'Shea analyzes the negotiation breakthrough, emphasizing that the release was achieved without a prisoner swap. This event highlights shifts in U.S. hostage diplomacy.
Photos and video emerged Wednesday showing Marine veteran Robert Gilman back on American soil following his release from Russian custody.

Gilman, a U.S. citizen who was arrested on Jan. 17, 2022, in Voronezh, Russia, and sentenced to a total of 10 years in prison, was freed on humanitarian grounds Tuesday after 1,666 days in prison. President Donald Trump said Gilman would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday night, and after speaking with him, "he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands."

"Our Marine is safely back on American soil," Sebastian Gorka, a deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X early Wednesday, sharing a video of an aircraft coming to a stop. "As President Donald Trump promised, Steve Witkoff brought Robert Gilman cheeseburgers and milkshakes!"
US MARINE VETERAN RELEASED FROM RUSSIAN PRISON AFTER 1,666 DAYS OF DETENTION

U.S. special envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, center, and Deputy Assistant to the President Sebastian Gorka, right, greeted Robert Gilman, left, upon his arrival in the U.S. following his release from Russia. (SEPeaceMissions/X.com)

"(I snuck him a cigar for when he’s fully recovered!)," Gorka added. "And a member of our broader White House team brought him his own USMC flag. There are very few jobs like this one. No American left behind."
In his own post, Witkoff, who is the U.S. special envoy to the Middle East, said it was a "special night welcoming an American citizen home to his family and country."
"Thank you POTUS for never leaving anyone behind," Witkoff also said, sharing an image of him and Gorka alongside Gilman on the plane following the landing.

"Robert is a patriot — a former United States Marine who served our country with honor. He can now finally return to his family and receive the medical care he needs," Witkoff said in a separate post. "His return is another testament to POTUS’s extraordinary leadership and unwavering commitment to bringing Americans home. Under his leadership, Marc Fogel and Ksenia Karelina were also brought home from Russia."
AMERICAN EX-MARINE FEARED NEAR DEATH AFTER WEEKS IN CATATONIC STATE IN RUSSIAN PRISON
Steve Witkoff and Sebastian Gorka are seen awaiting the arrival of Robert Gilman as he returned to U.S. soil following his release on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, from Russia. (SebGorka/X.com)

Gilman was convicted in 2022 of assaulting a police officer, initially receiving a sentence of three and a half years. Gilman’s troubles in custody then increased in 2024 when he was found guilty by Russia of attacking a prison inspector during a cell check, assaulting an investigator and beating another guard.
In December 2025, Russia once again extended Gilman's prison sentence after a regional court found him guilty of a new assault on prison staff.
However, the U.S. State Department referred to Gilman as a wrongful detainee.

Gilman is the third U.S. Marine to be taken prisoner in Russia in the last decade, following Russia's detention of Paul Whelan in 2018 and Trevor Reed in 2019. Both were later released in prisoner swaps.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis. We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place," Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
Gorka says he brought Gilman a cigar to enjoy when he is "fully recovered." (SebGorka/X.com)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Robert Gilman has been reunited with his wonderful mother, Nancy, who is also on the plane with him, and will soon get to see all of his loved ones," Trump added.
Fox News’ Emma Bussey, Robert McGreevy, Gillian Turner, Nick Kalman and Louis Casiano contributed to this post.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Decoy' Air Force One was protected by US fighter jets, official says
summary: U.S. fighter jets escorted the decoy Air Force One carrying the press corps and senior staff to the United Kingdom after Trump's secret plane swap.
story: President Donald Trump reportedly secretly boarded a third, smaller U.S. military aircraft, using an airport catering truck as cover and an older Air Force One jet as a decoy, to depart July’s NATO summit amid a credible threat from Iran.

The "decoy" Air Force One that President Donald Trump was snuck off of was protected by U.S. fighter jets on its flight to the United Kingdom, a senior Trump administration official told Fox News on Wednesday.

The revelation pushes back on media fears the press corps and staff might have been left vulnerable to the perceived threat from hostile actors seeking to strike Trump's flight out of Ankara, Turkey, last month.

The previously undisclosed security measure adds another layer to the extraordinary precautions surrounding the president’s plane swap, which left the aircraft normally associated with Trump continuing on to the U.K. without him aboard.

The press corps was joined on the "decoy" plane under U.S. fighter jet cover by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and were aware Trump was not on board, the official said.
TRUMP USED CATERING TRUCK, AIR FORCE ONE DECOY TO EVADE IRAN THREAT: REPORT
This photo shows the press boarding the Air Force One aircraft from Ankara, while a catering truck is located at the front of the plane. (Pool)
Staff and members of the traveling press pool had been instructed to keep the window shades closed throughout the flight, preventing them from seeing the fighter escort.

According to a pool report circulated Tuesday, there was little indication at the airport that anything unusual was happening. The press vans were positioned far back in the motorcade, and photographers did not see Trump board an aircraft from their usual position beneath the wing.
White House staff and reporters boarded the original plane as normal, where bags of snack mix bearing the presidential seal were waiting for them.
TRUMP’S SLY PLANE SWITCH RAISES EYEBROWS OVER SAFETY OF PASSENGERS LEFT BEHIND ON BOARD
President Donald Trump boards the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One at RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, Britain, after attending a NATO leaders summit in Turkey, on July 8, 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Once aboard, however, the press was told to keep the window shades down. A Secret Service agent later came to the press cabin to reinforce the instruction, according to the pool report. When a photographer briefly opened a shade, the photographer was quickly told to close it again.
A White House wrangler told reporters only that the closed shades had been requested by the Secret Service.
Trump said Tuesday night that the decision to switch aircraft was made at the direction of his security detail and the military.

"Well, it's only up to the Secret Service; I just follow what they'd like to do," Trump told reporters after traveling to Geneva, Ohio, for the Freedom 250 Patriot Games. "So I go by the Secret Service and the military."
TRUMP SAYS HE'S IRAN'S 'NO. 1' TARGET AS RENEWED CONFLICT RAISES ASSASSINATION FEARS

President Donald Trump speaks to reporters in the press cabin of the new, Qatari-gifted Air Force One after changing planes to return to Washington from RAF Mildenhall, Britain, July 8, 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)
"They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane, equal safety — but they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say."
The State Department declined to comment on the fighter jets.
Trump also suggested that the aircraft he ultimately traveled aboard may have faced greater danger once the swap was made.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk," Trump told reporters on the tarmac Tuesday night after news of the switch became public. "I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for."
Fox News' Nicholas Kalman contributed to this report.
Peter Doocy currently serves as a rotating anchor of The Sunday Briefing (Sundays, 11 AM/ET) alongside Jacqui Heinrich and senior White House correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC).

title: DOJ heavyweights throw monkey wrench in Dem plans to put Trump allies in hot seat
summary: President Donald Trump's private advisors can now claim executive privilege under a new Justice Department memo, and Democrats vow investigations.
story: Former special advisor to President Donald Trump Dr. Scott Atlas discusses Dr. Anthony Fauci facing questioning at a Senate hearing regarding COVID-19 origins, mandates and personal earnings. He invoked the Fifth Amendment 111 times, refusing to answer key inquiries.

President Donald Trump's private advisors and attorneys are now protected by executive privilege as long as their conversations relate to the president's official decision-making, according to a memo Tuesday from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel.
"The need for presidential confidentiality applies to communications with private advisers just as it does with government officials," the 21-page memo stated.
The memo, written by Assistant Attorney General Elliot Gaiser, comes months ahead of the midterm elections as Democrats battle for control of Congress.

Democrats have pledged to continue their investigations into Trump and his family's business dealings and financial investments, potentially using subpoenas and congressional hearings to advance those probes.
TRUMP AG PICK TODD BLANCHE FACES SENATE TEST IN FIRST MAJOR CONFIRMATION FIGHT SINCE GRAHAM’S DEATH
The Capitol and Donald Trump (Alex Wong/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Under the Office of Legal Counsel's new nonbinding memo, private citizens who have offered advice in confidential conversations with Trump or White House staffers about official presidential duties can claim executive privilege if they're subpoenaed by Congress.

"The presidential communications privilege is rooted in the need for confidentiality to ensure that [this] presidential decision-making is of the highest caliber, informed by honest advice and full knowledge," the memo stated. "Without a promise of confidentiality, the President’s ability to ‘decide and act quickly’ on matters of unrivaled importance would be seriously hindered."

The memo noted that the president may sometimes need expertise and guidance from an outside source who could be crucial to making the best decision. Gaiser also acknowledged that a private advisor to the president may be more hesitant to offer guidance because of concerns that doing so could negatively affect the advisor's livelihood.

"Such individuals may be reluctant to provide advice on controversial or unpopular policies based on a fear of public disclosure or potential ramifications for their personal endeavors," the memo stated.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appears before a Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing for his nomination to be attorney general at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Gaiser pointed to a long history of presidents seeking advice from people outside the federal government. Andrew Jackson had his informal "Kitchen Cabinet," while Franklin D. Roosevelt turned to a group of academics known as his "Brain Trust." The memo also noted that Grover Cleveland consulted financier J.P. Morgan during a Treasury gold shortage, and Lyndon B. Johnson sought advice from trusted friends outside the government during the Vietnam War.
SCHUMER DODGES QUESTIONS AFTER BOMBSHELL REPORT ALLEGES DEM SENATOR HAD RELATIONSHIPS WITH HOUSE STAFFERS
"Yet throughout history, Presidents have relied on private advisers (or, at minimum, advisers outside the Executive Branch) to perform their executive function," Gaiser wrote.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., interpreted the Justice Department memo as a sign that Trump is worried about what could come if Democrats win control of Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Donald Trump is scared," Schumer wrote on X. "He knows accountability is coming. He’s using his newly installed Attorney General/personal lawyer, Todd Blanche, to cover up his communications with private advisers and special interest cronies.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"These are the actions of someone with something to hide," Schumer continued. "And it shows he is petrified of the questions a Democratic Congress will demand answers to. We will not let Trump escape the accountability he deserves."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Peggy Flanagan was Minnesota's No 2 official as massive fraud scandal exploded under state's watch
summary: Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan just scored the Democratic nomination for Senate, but she's hampered by some heavy baggage: her role during the Minnesota fraud scandal.
story: Former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya joins ‘Fox Across America’ with Jimmy Failla to explain why she has decided to launch a bid for the U.S. Senate in Minnesota.
Minnesota's new Democratic nominee for Senate has baggage heading into the November election: the massive fraud scandal that rippled through the Land of 10,000 Lakes happened right under her nose.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan scored a major win for the insurgent progressive movement that's reshaping the Democratic Party from the outside on Tuesday, toppling the more moderate Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., in the process. But her role during the Minnesota fraud scandal has plagued her campaign, with both sides attacking her on the issue.
It became Craig's prime line of attack against her.

"The lieutenant governor, even as we sit here today, continues to take absolutely no accountability for any of the fraud issues, and she continues to blame the governor," Craig said during a debate with Flanagan on Minnesota Public Radio. "And I'm going to be honest: It's pissing me off."
PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE

Minnesota Democratic Senate nominee Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is riding the progressive wave this midterm election cycle, but before handing moderates a resounding defeat, she had a front row seat to the sprawling fraud scandal in her home state.  (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

During the campaign, Craig charged that Flanagan had largely shrugged off responsibility for the fraud scandal, despite having served alongside Walz as his No. 2 since the pair were first elected in 2018.
In an interview with the Minnesota Reformer, Flanagan said, "The governor has said that the buck stops with him, and he took the lead here," on the fraud scandal.

Notably, Flanagan did not mention fraud during her victory speech Tuesday night, instead focusing on hallmarks of her campaign thus far, such as vowing to "rip [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] apart" following the deadly shootings in Minnesota earlier this year.
Still, the scandal torpedoed Walz's re-election hopes, and Republicans plan to lean into it in the weeks leading up to Nov. 3.
HALL OF FAMER TONY DUNGY ENDORSES MICHELE TAFOYA IN CROWDED MINNESOTA REPUBLICAN PRIMARY FOR U.S. SENATE

Her opponent, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, has already pounced on the opportunity several times this election season and did so again shortly after being crowned the Republican nominee for Senate.
"Minnesotans of every political stripe are fed up. They're exhausted with this fraud," Tafoya told a Minnesota Fox affiliate.

"We cannot show our children that failure comes without accountability," she continued. "We've got to have accountability, but more than that, we've got to do things, everything we do, to make Minnesota more livable, more affordable, more safe, and without fraud, and we're gonna do that."
National Republicans are confident that she could win big in November.

While Minnesota is not on the NRSC’s target map of eight battleground seats, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, believes Tafoya is a serious contender to Democrats, who have held both Senate seats since 2009.
"The one thing that gets me excited when I think about this election cycle on the map is Minnesota," Scott told CNN. "I think Minnesota, we have a real shot with Michele Tafoya."
REPUBLICANS GET THE DEMOCRAT THEY WANTED AS SOCIALIST ABDUL EL-SAYED WINS MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY
Michele Tafoya says Peggy Flanagan represents a shift toward "Democrat socialism" in Minnesota. (Fox News Digital; Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
Republicans also see Tafoya’s more moderate leanings as a positive heading into November.
A GOP operative told Fox News Digital that she’s seen as a candidate who can unite swing, moderate and MAGA voters in a winning coalition.

"Tafoya has the power to appeal to a broader electorate that’s starving for authenticity," the operative said. "Her career as a sideline reporter for NBC’s ‘Sunday Night Football’ makes her relatable to a mainstream crowd."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Her position on abortion, for example, could attract swing voters.

In an open letter to Minnesotans, Tafoya wrote that, as a senator, she would oppose taxpayer-funded abortions, support conservative, strict-constructionist judges and remain "completely aligned with President Donald Trump on this issue." She also expressed support for the Dobbs decision.
But she won’t support a total ban on abortion.

"I do not support an outright ban on abortion, and I believe there should be reasonable access in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy," Tafoya wrote. "Further, I believe that states who restrict access to fertility treatments like IVF are also acting wrongly — being pro-family is pro-life."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Mamdani's team said NYPD would accompany his wife on Middle East vacation — cops say that's not true
summary: The NYPD denied it would send officers to Syria and Lebanon with Rama Duwaji, contradicting Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office on the security detail.
story: Police security escorts are denied for the wife of NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani during her upcoming trip to Lebanon and Syria. Nate Foy breaks down the NYPD decision. Mamdani's office initially claimed security would join her, later blaming a miscommunication.

The New York Police Department (NYPD) will not provide a security detail to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's wife during her upcoming vacation to two terror hotspots in the Middle East, despite the mayor's office claiming otherwise.
"The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level 4 travel advisories for discretionary reasons such as personal travel," a spokesperson for the law enforcement agency told Fox News.

Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, is planning to travel to Syria and Lebanon to visit family in September, according to the New York Post. Both of those countries are on the State Department's "Do Not Travel" list due to terrorism concerns.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his wife, Rama Duwaji, smile as confetti falls after his ceremonial inauguration as mayor at City Hall on Jan. 1, 2026, in New York. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)
MAMDANI'S WIFE CO-HOSTS LUXE MUSLIM RETREAT CASTING VIRGIN MARY AS ‘PALESTINIAN WOMAN’ UNDER OCCUPATION
The mayor's office had previously confirmed that Duwaji would have an NYPD security detail on the trip.

"Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the first lady’s security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon," Mamdani’s spokeswoman Dora Pekec reportedly said.

But later, as it became clear that the NYPD would not be making the overseas trek, the mayor chalked the confusion up to a staff "miscommunication" when asked about it by news outlet PIX11 on Tuesday.
NYPD Detectives’ Endowment Association (DEA) President Scott Munro furiously slammed the implication that NYPD detectives would accompany the city's First Lady to the Middle East.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch speak at a Sunday morning news conference after a spate of weekend shootings in Brooklyn. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu)
MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS

"Our detectives put themselves in harm’s way every day protecting New Yorkers," said Munro. "The DEA would never remain silent if our members were asked to travel to a dangerous, off-limits foreign country for anything other than a legitimate law-enforcement or intelligence operation."
"Our detectives are needed here in New York City protecting residents and fighting crime," he added.

Mamdani has a long history of trashing the very police department he thought would accompany and provide security for his wife to the dangerous Middle Eastern countries on New York City taxpayer's dime.
"There is no negotiating with an institution this wicked & corrupt. Defund it. Dismantle it. End the cycle of violence," Mamdani said in reference to the NYPD in a viral 2020 post on X.

Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, holds up bananas labeled with a 30% off sticker during an announcement on municipal grocery stores at a Campaign for Hunger community food distribution center in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"We don't need an investigation to know that the NYPD is racist, anti-queer & a major threat to public safety," he said in another 2020 post, adding in a follow-up: "What we need is to #DefundTheNYPD."
JON STEWART PRESSES MAMDANI ON WHERE HE BREAKS WITH FELLOW DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ON PRISONS AND BORDERS
"Queer liberation means defund the police," he said in yet another post.

The mayor, who has also faced scrutiny for his anti-Israel views and recently called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" while calling for his arrest, derogatorily linked the NYPD to the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF).

"We have to make clear that when the boot of the NYPD is on your neck, it’s been laced by the IDF," Mamdani, who was a keynote speaker, said during a panel discussion at the Democratic Socialists of America's 2023 national convention.

Jessica Tisch speaks after being sworn in as the next Commissioner of the New York Police Department (NYPD) during a ceremony at One Police Plaza on November 25, 2024, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
During his campaign for mayor of the most populated U.S. city, Mamdani said the exact opposite, explicitly stating that he did not want to defund the police.
SEE IT: MAMDANI BOOED OFF STAGE AT NEW YORK CITY PRO-POLICE CELEBRATION: ‘WALKED OFF IN SHAME’
Still, it appears there is no love lost between Mamdani and the NYPD.
Just last week, he was booed offstage when he tried to speak at a pro-police event in Staten Island.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Dem in key swing race missed nearly half her state House votes while taking taxpayer salary: 'No show'
summary: Former Iowa Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan missed 45% of Iowa House floor votes in 2022 while campaigning for a congressional seat.
story: Christina Bohannan warned in 2021 that Iowa would become a ‘backwater’ if lawmakers barred transgender athletes from girls and women's sports. Iowa enacted the ban in 2022. (Credit: YouTube/City of Iowa City — April 2, 2021)

FIRST ON FOX: Former Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan missed nearly half of her votes in Iowa's House of Representatives during her final year in office as she campaigned for a congressional seat in the battleground district, records show.
In 2022, Bohannan missed 348 of 773 floor votes, or about 45% of all votes, according to the legislature’s records, despite stressing the importance "for leaders to show up" three years later.

Bohannan is running for Congress in Iowa's 1st Congressional District, a race the Cook Political Report ranks as a "toss up" in November as Republicans attempt to preserve their razor-thin majority in the House of Representatives.

Some of the skipped votes involved bills addressing protections for sexual abuse victims, volunteer firefighters and first responders, Iowa’s dairy industry, agricultural programs, emergency 911 services and juvenile justice reform.
IOWA DEM WHO TOUTED 'STRONG WORK ETHIC' MISSES MORE THAN HALF OF HER HOUSE VOTES

Former Iowa Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan missed nearly half of her state House votes while campaigning for Congress, records show. (Iowa Legislature ; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Liberal Christina Bohannan says leaders should ‘show up’ and then is a no-show herself," Emily Tuttle, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"Missing half your job while collecting your taxpayer-funded paycheck isn’t leadership worthy of a promotion. It’s the kind of performance that would get you fired anywhere else."

The absences stand in contrast with Bohannan’s past comments. In an Oct. 6, 2025, post on X, she wrote that she had the "honor of speaking" with more than 100 voters at a candidate forum representing five Iowa counties.
"At a time when so much is uncertain, it’s more important than ever for leaders to show up and talk directly with Iowans," she added.

Similarly, in a 2021 interview with Bleeding Heartland, an Iowa politics blog, Bohannan was described as planning to spend "a lot of time on legislative work during the 2022 session" with the rest of her efforts focused on her congressional campaign.
Bohannan served one term in the Iowa House from 2021 to 2023 before launching her first campaign for Congress.
BATTLEGROUND DEM CALLED PATRIOTISM 'SENSITIVE AND CONTROVERSIAL' DURING DEBATE OVER THE PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE
Christina Bohannan, candidate for Iowa’s first congressional district, listens during a roundtable on affordable housing Oct. 23, 2024 in Iowa City, Iowa. (Iowa City Press-Citizen)

She is challenging incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, for a third time in the 1st Congressional District, which includes Davenport and Iowa City, after losing by about seven points in 2022 and roughly 800 votes following a recount in 2024.

But Bohannan remained on the state’s legislative payroll during that period. According to state legislative records, Iowa lawmakers earned a $25,000 annual salary in 2022, plus $175 per day per diem for up to 100 days, or $17,500.
The Democratic lawmaker has also faced mounting criticism for her past comments and middle-class messaging on the campaign trail.
'QUEEN OF DEI' RUNNING FOR CONGRESS RIPPED HER RURAL STATE AS 'BACKWARDS' ON PODCAST
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, attends a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center after a meeting of the House Republican Conference Dec. 16, 2025. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital previously reported that Bohannan warned Iowa could be seen as "backwards" over limits on diversity training at public schools and universities and "look like a backwater" over restrictions on transgender athletes.

Other reports revealed that Bohannan and her husband owned a waterfront Sarasota, Florida, condo valued between $500,001 and $1 million, in addition to a $1.55 million Iowa City home while campaigning as a hard-working, middle-class advocate who understands what it's like "to still struggle to put food on the table."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Bohannan’s campaign for comment.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Tafoya makes 'common sense' pitch to disaffected Democrats as she vows to fight Minnesota’s ‘socialist lurch’
summary: Michele Tafoya won the Minnesota GOP Senate primary and now faces Peggy Flanagan, pitching common sense to voters across the political spectrum.
story: GOP Minnesota Senate candidate Michele Tafoya told Fox News Digital she’s offering voters a ‘common sense’ alternative

EDINA, MN - As socialist candidates continue to score victories across the country and take more control of the Democratic Party, Minnesota GOP Senate nominee Michele Tafoya is making her pitch to voters from all parties who still believe in "common sense."

"We do not want to see a socialist lurch anywhere in this country, and in particular in Minnesota, so I will do whatever I can to stand up against this movement toward Democrat socialism," Tafoya told Fox News Digital on Tuesday shortly after voting in a suburb outside Minneapolis. "Socialism does not work."

"There is absolutely a home for every voter in Minnesota that wants common sense, that wants a return to sanity, that wants to see kids learn in school again, that wants accountability for this fraud, who wants the fraud never repeat itself, who wants crime rates to go down again," Tafoya told Fox News Digital. "There is room for you. We are the common sense candidacy and we're gonna represent a lot more than just conservatives in this state."

Hours later, Tafoya went from Republican Senate candidate to Republican Senate nominee as she convincingly won her primary and moves on to face Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the general election in November.
MINNESOTA HOUSE SPEAKER LISA DEMUTH WINS GOP GUBERNATORIAL PRIMARY TO REPLACE TIM WALZ IN NOVEMBER
Michele Tafoya says Peggy Flanagan represents a shift toward "Democrat socialism" in Minnesota. (Fox News Digital ; Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
When reached by phone after her victory, Tafoya reiterated her commitment to crossing party lines to reach disaffected Democrats.

"Our state has been going in the wrong direction at the speed of sound and people who love Minnesota are brokenhearted, and we see that this has happened under the watch of career politicians single-party rule, for many years now they've brought us to this place it's time for change and I think we're going to appeal to voters across the political spectrum to stand up and say we're not going to continue to re-elect the people that got us to this place to begin with," Tafoya told Fox News Digital.
FAILED PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE WINS DEM PRIMARY FOR MIDWEST GOVERNOR AMID FRAUD SCANDAL FALLOUT
Tafoya is aiming to become the first Republican to win statewide office in Minnesota since 2006.

Tafoya's opponent in November, progressive Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, has drawn criticism over the massive fraud scandal in the state that forced Gov. Tim Walz to drop his re-election bid, given that she has served alongside him since 2019, as well as her far-left positions that include abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Michele Tafoya and Kevin O’Leary visited "Outnumbered" at Fox News Channel Studios on April 18, 2024, in New York City. (Roy Rochlin/Getty Images)

"It is time to hold them accountable, and we're going to do that by firing them," Tafoya said. "And we're gonna hire people who are outsiders, who are willing to come in and fix this with new ideas and not just bend to party politics as the establishment always does."

Tafoya, whose message to disaffected Democrat voters is similar to the pitch Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers made last week in his race against his opponent Abdul El-Sayed, told Fox News Digital she is looking forward to speaking to Democrats and independents in the coming months.

"When you run in a primary, you're talking to mostly your own voters," Tafoya said. "Now I'm excited to reach out to those disaffected Democrats who feel that the party has left them, who feel like they're homeless politically. We're gonna open the doors to them and I can't wait to talk to all those independents and share their ideas. So that's what I'm looking forward to."
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Blakeman cuts into Hochul's New York governor's race lead in new poll, as likely voters give DSA judgment
summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s lead over Bruce Blakeman narrowed from 20 points among registered voters in Siena’s June poll to 10 points among likely voters in its latest poll.
story: New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman joins 'Sunday Morning Futures' to discuss New York Gov. Kathy Hochul's far-left policy shift, budget comparisons with Florida and the rise of progressive influence in New York politics.

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul’s lead over Republican candidate Bruce Blakeman is slipping, according to a new Siena University poll released Wednesday, as likely voters in New York also gave a negative 30-47% favorability rating to the Democratic Socialists of America.

With under three months to go until Election Day, Hochul leads Blakeman 49-39% among likely New York State gubernatorial voters, down from 52-32% when registered voters were asked the same question in June.

"At this point four years ago, August 2022, when Hochul was just finishing her first year as governor, she led her opponent, former Republican Congressman (and current EPA Administrator) Lee Zeldin by 14 points, 53-39%, before going on to ultimately win the election by six points, 53-47%," Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said in a statement.

Blakeman, who is the current Nassau County executive, said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Wednesday that "All of the polls we have seen in the last two months have us virtually tied with Kathy Hochul," and, "This poll is always off and continues to be off."
HOCHUL SAYS STEFANIK WOULD'VE BEEN TOUGHER GOP OPPONENT THAN BLAKEMAN IN SURPRISING SWIPE AT RIVAL
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images/Getty Images; Alexander MacDougall/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)

"We know and she knows this race is neck and neck. Kathy Hochul is desperate for people to believe that she is way ahead when she knows that her high taxes, soaring electric bills, and increased crime have made her the worst governor in America," Blakeman added.

The latest Siena University Poll was conducted between Aug. 3–6 among 811 New York likely voters, with an overall margin of error of +/- 4.6 percentage points for those who answered the entire survey.

Hochul Campaign Spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki told Fox News Digital on Wednesday that "The difference in this race is crystal clear: Governor Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets at every opportunity, invested billions in public safety, and stood up against Donald Trump’s endless attacks on this state – ‘MAGA all the way’ Bruce Blakeman, who’s literally campaigning with Trump himself, jacked up property taxes and let violent crime spike to decade highs on his watch – and that’s what we continue to see voters respond to."

The Siena poll found that likely voters believe Hochul will do a better job than Blakeman on making prices more affordable for average New Yorkers, 48–41%, and increasing the supply of affordable housing, 51–35%.
NEW YORK SHERIFFS 'MAD AS HELL' AS HOCHUL PUSHES TO BAN KEY LAW ENFORCEMENT PARTNERSHIP

Then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul hold hands on stage as they attend a "New York is Not For Sale" rally at Forest Hills Stadium, in the Queens borough of New York City, on Oct. 26, 2025. (Reuters/Eduardo Munoz)

Respondents were more divided over the issues of keeping New Yorkers safe, where Hochul led 47-44%, and addressing undocumented immigrants living in the state, where she was ahead 45-44%, according to the Siena Research Institute.

"Not surprisingly, both candidates are holding on to their partisan bases, as Hochul leads among Democrats 80-8% and Blakeman leads among Republicans 84-9%. Likely independent voters favor Blakeman by a narrow five-point margin, 45–40%," Greenberg said.

"Hochul holds a commanding 64-19% lead in New York City, but trails Blakeman in the downstate suburbs by eight points, 49-41%. They are running virtually even in upstate, as well as among men and with white voters; Hochul has large leads with women, Latinos and Black voters," he added.

Bruce Blakeman, Nassau County executive and Republican candidate for New York governor, who is running to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and has secured President Donald Trump's endorsement. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The Siena Research Institute also said it asked voters about the Democratic Socialists of America for the first time. The progressive political group has been exerting its influence on elections across America, with member Zohran Mamdani winning the New York City mayoral race last year.
The poll found that the group had a negative favorability rating.

title: Spanberger’s rough rural reception draws Hillary Clinton parallels
summary: Del. Wren Williams compared Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's Galax visit to Hillary Clinton's hot sauce moment, saying nobody was buying it.
story: Virginia Democrat Gov. Abigail Spanberger was met with loud boos in a brief appearance on stage on the final day of the annual Old Fiddlers' Convention in Galax, Virginia.

Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger was roasted for her visit to a nearly century-old fiddling convention in southwestern Virginia, with the area’s state delegate comparing her unfavorably to failed presidential candidate Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Clinton famously surprised the hosts of New York’s "Breakfast Club" radio program in 2016 when she said she regularly carries hot sauce in her purse — a remark critics said echoed Beyoncé Knowles and amounted to political pandering to Southern and Black voters during her 2016 race against then-businessman and reality TV star Donald Trump.

Del. Wren Williams, a Republican who represents Galax, where the 90th Annual Old Fiddlers’ Convention took place, told Fox News Digital he was proud of constituents who made their feelings about the governor known peacefully but strongly.
DEM GOVERNOR BOOED AT VIRGINIA OLD FIDDLERS' CONVENTION
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, left; Hillary Rodham Clinton, right. (Mike Kropf/Getty Images; David Dee Delgado Getty Images)

Williams said it was clear to those assembled that Spanberger was trying to "pander" to rural residents, who have pushed back on several of the governor’s priorities, including the judicially halted redistricting effort and a slew of what Richmond Republican leaders have called "the bad bills."
"[It was] about like Hillary Clinton and her hot sauce – nobody was buying it," Williams said.

Over the weekend, Spanberger and her public safety chief, Galax native Stanley Meador, were booed after Meador introduced the governor. Meador previously served as special agent in charge of the FBI’s Richmond Field Office during the "anti-Catholic memo" controversy that drew congressional scrutiny.

Williams told Fox News Digital that people in Galax and surrounding Carroll County — atop the Blue Ridge and just over the border from Andy Griffith’s "Mount Pilot" area of North Carolina — have felt ignored by Spanberger and said their reaction was justified.
SUPREME COURT DEALS BLOW TO VIRGINIA DEMOCRATS IN FIGHT OVER STATE COURT ELECTION MAP RULING

"These are my constituents, the same ones that she just disarmed, tried to force into one single congressional district that represented their political views, and lied every step of the way while jockeying for the national Democratic Party nod for her shot at first female president," Williams said, referring to another parallel between Spanberger and Clinton.

Galax, currently represented in Congress by Rep. Morgan Griffith, R-Va., would have sat at the edge of the only remaining Republican-held district under Richmond Democrats’ proposed 10-1 congressional map, which a bipartisan group of Virginia Supreme Court justices blocked earlier this year.

Virginia's top state Republican — whose district is not far west of where Spanberger got booed — told Fox News Digital the incident proved to the governor that her policies run counter to what his neighbors want from Richmond:
"Southwest Virginians have never been shy about standing up for their values and their way of life," said House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore of Gate City.

"When you try to take away their voice in Congress, go after their Second Amendment rights, and drive up their power bills to pay for a green energy agenda they don’t want and can’t afford, folks are going to let you know how they feel," he said.
Former Attorney General Jason Miyares, a top figure in the "Vote No" coalition opposing Spanberger’s redistricting effort, said in a statement that the crowd’s response was predictable.

"Governor Spanberger booed in Galax. Turns out when you break your campaign promise, attempt a leftist power grab pushing an unconstitutional gerrymandering effort in order to silence rural Virginia voices, coupled with massive tax increases, it results in a frosty reception," Miyares said.
WATCH: SPANBERGER KNOCKED FOR ‘BAIT AND SWITCH’ HYPOCRISY AS POPULARITY PLUMMETS AMID REDISTRICTING FIASCO
"Spanberger finally had to face the music," another Virginia user wrote on X.
Other critics contrasted Democrats’ strength in Northern Virginia with opposition to Spanberger in more rural parts of the state.
"These folks booing are showing how the vast majority of those of us in Virginia feel… not those communists in the blue suburbs of DC," Diane Cheesbrough wrote on X.
"She needs to go and take Tim Kaine and Mark Warner and Eugene Vindman with her."
TRUMP BLASTS SPANBERGER AHEAD OF VIRGINIA MEETINGS, SAYS STATE FACES TAX BASE EXODUS LIKE NEW YORK, CALIFORNIA
Radio host Scott Adams added that rural voters "are not forgetting" the redistricting controversy.
"Southwest Virginia just delivered the message in person," he said.
"Virginians are done with her," added former Rep. Matt Gaetz, R-Fla.
Some observers, however, credited Spanberger with going to Galax and Carroll County despite her weak electoral support in the area.
VIRGINIA VOTERS CEMENT SWING DISTRICT REMATCH AFTER DEMS’ REDISTRICTING FAIL
"Abigail Spanberger lost [the independent city of] Galax 68 to 32 and showed up anyway," said Democratic strategist Matt Royer.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"A Republican would have tucked tail and stayed at home when it comes to events in places they lost, like Jason was yesterday. She won Virginia by 15 and still went to one place that booed her. That is the job."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Spanberger and Clinton for comment.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Trump-backed Michael Alfonso wins crowded GOP primary for his father-in-law's former Wisconsin seat
summary: Michael Alfonso, Sean Duffy's 26-year-old son-in-law, defeated a crowded field to win the Republican nomination for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District.
story: Wisconsin congressional candidate Michael Alfonso joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze key primary results shaping the upcoming midterm elections. Alfonso reacts to veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warning his party against far-left progressives like Hasan Piker. As inflation and economic worries dominate voter concerns, Alfonso explains why conservative solutions resonate with everyday Americans.

Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy, has won the Republican Party’s nomination in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.

The 26-year-old, endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated a crowded field of contenders as he seeks the same northern Wisconsin congressional seat once held by his father-in-law, who represented the district from 2011 to 2019.

"It is my Great Honor to endorse MAGA Warrior, Michael Alfonso, a young ‘STAR’ who is running to represent the incredible people of Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District," Trump wrote on Truth Social on the eve of Tuesday’s Election Day.

"As your next Congressman, Michael will work tirelessly to Grow our Economy, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Champion our Amazing Farmers and Ranchers, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE, Keep our Border SECURE, Stop Migrant Crime, Support our Military/Veterans, Safeguard our Elections, and Protect our always under siege Second Amendment," Trump added.
DEMOCRAT ESTABLISHMENT STRIKES BACK AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATE DOWNED IN BATTLEGROUND PRIMARY

First lady Melania Trump, Michael Alfonso, President Donald Trump and Evita Duffy-Alfonso are seen in this photo. On Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, Alfonso won the Republican nomination in the race for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District. (Alfonso for Wisconsin)
The seat is currently held by Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., who on Tuesday won the Republican nomination in the Wisconsin governor’s race.
Tiffany was first elected to the seat in a May 2020 special election after Duffy resigned due to one of his children's health issues.

District 7 has been under control of Republicans for 15 years, and it is deemed a solid Republican by Cook Political Report. Trump carried the district with about 60% of the vote during the 2024 presidential election.
NEW MIDTERM BATLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES
Michael Alfonso, a candidate for U.S. House in Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, speaks during a campaign event Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in New Richmond, Wis. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)
Alfonso will face off against Fred Clark in November, who won Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.
Clark, a former Wisconsin state assemblyman, said on his website that he believes northern Wisconsin has the "makings of a new rural majority."

Michael Alfonso, Republican U.S. congressional candidate for Wisconsin, attends a roundtable with President Donald Trump at Custer Farms Inc. in Chippewa Falls, Wis., on Friday, June 5, 2026. (Steven Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"That’s a majority not based on old right wing and left wing politics, but a majority made up of real people who live and work in our communities," Clark’s website said. "Fred Clark will become part of a new majority of leaders in Congress who will stand up, represent their communities, and do the work we expect from our elected representatives."
Fox News Digital’s Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

title: Fired Texas judge speaks out as dirty water firestorm engulfs town
summary: Jennifer Combs' Facebook post about Trinidad water led to her felony arrest, a fired judge, and a Texas Rangers investigation now rocking the city.
story: Former Trinidad, Texas, Municipal Judge Shellena Bivens explains why she was dismissed from her position on ‘The CyberGuy Report’ Podcast.

When we first introduced you to Jennifer Combs, the facts already sounded hard to believe. The Texas mom said police arrested her after she used Facebook to collect complaints about discolored water in Trinidad.

Combs spent 23 hours in jail on a felony false alarm or report charge. A Henderson County grand jury later declined to indict her. She has since filed a federal lawsuit alleging political retaliation. You can read our original article on Jennifer Combs and the Trinidad, Texas, water controversy.

Her arrest, however, did not end the controversy. Police later arrested a man who protested outside Trinidad City Hall. The judge who dismissed his charge says city officials fired her one week later.
TEXAS MOM JAILED OVER DIRTY WATER FACEBOOK POST

Police escort a Texas mother from her home after a Facebook post about Trinidad’s discolored water led to a felony arrest. (Jennifer Combs)
Judge Bivens describes what happened inside her courtroom

Former Trinidad Municipal Judge Shellena Bivens joined me on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast at CyberGuy.com to explain why she dismissed the protest case and what happened after that decision. Bivens had served as a judge for 16 years. She described herself in a way that was direct and deeply personal.
"I've been a damn good judge," Bivens said. "I've tried to be human."

The case involved Winston Noles, a citizen journalist known online as Otto the Watchdog. He went to Trinidad after learning about Combs' arrest. Noles stood outside city hall with a sign that used an expletive to criticize "bad cops." Trinidad police arrested him and charged him with misdemeanor disorderly conduct. The department's case centered on a claim that his sign had offended the city's water clerk. Bivens said the evidence presented to her did not support that charge.
Judge Bivens says she repeatedly told police to release him
Bivens recalled an officer entering her courtroom and presenting two possible outcomes. Police could take Noles to jail or bring him before her for arraignment. Her response was clear.
"You need to let him go," Bivens said. "I said that multiple times. You need to let him go."

Bivens dismissed the disorderly conduct charge. She said Noles had not committed a crime by displaying the sign. Local reporting also found that the former water clerk, Colby Reyes, said in writing that Noles had not offended her. Reyes later joined another former city employee in a wrongful termination lawsuit against Trinidad.

The lawsuit alleges that city officials fired Reyes because she "refused to lie" about her reaction to the protest. Those allegations have not been proven in court. During our interview, Combs described the situation.
"She would not sign a statement that said she was offended," Combs said. Then came the part that still seems unbelievable. "The judge dropped it. They fired the judge," Combs said.
CARIBBEAN HOT SPOT GRIPPED BY WATER CRISIS, AND TOURISTS SCRAMBLE TO RESCHEDULE PLANS
Former Trinidad Municipal Judge Shellena Bivens was fired after a decision about a local police officer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Trinidad City Council voted to dismiss Bivens

The Trinidad City Council voted 3-1 to dismiss Bivens during a May 28 meeting. Her attorney argued that the council's action was unlawful. The city proceeded with the dismissal. Bivens told me she returned to work and discovered she could no longer enter her office.
"They changed my code when I came in to work on Tuesday," she said. "My security code was changed."

She said city leaders ended her 16-year judicial career without giving her a valid reason. When I asked whether she expected a Facebook post about water to cause this much upheaval, she answered quickly.
"Absolutely not. No," Bivens said. "This has been such a crazy journey."

Bivens has said publicly that she believes the city retaliated against her because she dismissed Noles' charge. Her attorneys have considered legal action. The city has not admitted that retaliation motivated its vote.
CyberGuy sent a request for comment to the mayor and city council through the city’s published contact information but did not hear back before our deadline.
Bivens makes an allegation about the former police chief

During our interview, Bivens also described an alleged conversation with Charles Gregory, who served as Trinidad's police chief when police arrested Combs. According to Bivens, Gregory entered her office after Combs published her Facebook post.
"I know who it is, and I'm, I'm F---ing getting her. I'm getting her," Bivens recalled him saying.

That is Bivens' account of the conversation. CyberGuy has not independently verified that Gregory made the statement. Gregory previously defended the department's decision to pursue Combs. He said her Facebook post created "fear, panic, or unnecessary emergency response within a community." He later resigned, with June 19 reported as his final day.
We reached out to the Trinidad Police Department for comment about Bivens' allegations and the department's handling of the arrests. We did not hear back before our deadline.
In our earlier CyberGuy report, an attorney representing Trinidad said the city could not discuss details because of active lawsuits.
"The claims against the City of Trinidad will be answered where they belong, in a court of law," attorney Zachary Smith wrote.
A former Trinidad municipal judge discusses why she dismissed a protester’s disorderly conduct charge and what happened afterward. (GFA Law/YouTube)
Another judge questioned the information police provided

The warrant process later faced scrutiny from another judge. Henderson County District Judge R. Scott McKee approved the warrant connected to Combs' arrest. He later sent Gregory a letter questioning information that two Trinidad officers had presented. McKee questioned the "accuracy, completeness, and reliability" of the officers' information. According to the letter, the officers failed to disclose citizen complaints and water-quality concerns. They also left out information that could explain the basis for Combs' Facebook post.

McKee ordered the two officers to appear before him in person when seeking future warrants. They had previously been allowed to submit requests electronically. That development is important. A judge can only evaluate probable cause using the information police provide. Missing context may change how a judge views the entire case.
State investigators documented Trinidad water violations

State investigators confirmed that Trinidad's water system had real problems. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality released findings from two investigations on July 1. The first investigation found that Trinidad's system failed to meet state minimums involving total chlorine and iron. The report said the system had returned to compliance by April 22 after a boil water notice.

A second investigation began May 15. It resulted in four violations. Investigators documented problems with required chloramine-effectiveness sampling. They also found maintenance issues at the surface water treatment plant. In one sample, investigators recorded 20 color units. The EPA and TCEQ recommend a maximum of 15 color units. These findings do not confirm every medical claim posted online. However, they show that residents were raising concerns about a system with documented deficiencies.
Family says teenager suffered burns after showering

Combs and Bivens also discussed a Trinidad family that said its 16-year-old daughter developed a serious skin reaction after showering. Medical records obtained by a local TV station described the condition as "most likely chemical burn/severe dermatitis from water she was exposed to." However, the report also stated that it remained unclear whether Trinidad's water treatment process caused the reaction. The family was considering legal action at the time of the report.
Bivens told me she knew the family and had seen photographs of the teenager's injuries.

]"I've seen the pictures," Bivens said. "I know the family of the young girl that got burned." The family's allegation and the medical assessment deserve attention. Still, a final legal or regulatory determination about the cause has not been made.
Texas Rangers investigate Trinidad as City Hall staff resigns
On July 10, the Texas Rangers confirmed they had opened an investigation involving Trinidad.
"We can confirm the Texas Rangers are investigating," the agency told Dallas affiliate FOX 4. Because the investigation remains active, the Rangers did not disclose its scope.

Then, on July 16, all three members of Trinidad's city hall staff resigned. The departing officials were City Manager Cynthia Dosier, City Clerk Sandra Rojas and Municipal Judge Susan Carver. Carver had taken over the municipal judge position after Bivens' dismissal. Mayor Dennis Haws warned that the resignations would create operational problems while the city worked through the transition. The resignations do not prove wrongdoing. They do show how far this controversy has spread since Combs published her original Facebook post.
Facebook's role in the Trinidad water fight
Combs says people associated with a small group in Trinidad mass reported her Facebook post. The platform then removed it. During our interview, Bivens directed a message at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.
"Stop trampling on people's rights," Bivens said. "Stop trampling on free speech."
We reached out to Meta for comment on Bivens' message, but did not hear back before our deadline.

Facebook's content-moderation system did not arrest Combs. Still, removing a post can erase evidence of what someone said and how other people responded. That is why screenshots matter. Save the original post and relevant comments when documenting a public concern. Keep copies of notices or messages you receive from officials.

You should also separate confirmed facts from reports that still need verification. Phrases such as "residents reported" or "we are asking the state to investigate" make that distinction clear. For more ways to control what social platforms collect and preserve your account security, see our five simple tech tips to take back control of social media.
Kurt's key takeaways

Jennifer Combs says she used Facebook to gather water complaints from people who felt ignored. Police responded with a felony charge, yet a grand jury declined to indict her. Winston Noles then protested her treatment. Judge Shellena Bivens dismissed his disorderly conduct charge because she said the evidence did not support it. Trinidad's City Council fired her one week later.

Since then, another judge has questioned the police warrant process. State investigators have documented water-system violations. The Texas Rangers are also investigating, although they have not revealed the scope. Public officials have every right to correct false information. They also have a duty to respect lawful criticism. Arresting people who question local government creates a chilling effect that can reach far beyond one small town. For more on how this controversy unfolded, check out the full conversation with Judge Bivens on The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com.

When a Facebook post about dirty water can lead to two arrests, a fired judge and a Texas Rangers investigation, how safe would you feel speaking up in your own community? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake rental listing scams can cost you thousands
summary: FBI real estate fraud complaints jumped from 9,359 in 2024 to 12,368 in 2025 as fake rental listing scams grow more convincing with stolen photos.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You find a charming rental in the right neighborhood. The price sits slightly below other homes nearby. Better yet, it becomes available right when your current lease ends. Then the pressure begins. Consider a Southern California renter who recently found a two-bedroom bungalow near family. The supposed landlord said she could not tour it because the current occupants had not moved out. Instead, he sent her a professional video of the home.

The video looked convincing because it was real. However, the scammer had copied it from an earlier property listing. After collecting an application fee, the fake landlord requested a deposit through Zelle. A phone conversation helped ease the renter's concerns. He also promised receipts and said the deposit was refundable.

She sent more than $2,500. When she asked for the money back, the calls stopped and the messages went unanswered. The actual homeowner still lived in the house and had never offered it for rent. That experience shows how quickly fake rental listing scams can turn a hopeful move into a financial crisis.
