WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Scammers often copy real property photos and repost them with fake contact information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Fake rental listing scams are spreading online

Rental scams have been around for years. However, criminals now have more places to reach people who need housing quickly. Fake listings can appear on established real estate websites. They also circulate through Facebook, TikTok and other social platforms with less oversight. That wider reach gives scammers access to renters who feel worn down by rising prices and fierce competition. When an affordable home appears, people may worry that taking an extra day to investigate will cost them the opportunity. Criminals count on that reaction.

The FBI received 12,368 real estate fraud complaints in 2025. That was up from 9,359 complaints in 2024. Reported losses climbed from about $174 million to more than $275 million. The FBI category covers more than fake rental advertisements. Still, the jump shows how much money people are losing through property-related fraud.

CyberGuy has previously covered how rental scams work and what renters should watch for. Today's fake listings can look even more convincing because scammers have access to professional property photos, video tours and AI tools.
How scammers create convincing rental ads

Many scammers do not need to invent a property. Instead, they steal an existing listing. They copy the photos and property description. They may also download a real estate agent's video tour. Then they replace the contact details and post the home on another website or social platform. When you respond, every message goes directly to the scammer.

The Federal Trade Commission says criminals may collect application fees or deposits from several people before anyone discovers the property was never available. They may also use rental applications to steal sensitive information such as a Social Security number or driver's license image. Artificial intelligence can make the operation look more polished. A scammer can use it to improve awkward messages or create professional-looking documents. However, many scams still rely on copied photos and a believable excuse. The FBI recorded 115 real estate fraud complaints that referenced AI during 2025. Those complaints reported nearly $2.7 million in losses. That does not mean AI powered most rental fraud. However, it shows that the technology has become part of some real estate schemes.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
A polished video tour may come from an old listing and does not prove the sender can rent the home. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why fake rental listings fool smart people

Rental scammers understand timing. You might need to move before school starts. Your lease may expire soon. Perhaps you found a home closer to work or family. When the market feels competitive, waiting can seem like losing your chance. Scammers use that pressure to keep you moving forward.

First, they explain why you cannot tour the property. Then they provide a video that appears to answer your concerns. If you question the payment recipient, they may claim that the person handles applications. Each answer sounds possible on its own. A phone call can also create false confidence. Hearing a real voice proves that a person exists. It does not prove that the person owns the home. Likewise, a video proves that somebody filmed the property. It does not prove that your contact can rent it to you. The FTC warns that even a virtual tour cannot guarantee that a home is available.
Warning signs of a fake rental listing

Watch closely when the rent falls far below similar homes nearby. A small discount may seem reasonable. A bargain combined with immediate pressure deserves more scrutiny. You should also pause if the landlord refuses an in-person tour. Scammers often blame current tenants or an unexpected trip. They may tell you to drive past the home instead.

Another warning appears when a listing vanishes but the supposed landlord continues contacting you privately. A scammer may claim the ad attracted too many applicants. In reality, the platform may have removed it. Be cautious when the payment recipient has a different name. Claims involving an assistant or secretary require independent verification. Finally, walk away when someone demands money before you confirm who owns or manages the home. A professional video and friendly conversation do not replace that step.
Verify the landlord, tour the property and review the lease before sending a deposit or accepting the keys. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to avoid fake rental listing scams
A little extra checking can protect your moving budget and your identity.

Search the full address using more than one search engine. Look for older sales pages and active rental advertisements. Compare the photos, monthly rent and contact details. If another agent or property management company appears, contact it directly. Use the number on the company's official website rather than one supplied by the person texting you. Also, search the owner's or property manager's name with terms such as "scam," "complaint" or "review." The FTC recommends this step when checking a rental.

Use Google Lens or another reverse-image tool to see where the property photos appeared before. You may discover that the home recently sold or that the images belong to an unrelated listing. CyberGuy's guide explains how to reverse-search an image on your phone. Still, finding only one version of a photo does not guarantee the advertisement is legitimate. The original page may no longer be online.

Visit the home and step inside before sending an application fee or deposit. When you cannot go yourself, ask a trusted friend to attend the showing. A live video call can provide more confidence than a prerecorded tour, but you should still verify the person conducting it. The FTC advises renters to keep looking when a landlord insists on collecting money before showing the property.

Check the county assessor's property records for the owner's name. Keep in mind that these records may not reflect a very recent sale. Then ask the landlord for identification and documentation showing that the person can rent the property. For an apartment building, call the leasing office directly. Do not use a phone number from an unexpected text or social media message.

A scammer may use the name and photo of a real estate agent. Search for that agent's official brokerage page. Then call the office number shown there and ask about the rental. Do not rely on a profile or phone number supplied within the advertisement.

Payment apps make sending money easy. Unfortunately, an authorized payment can be difficult to reverse. Before using Zelle, confirm that the recipient is someone you know and trust. Learn more about the warning signs in CyberGuy's guide on how to avoid getting scammed on Zelle. Also, avoid anyone who demands gift cards, cryptocurrency or a wire transfer. Those methods give scammers a better chance of disappearing with your money. When a legitimate rental company accepts credit cards, that option may offer stronger dispute protections than a peer-to-peer payment.

Do not send your Social Security number or driver's license until you verify the property and landlord. Be cautious when someone directs you to a credit-check website through a texted link. The page could collect your personal information or payment card details. Instead, ask which screening company handles the application. Then find that company's official website yourself.

A polished profile does not prove someone is a legitimate landlord. Look at when the account was created. Review its earlier posts and check whether real people interact with it. You should also watch for copied profile pictures or an account that suddenly changed names. CyberGuy's guide to protecting yourself from social media scammers includes more ways to evaluate suspicious accounts.

Scammers want you to believe this rental is your only chance. It isn’t. Walking away from an affordable home can feel frustrating, especially after weeks of searching. However, losing thousands of dollars could leave you unable to secure the next legitimate rental.
If you sent money to a fake landlord, act quickly to protect your finances and improve your chance of recovery.

Contact your bank and payment service immediately.Report the transaction as fraud and ask whether it can be stopped or recalled. Recovery isn’t guaranteed, but acting quickly gives you the best chance.Next, save every piece of evidence. Take screenshots of the listing, messages and social media profiles. Keep payment receipts, email addresses and phone numbers.Then report the advertisement to the website or platform where you found it. Contact local law enforcement and file a complaint online with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. Be sure to include the listing, messages, email addresses, phone numbers and payment details connected to the scam.The FBI encourages people to report online scams even when they are unsure whether the crime qualifies. Reports can help investigators connect victims to a larger operation.You should also submit a report to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you cannot file online, call the FTC's Consumer Response Center at 1-877-382-4357.If you shared your Social Security number or other sensitive data, create a recovery plan at IdentityTheft.gov. Review your financial accounts and consider placing a freeze with all three credit bureaus. CyberGuy's step-by-step guide shows how to freeze your credit and clean up exposed personal data at Cyberguy.com.Change any password that you entered into a website linked to the scam. If you reused it elsewhere, update those accounts as well. A password manager can create and store a different strong password for each account.
Contact your bank and payment service immediately.
Report the transaction as fraud and ask whether it can be stopped or recalled. Recovery isn’t guaranteed, but acting quickly gives you the best chance.
Next, save every piece of evidence. Take screenshots of the listing, messages and social media profiles. Keep payment receipts, email addresses and phone numbers.

Then report the advertisement to the website or platform where you found it. Contact local law enforcement and file a complaint online with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. Be sure to include the listing, messages, email addresses, phone numbers and payment details connected to the scam.
The FBI encourages people to report online scams even when they are unsure whether the crime qualifies. Reports can help investigators connect victims to a larger operation.
You should also submit a report to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you cannot file online, call the FTC's Consumer Response Center at 1-877-382-4357.

If you shared your Social Security number or other sensitive data, create a recovery plan at IdentityTheft.gov. Review your financial accounts and consider placing a freeze with all three credit bureaus. CyberGuy's step-by-step guide shows how to freeze your credit and clean up exposed personal data at Cyberguy.com.

Change any password that you entered into a website linked to the scam. If you reused it elsewhere, update those accounts as well. A password manager can create and store a different strong password for each account.
Kurt's key takeaways

Fake rental listing scams succeed because criminals borrow real property advertisements and add a story that explains why you cannot tour. The strongest defense is verification. Confirm who owns or manages the home before you complete an application or send money. Also, do not let a deadline silence your instincts. A caller can sound friendly while using stolen photos and a fake lease. When something feels wrong, pause and check the address through an independent source. That brief delay could protect your savings and your identity.

title: Shared VPN vs dedicated IP: Which one is right for you?
summary: Shared VPN IPs blend your activity with thousands of users for maximum privacy, while dedicated IPs reduce captcha requests and login issues.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

If you've started shopping for a VPN, you've probably come across the terms shared IP and dedicated IP. While they may sound technical, the difference is actually pretty straightforward, and choosing the right one can make your online experience smoother.

Both options encrypt your internet traffic and protect your connection, but they serve different purposes. One prioritizes maximum privacy by blending your activity with thousands of other users. The other gives you your own personal IP address, making it easier to access certain online services without additional verification.
Here's what each option does, and how to decide which one is right for you.

IS ID.ME SAFE TO USE? WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
Shared and dedicated VPN IP addresses both encrypt internet traffic, but they offer different advantages for privacy, convenience and online logins. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What is a shared VPN IP?

A shared IP is exactly what it sounds like: multiple VPN users connect through the same public IP address. When dozens, or even hundreds, of people are using the same IP at different times, it becomes much harder for websites or other observers to associate online activity with any one individual. That's one reason shared IPs are the default choice for most VPN services.

The trade-off is that shared IPs can sometimes trigger CAPTCHAs, blocked logins or extra verification if a website sees too much activity coming from the same address. That is one reason some people look for ways to fix a VPN that keeps getting blocked.
What is a dedicated VPN IP?

A dedicated IP is reserved exclusively for you. No one else using the VPN service shares that IP address. Because your IP remains consistent every time you connect, websites and online services recognize it as the same connection. That can make certain activities more convenient, especially if you regularly access accounts that use IP-based security checks.
For example, some businesses only allow employees to log in from approved IP addresses. Using a dedicated IP allows your company to "whitelist" this IP so that you can log in smoothly every time.

A dedicated IP can also reduce the number of verification requests you receive when signing in to banking websites, business software, or other accounts that flag unfamiliar locations. If you've ever been annoyed by a CAPTCHA (e.g., "which one of these photos is of a motorcycle?") when trying to log in from a new location, you'll appreciate the consistency of a dedicated IP address.

Some people might argue that letting your VPN provider assign you a dedicated IP inherently makes you less private. This is where your choice of VPN provider is important. A reputable VPN provider distributes IP addresses with a zero-knowledge allocation system, meaning not even the provider can trace it back to you.
With this kind of dedicated IP, you still receive the privacy and encryption benefits of a VPN; the difference is simply that your VPN IP belongs only to you.
INHERITANCE SCAM EMAIL LOOKS REAL BUT STEALS YOUR DATA
Shared VPN IP addresses mix traffic from many users, while dedicated IP addresses stay assigned to one VPN customer. (Akos Stiller/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Shared VPN vs. dedicated IP: Which one should you choose?

The answer depends on how you use the internet. A shared IP is usually the better option if your main goals are privacy, anonymous browsing, and protecting your data while traveling or using public Wi-Fi. Since many people are using the same address, your online activity is more difficult to distinguish from everyone else's.

A dedicated IP makes sense if convenience is your priority. If you frequently work remotely, access company resources with IP restrictions, manage servers remotely, or want fewer login challenges from websites that recognize your connection, having your own VPN IP can save time. Neither option is inherently more secure than the other. Both encrypt your internet traffic and hide your original IP address from the websites you visit. The main difference is whether you want to share your VPN identity with other users or have one reserved just for yourself.

A shared VPN IP can provide greater anonymity, while a dedicated IP gives one user a consistent address for websites and online services. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Choose a VPN built for speed and security
For this kind of VPN setup, look for strong privacy protections, fast speeds and the option to add a dedicated IP if your needs change.

A strong VPN should use modern encryption, follow a verified no-logs policy and include a kill switch that blocks internet traffic if the VPN connection drops. It should also work across iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac and compatible routers.

Look for a provider with servers in many countries, support for streaming and secure browsing, multiple simultaneous device connections and responsive customer support. A money-back guarantee can also give you time to test its speed, reliability and ease of use before committing.
For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt’s key takeaways

Both shared and dedicated VPN IP addresses offer the core benefits people expect from a VPN: encrypted internet traffic, improved online privacy, and protection on public networks. The right choice comes down to how you use the internet. For most people, a shared IP provides the best balance of privacy and simplicity. If you need a consistent online identity for work, secure logins, or specialized services, a dedicated IP may be worth considering. Whichever option you choose, using a trusted VPN helps keep your internet activity more private and your connections more secure across your computers, smartphones, tablets, smart TVs, and other devices.

title: Cleveland Clinic launches prescription drone delivery
summary: Cleveland Clinic launched prescription drone delivery with Zipline near Beachwood, Ohio, covering eligible patients within five miles of its campus.
story: A medical drone takes off during testing as part of a program aimed at speeding up the delivery of critical healthcare supplies. The effort is focused on transporting lab samples, blood and donor matching materials between smaller communities and larger hospital hubs, where timing can impact diagnoses and treatment. Developers say faster, on-demand flights could help reduce delays for rural patients, who often face longer travel times for care, with future plans to expand the technology to carry transplant-related materials.

A trip to the pharmacy can feel like a routine errand on a normal day. When you feel sick or care for someone else, that same trip can become a serious burden. Now, some Cleveland Clinic patients can skip the drive and have eligible prescriptions lowered into their yards by drone.
Cleveland Clinic just announced the launch of its prescription drone delivery program with Zipline. The first successful deliveries took place in and around Beachwood, Ohio.

Cleveland Clinic describes the launch as the first long-term deployment of a prescription drug drone delivery program by a U.S. health system. While other hospitals have tested medical drone services, this program is designed for ongoing delivery to patients' homes.

DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Zipline drones can deliver eligible Cleveland Clinic prescriptions within minutes while remaining hundreds of feet above patients’ homes. (Zipline)
Cleveland Clinic drone delivery starts in and around Beachwood

The service currently covers eligible addresses within five miles of Cleveland Clinic's Beachwood Administrative Campus. That location serves as the home base for Zipline's electric drones. Initially, Cleveland Clinic is offering the service to certain patients who already use its pharmacy home delivery program. The pharmacy team will notify eligible patients through their electronic patient portal.

Patients do not have to use a drone. The delivery option is voluntary, and Cleveland Clinic says it will not charge an additional fee. According to Zipline, the program initially covers shelf-stable prescriptions. Controlled substances will not travel by drone at this time.
How prescriptions arrive by Zipline drone

The process begins inside a Cleveland Clinic pharmacy. A pharmacy technician places the packaged medication into a secure Zipline drop box. Next, an autonomous drone retrieves the order and flies to the patient's address. When the aircraft reaches its destination, it remains as high as 300 feet above the ground. A small delivery pod then descends on a tether. The pod places the prescription at the selected delivery location before rising back to the drone. The aircraft returns to its charging station after completing the delivery.

Since the drone stays in the air, it does not need to land in your yard. You also do not need to clear space for a landing pad. Once a pharmacy order enters the Zipline drop box, it can reach the patient's home within minutes. According to Zipline, its average flight time is under five minutes.

Patients can follow the delivery through a tracking link in the MyChart messaging portal. Because delivery information arrives through a health portal, be careful with unexpected texts or emails claiming to contain a tracking update. Open the official MyChart app or type the portal address into your browser instead of tapping an unplanned link. CyberGuy's guide to using health apps and patient portals safely explains why going directly to the official app can help you avoid phishing attempts.
Who can use Cleveland Clinic prescription delivery

For now, eligibility remains narrow. You must live within the initial delivery zone near Beachwood. You must also participate in Cleveland Clinic's pharmacy home delivery program. Cleveland Clinic patients who are interested in participating should ask their doctor if they are eligible. The Beachwood launch gives the Cleveland Clinic and Zipline a chance to incorporate the experience during regular pharmacy operations.
REMOTE ROBOT SURGERY REMOVES CANCER 1,500 MILES AWAY
Cleveland Clinic patients near Beachwood, Ohio, can now receive eligible prescriptions by Zipline drone, with deliveries lowered by tether into their yards. (Zipline)
Patients can choose where the package lands

Eligible patients can select a delivery location on their property. According to Zipline, that location will typically be in the front yard or backyard. Patients can also schedule delivery for a time when they expect to be home. After the pod places the package on the ground, the patient can collect it without touching the drone or the delivery pod. That setup may help keep a prescription from sitting outside longer than necessary. It also gives patients more control over where the package appears on their property.
How Zipline handles privacy and flight monitoring

Zipline says it does not know what is inside a Cleveland Clinic order. The company receives only the information it needs to complete the delivery and follow healthcare requirements, including package handling or temperature instructions. The drones do not send a live video or image feed to Zipline employees. Instead, trained specialists monitor flights at the fleet level through operational dashboards. Each drone and delivery pod flies autonomously using onboard sensors. Those sensors help the system navigate the airspace and avoid obstacles near the delivery area. Cleveland Clinic and Zipline say they worked together to meet the regulatory and technical requirements for the program.
Zipline has delivered medical products since 2016

While a prescription hovering over an Ohio neighborhood may seem unusual, Zipline has spent years building autonomous medical delivery networks. The company began delivering blood and other medical products in 2016. Today, Zipline says it serves more than 5,000 hospitals and health facilities around the world. It has delivered tens of millions of medical products through its network.

CyberGuy first examined how Zipline planned to deliver medicine and food when the company revealed its Platform 2 system in 2023. That design introduced the tethered pod that can place a package in a precise location while the main aircraft stays overhead. Since then, Zipline has moved further into everyday U.S. delivery. To date, the company reported more than 2.7 million commercial deliveries. Roughly 70% of its flights now take place in the United States. Outside healthcare, Zipline carries restaurant orders and retail products. In parts of Texas, customers can receive drone deliveries from national brands and local businesses.
CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'
Cleveland Clinic says its new drone service gives some patients another way to receive shelf-stable prescriptions without making a pharmacy trip. (Zipline)
Drone delivery can continue through difficult weather

Cleveland Clinic's program arrives as drone delivery becomes more visible in the U.S. CyberGuy recently covered a drone food delivery pilot in New Jersey. That service also uses a tether to lower orders while the aircraft remains in the air. Food delivery gives companies a way to test flight paths and neighborhood acceptance. Delivering medicine raises the stakes because patients may rely on the package for their care.

According to Zipline, its drones can operate in rain, wind, storms and cold conditions that may slow road traffic. However, weather or another issue could still make a drone flight unavailable. In that situation, Cleveland Clinic would use another delivery option. Zipline says the prescription would typically travel by ground courier instead. According to Cleveland Clinic, each Zipline drone performs more than 500 safety checks per second while flying.
Cleveland Clinic plans to expand medical drone delivery

Prescription medication is the starting point. Over time, Cleveland Clinic plans to add other medications and lab samples. The program may also transport medically tailored meals and medical supplies.

Zipline has already announced its next expansion will be to Austin, Texas. Zipline's president of U.S. healthcare, Hillary Brendzel, described the immediate benefit in simple terms: "That's one less errand to run, and more time back in people's days." That may sound modest compared with the technology involved. However, saving one pharmacy trip can matter when someone feels ill or cannot easily drive. In fact, in Texas, according to Zipline, its most frequent customers are older adults and busy parents.
Kurt's key takeaways

What caught my attention here is how ordinary the problem is. People need medicine, but getting to a pharmacy can be difficult when they are already dealing with an illness or mobility problem. Cleveland Clinic and Zipline are using drone technology to remove that errand for some patients. The drone stays above the property while a tethered pod handles the final delivery. Patients can track the order through MyChart without paying an extra fee. The average flight takes under five minutes, according to Zipline. Patients can choose where the package arrives and schedule the delivery for a time when they will be home. If the drone cannot fly, Cleveland Clinic can use a ground courier instead. Zipline also says it does not know what medication is inside the package, and its drones do not provide employees with a live video feed. Those details may reassure patients who have questions about privacy. Still, the launch remains limited to a small area near Beachwood. Only shelf-stable prescriptions qualify at first, and controlled substances are excluded. If this works reliably, prescription delivery could become one of the most meaningful uses for autonomous drones.

title: 100 Kodiak driverless trucks are headed for public roads
summary: Atlas Energy Solutions plans to grow its Kodiak driverless truck fleet from 28 to 100 by mid-2027, with public highway driving in Texas and New Mexico.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson spoke with Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, about how attitudes toward autonomous trucks have shifted over time.
Atlas Energy Solutions is expanding its fleet of Kodiak-powered driverless trucks across Texas and New Mexico. The trucks already haul sand to oil and gas well sites without anyone inside the cab.

Now, Atlas and Kodiak plan to grow the fleet from 28 driverless trucks to 100 by mid-2027. They also expect the trucks to begin operating on public roads in early 2027. However, that timeline still depends on operational milestones.
The expansion gives us a clearer look at how driverless trucking could move from private industrial roads onto highways.

NEW YORK SCHOOL PAUSES HUMANOID CLASSROOM ROBOT PILOT PROGRAM

Kodiak-powered driverless trucks haul sand across the Permian Basin as Atlas Energy Solutions prepares to expand its autonomous fleet from 28 trucks to 100 by mid-2027. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kodiak driverless trucks expand to a second depot

Atlas previously operated its driverless trucks from one load-out location at a time. It now runs them simultaneously from two depots about 90 minutes apart. One site is in Texas while the other is in New Mexico. The wider footprint lets Atlas reach more well sites across the Permian Basin. It can also respond faster when customers need more sand delivered. The operation connects with Atlas' 42-mile Dune Express conveyor system. That system moves sand closer to the well sites before the trucks complete the final portion of the trip.

Don Burnette, founder and CEO of Kodiak, said the two companies have built the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks: "Together, Atlas and Kodiak have deployed the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks. We've demonstrated that autonomous trucking is delivering meaningful results today. Our expanding partnership, which now covers two unique locations, is creating a blueprint for how autonomy can transform logistics by improving efficiency, increasing productivity, and delivering lasting value for customers at commercial scale."
The driverless fleet is growing from 28 trucks to 100

As of March 31, 2026, Atlas's driverless program operated 28 driverless trucks across 15 routes. Those trucks had carried about 7,000 loads and hauled more than 450,000 tons of sand. The fleet also logged more than 23,500 driverless operating hours during the first quarter of 2026. On July 20, Kodiak-powered trucks delivered 176 loads in one day. The companies called it a daily record for the 18-month deployment.

Earlier in 2026, Kodiak and Atlas also introduced a driverless truck that can pull three connected trailers. The combined loaded weight tops 135 tons. That kind of load would grab anyone's attention. It also raises an obvious question. What happens when these trucks leave private roads and begin driving beside the rest of us?
Public highway driving could begin in 2027

Kodiak plans to launch driverless highway operations by the end of 2026. Atlas expects its Kodiak-equipped fleet to follow onto public highways in 2027. The company is not alone in moving toward humanless highway freight. A separate autonomous truck recently completed a 230-mile commercial delivery in Texas with nobody in the cab.

Burnette told CyberGuy that other motorists should not expect unusual behavior from Kodiak-powered trucks: "Kodiak-powered trucks already operate autonomously on highways across the southern United States with a safety driver in the cab to oversee the system.The Kodiak Driver is engineered to be a safe and cautious driver and to follow normal driving etiquette, so other motorists should not notice anything unusual."

That may sound reassuring. Still, most drivers will want more than a smooth lane change before they feel comfortable beside a truck with no human behind the wheel. CyberGuy recently took a closer look at whether autonomous trucks can make highways safer, including Kodiak's arguments about fatigue, distracted driving and real-world testing.
How driverless trucks handle extreme weather

The Permian Basin can be brutal on vehicles. Trucks can face triple-digit temperatures, dust storms, sudden flooding and high crosswinds. Dense morning fog can also make visibility difficult. Kodiak equips its trucks with a sensor suite built around cameras, with radar and lidar support. These systems give the truck a detailed view of the surrounding environment.

However, more sensors cannot make every condition safe. Burnette said the truck will stop instead of pushing through dangerous weather: "And if conditions aren't safe, the truck won't keep driving. It slows down and safely pulls over." Kodiak says its system responds to construction zones and emergency vehicles as part of normal driving. It also adjusts to changing road conditions. Severe fog or other hazardous weather can still stop an autonomous trip. According to Burnette, Kodiak-powered vehicles will remain parked when conditions become unsafe.
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

Atlas Energy Solutions is expanding its fleet of driverless big rigs across Texas and New Mexico, with public highway operations expected to begin in 2027. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What happens when a driverless truck has a problem

A damaged component or communications failure can create a serious problem in any large truck. The stakes may feel even higher when nobody is sitting in the cab. Burnette said the Kodiak Driver checks both the truck and its autonomous system while it operates: "The Kodiak Driver continuously monitors the truck and its autonomous driving system. If it detects a critical problem, such as a mechanical, sensor or communications failure, it can execute a fallback maneuver that safely pulls the truck out of traffic and brings it to a stop in a safe location."
According to Burnette, "The health and safety of all trucks are overseen by Kodiak's command center, and a human can remotely provide assistance should a truck need additional help."
Kodiak points to an independent safety score

Kodiak also cites a safety evaluation from Nauto, an AI-powered fleet safety company. The Kodiak Driver earned a VERA safety score of 98 out of 100. That result tied for the highest score among more than 1,000 commercial fleets in Nauto's network. The other fleets used human drivers. The system earned a perfect score for inattentive driving and high-risk driving. It also earned 100 for traffic violations. Its aggressive driving score was 95. You can read CyberGuy's full breakdown of the Kodiak Driver's independent safety score. Burnette pointed to the evaluation in his response: "We are proud that an independent evaluation by Nauto, a leader in AI-powered fleet safety technology, gave Kodiak the highest score in a safety study, tying for first place and outperforming 1,000 human-driven fleets."
How Kodiak protects driverless trucks from hackers

Driverless trucks create another concern that has nothing to do with rain or road debris. A connected vehicle can become a cybersecurity target. Kodiak does not publicly detail every safeguard. Publishing a complete security blueprint could help attackers. Burnette said Kodiak treats cybersecurity as part of its safety work: "Cybersecurity is something we take extremely seriously because safety starts long before a truck ever reaches the road."

He said Kodiak uses multiple security layers and continuously watches for suspicious activity. The company also tightly limits access to its systems. "We build multiple layers of security into our vehicles and systems to help protect against unauthorized access, and we continuously monitor for unusual activity. For security reasons, we don't discuss the specific safeguards we use or how they're implemented. But access to the systems is tightly controlled and if it detects something unusual, it will bring itself to a safe stop rather than continuing to operate." Kodiak's public technology materials say the company isolates safety-critical functions from external communication ports. It also says it protects vehicle infrastructure with end-to-end encryption.
What this means to you

You probably will not wake up tomorrow and find every delivery truck driving itself. Early public deployments will likely focus on routes where operators already understand the conditions. Still, the Atlas expansion shows that fully driverless trucking has entered commercial service. These trucks are already working without a person in the cab.

The next major step will bring them onto roads used by commuters and families. Other truck drivers will also begin sharing lanes with autonomous rigs. For you, the biggest issue is how the system responds when normal driving suddenly becomes abnormal. Dangerous weather can change a trip in seconds. So can equipment failures, cyberattacks or unpredictable motorists.

Kodiak says its system will reduce speed and move toward a safe stop when conditions become unsafe. Human teams will also monitor the fleet through a command center. The technology could eventually affect deliveries and transportation costs. It may also change trucking jobs, an issue CyberGuy explored in a closer look at whether autonomous trucks could replace drivers by 2027.

As these vehicles reach public highways, transparency will become even more important. Drivers deserve clear information about crash reporting and emergency response. They also need to understand the limits of remote assistance. Regulators will need to test company safety claims against real-world results. A strong safety score provides a starting point, but public trust will depend on consistent performance over time.
OUR ENEMIES FOUND A WEAKNESS IN ESSENTIAL TECHNOLOGY. WE MUST FIX IT … FAST

Kodiak-powered trucks already move heavy loads without anyone in the cab, logging more than 23,500 driverless operating hours in the first quarter of 2026. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Kodiak and Atlas are rapidly expanding a commercial driverless truck operation that already moves heavy loads without anyone in the cab. The plan to grow from 28 trucks to 100 by mid-2027 shows how quickly autonomous trucking can scale inside a demanding industrial environment. Public highway use will bring a new level of scrutiny. Drivers will want answers about severe weather, system failures, public-road emergencies and cybersecurity. Kodiak says its trucks can stop when something goes wrong. Human teams also remain available through a command center. However, the technology must prove that those protections work reliably as more trucks enter service. The expansion could reshape how companies transport essential materials. Yet public trust will depend on what happens when these trucks encounter the unpredictable moments every driver knows too well.

title: Brinks Home data breach puts 1M customers on alert
summary: Brinks Home confirmed unauthorized access to its IT systems, and the ShinyHunters group claims it stole 4.9 million Salesforce records from it.
story: Cybersecurity expert Theresa Payton breaks down age verification, AI tools and how to protect kids online without collecting biometric or personal data that can be hacked.

You hire a home security company to help protect your house. So, hearing that hackers broke into the company's own computer systems may feel especially unsettling. Brinks Home has confirmed that an unauthorized party accessed part of its IT environment. The Dallas-based company says its alarm monitoring and security systems continue to work normally.

However, the intruder has threatened to release information it claims to have stolen. The Brinks Home data breach could affect a wide audience. Brinks Home says it serves residential customers in all 50 states. It also says it protects more than 1 million people across North America. For now, customers face a frustrating gap. Brinks Home has not confirmed exactly what information was accessed or who may be affected.

COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?

Brinks Home confirmed an unauthorized party accessed part of its IT environment, though the company says its alarm monitoring and security systems continue to operate normally. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What Brinks Home confirmed about the cyberattack

Brinks Home discovered unauthorized access to part of its systems on July 20, 2026. The company activated its incident response procedures and moved to contain the intrusion. It also brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. William Niles, CEO of Brinks Home, said the company was working with leading forensic experts to address the incident.

CyberGuy reached out to Brinks Home for additional comment. The company confirmed that its response began as soon as it detected the intrusion. "Brinks Home recently identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party gained access to certain company systems. Upon discovering the incident, we immediately activated our incident response plan, contained the activity, and engaged an industry-leading cybersecurity forensics firm to investigate," Brinks Home told CyberGuy.

The company's most reassuring update involves its security services. Brinks Home says the incident did not involve its products or monitoring services based on what it knows so far. Your security panel and sensors should continue working. Emergency monitoring should also remain available without interruption. However, the investigation has not determined the full scope of the incident.

Brinks Home stressed that its investigation remains in the early stages. "Our investigation is early and ongoing. Our systems are secure, and we are continuing to assess the full scope and potential impact of the incident while closely monitoring our environment," the company said. "If we determine that your information was affected, we will notify you and explain what steps, if any, you should take," the company says in its cybersecurity FAQ.
Hackers claim they stole 4.9 million Brinks Home records

The ShinyHunters extortion group has claimed responsibility for the attack. The gang alleges that it stole more than 4.9 million records from Brinks Home's Salesforce environment. That number refers to database records. It does not mean 4.9 million separate people were affected. One customer may appear in several records.

According to ShinyHunters, the stolen information includes more than 1.1 million rows from a Salesforce customer contacts database. The hackers also claim they obtained more than 4,000 employee records. Those records allegedly contain names, email addresses, job titles and phone numbers. In addition, the group claims it stole around 3.8 million customer support chat logs from the Brinks Care Cresta platform. Those claims have not been independently verified.

BleepingComputer says it has not reviewed the allegedly stolen data. The publication could not confirm the hackers' figures or descriptions. Brinks Home has not confirmed that those specific records were taken. It also has not confirmed that personal information was compromised. That distinction is important. Criminal groups often mix real information with inflated claims to increase pressure on a company. The FBI has warned that ShinyHunters uses real or exaggerated claims while demanding payment. The gang may also use threatening messages or harassing phone calls.
A voice phishing call may have opened the door

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer that it entered Brinks Home's systems on July 13. The group claims it used a Microsoft Entra voice phishing attack. This type of attack is also called vishing. During a vishing attack, a criminal calls an employee while pretending to work for the company's technology department.

The caller may say the employee needs to complete an account update. The criminal then guides the employee through an authentication or device registration process. If the employee approves the request, the hacker may gain access to the account and its connected business tools. Brinks Home has not confirmed this version of events. Its FAQ says the company is still investigating the incident.

Still, the allegation highlights a growing problem. A hacker may not need to crack a password when an employee can be persuaded to approve access. Voice phishing has helped criminals break into other corporate cloud accounts. That makes unexpected login requests especially dangerous.
Why stolen customer support chats could fuel convincing scams

A customer support chat may sound less sensitive than a password. However, those conversations can contain useful personal details. You may have discussed an installation date or a billing problem. Perhaps you mentioned the equipment installed in your house. A chat could also reveal your contact details, previous service issues or the names of authorized account users. Criminals can use those details to make a scam feel familiar.

For example, a caller might know that you recently contacted Brinks Home. The person could mention your equipment before claiming that an urgent security update is required. That context may make the call sound legitimate. It can also lower your guard before the criminal asks for a password or authentication code. The FBI warns that criminals can use stolen real-world context to create highly convincing phishing campaigns. You can learn more about how exposed contact information helps criminals launch attacks in our guide to ways scammers can use your phone number.
Brinks Home warns customers about follow-up scams

Brinks Home is warning customers to stay alert for suspicious communications related to the breach. A scammer might pretend to represent Brinks Home. The person could also claim to be a cybersecurity investigator or another party involved in the response. The message may say that your data will be released unless you act immediately. It could direct you to a fake login page or ask you to confirm account credentials.

Brinks Home says it will never ask you to provide sensitive information through an unsolicited communication. That warning deserves your attention even though the company has not confirmed whose data was involved. Hackers do not need a complete customer database to start sending scams. They may use public information or previously stolen data to target people while news of the breach spreads.
Has the alleged Brinks Home data been released?

ShinyHunters threatened to release the alleged data if Brinks Home did not respond by July 30, 2026. That deadline has passed. However, as of today, Brinks Home had not publicly confirmed that customer information had been released. Its official update continued to say that the company was investigating what information may have been involved.

The absence of a confirmed leak does not prove that the hackers lack the information. At the same time, the group's claims should not be treated as established facts without evidence. Customers should focus on what they can control now. That includes securing their accounts and becoming more suspicious of unexpected requests.
Tips to stay safe after the Brinks Home data breach
These steps can help protect your accounts, devices and identity while Brinks Home continues its investigation.

Be cautious if someone contacts you about the breach and asks you to confirm personal information. A scammer may claim that your alarm will stop working. The person might also say your account needs an urgent security update. Do not use a link or phone number included in the message. Instead, open the official Brinks Home app yourself. You can also type the company's website address directly into your browser.

Do not trust a caller simply because the person knows your name or account details. Hang up and contact Brinks Home through the app or its official website. Avoid calling a number supplied by the person who contacted you. The FBI recommends verifying unusual requests through a separate communication method before responding.

A legitimate representative should not ask you to read aloud a one-time security code. That code may be the final step a criminal needs to enter your account. End the call if someone asks for one. Also, never approve an unexpected login notification. Select deny or reject when you did not initiate the request.

Change your password if you reused it on another website. You should also change it if you notice unusual account activity or receive an unfamiliar login alert. Create a long password that you have never used for another account. A password manager can create and store a different password for every login. That way, one exposed password cannot unlock several accounts. Pay close attention to your email password. Your email account may control password resets for Brinks Home and many other services.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA

Hackers linked to the ShinyHunters extortion group say they stole millions of records from Brinks Home, but the company has not verified those claims. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A data removal service can request that data brokers and people-search websites remove your personal information. This may include your home address, phone number and relatives' names. Removing those details can make it harder for scammers to combine breached records with information found elsewhere online. However, a data removal service cannot erase information already taken from Brinks Home. It also cannot guarantee that stolen data will disappear from criminal forums. Its value comes from reducing the extra information scammers can use to build a convincing profile about you. Data broker profiles can reappear, so ongoing monitoring and repeated removal requests may be necessary. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Multifactor authentication adds another check after you enter your password. An authenticator app or physical security key can offer stronger protection than a code sent through a text message. Turn on the strongest option available for your Brinks Home account. You should also protect your primary email account. Our guide to the top multifactor authentication apps explains how these tools work.

Open the Brinks Home app or customer portal and review your account information. Check your email address and phone number. Look for unfamiliar authorized users or account changes. Confirm that your emergency contacts and recovery information remain correct. If you ever shared an alarm code or verbal security password in a support chat, contact Brinks Home through an official channel. Ask whether that credential should be changed. Do not change settings through a link sent in an unexpected message.

An exposed phone number can help a criminal attempt a SIM swap or number transfer scam. Contact your wireless carrier and add an account PIN. Ask whether it offers a port-out lock or number transfer lock. These protections can make it harder for someone to transfer your phone number and intercept security codes. You should also use an authenticator app instead of text-message codes when an account offers that choice.

Install strong antivirus software on your computer and mobile devices. This protection can help detect malicious links, fake websites and suspicious downloads before they cause harm. It may also warn you when a phishing page tries to steal your password. Antivirus software cannot reverse the Brinks Home breach. However, it can provide another layer of defense against scams that follow it. Keep the antivirus software updated and allow it to run automatic scans. You should also install operating system, browser and app updates as they become available. Strong antivirus tools can block malware, dangerous websites and unsafe downloads in real time. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Brinks Home has not confirmed that Social Security numbers or financial account details were involved. Therefore, customers do not currently have evidence that they all need to replace payment cards. Still, review your bank statements and credit card activity. Watch for small charges that you do not recognize. Check your credit reports for new accounts or unfamiliar inquiries. Our guide to quiet signs of identity theft explains what can appear before larger problems surface. You may also consider an identity theft monitoring service if Brinks Home later confirms that sensitive personal information was exposed.

A credit freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new account in your name. You must place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Adding or removing a freeze is free. However, a credit freeze cannot stop misuse of an existing bank or credit card account. Brinks Home has not confirmed that customers need to freeze their credit because of this incident. That recommendation could change if the company identifies exposed identity information.

Brinks Home tells customers not to respond to a suspicious message or click its links. However, the company also says not to delete the communication right away. Take screenshots and preserve the sender's details. Save the date, time and phone number or email address involved. Then report the message using the contact information listed in the official Brinks Home incident FAQ. The company lists 469-391-4024 as a reporting number. You can also report online fraud or extortion attempts to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.

Brinks Home says it will contact affected individuals if its investigation confirms that personally identifiable information was involved. However, criminals may send fake breach notices first. Compare any notice with information posted on the official Brinks Home cybersecurity update at brinkshome.com/cybersecurity-update. Contact the company directly when something looks unusual. Do not pay anyone who threatens to release your information.

Brinks Home says it plans to provide more information once its investigation produces verified findings. "Protecting the information entrusted to Brinks Home remains a top priority, and we take our data security responsibilities very seriously. We appreciate the patience and understanding of our customers as we work through this process. We will provide additional updates as appropriate when more verified information becomes available," the company told CyberGuy.

While Brinks Home serves more than 1 million customers nationwide, its recent cybersecurity incident shows that even a company trusted to protect homes can face digital vulnerabilities, despite assurances that alarm monitoring and system functionality continue without interruption. There are many other options in the market, whether you prefer a professionally installed system or a do-it-yourself one.

For reference, you can check out my guide on the best home security systems at Cyberguy.com, where I’ve listed four of my favorite options. You might also want to find out if your home insurance offers a discount for installing robust security protection.
IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?

Brinks Home says it discovered unauthorized access to certain company systems July 20 and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

The Brinks Home cyberattack feels personal because this company may hold information connected to your household. So far, Brinks Home has confirmed unauthorized access to part of its IT environment. It has not verified the hackers' claim that they stole 4.9 million Salesforce records. The company says its alarm monitoring and security products continue to work normally. Customers do not need to disconnect their systems based on the information available now. The immediate danger may come from phishing. A criminal who knows your name or previous support issue can build a message that sounds convincing. Slow down when someone creates urgency. Contact Brinks Home through an official channel and never hand over a security code.
When a company is trusted to help protect your home, should it face a higher standard for guarding the personal information connected to it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Apple Pay text scam threatens $8,250 loss in 35 minutes
summary: Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an Apple Pay scam text claiming $8,250 was charged and a duplicate would auto-approve within 35 minutes.
story: JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an alarming text claiming Apple Pay had already charged him $8,250 and another $8,250 would go through in 35 minutes. That is the kind of message designed to make your stomach drop before you have time to think.
Paul did the smart thing. He stopped, avoided the callback number and sent the text to us. Let's break down every red flag and show you how to verify a charge without handing control to a scammer.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
A scam text falsely warns of an $8,250 Apple Pay charge and threatens another $8,250 transaction within 35 minutes to pressure recipients into calling scammers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The Apple Pay scam text Paul received

The message claimed $8,250 had already been charged through Apple Pay and warned that a duplicate $8,250 transaction would "auto-approve" in 35 minutes. It told Paul to call an 855 number, quote "Case CA-3321" and "verbally kill the pending charge." We partially masked the callback number so no one calls it accidentally.
Every red flag hiding in this Apple Pay scam text
The message looks chaotic, but nearly every phrase has a purpose. The sender uses dramatic wording, fake authority and a tight deadline to push Paul toward one action: calling the number in the text.

The message came from a number beginning with +44, the international calling code for the United Kingdom. Yet it claims to come from "Apple Pay Account Services" and tells Paul in Washington, D.C., to call a separate 855 toll-free number. A different callback number does not automatically prove fraud. However, an overseas sender directing a U.S. recipient to an unrelated support line should make you stop before calling.

The text uses the Apple Pay name several times and signs off as "Apple Pay Account Services." It also arrived as a blue iMessage with the word "Encrypted" shown beneath it. Those details can make the message feel official. However, encryption only means the message was protected while traveling between devices. It does not confirm that Apple sent it. The signature also sounds generic. It does not name Paul's bank, identify the card involved or provide an official Apple support channel.

The first line reads: "$8,250.00 APPLE PAY - 35-MINUTE DEADLINE." The message then claims $8,250 has already disappeared and warns that a duplicate $8,250 charge will be approved in 35 minutes. That raises the threatened loss to $16,500. The exact 35-minute deadline feels calculated. It gives Paul enough time to call while discouraging him from checking Wallet, opening his bank's app or asking someone else for advice.

The message says Paul's Apple Pay account has "hemorrhaged" money. It calls the situation a "catastrophic fraud event" and claims his contactless limit has been "crushed" to $0. It later tells him to "verbally kill the pending charge." Those words sound dramatic because they are meant to produce fear. A legitimate financial alert would normally use clear terms such as charged, declined, frozen or pending. It would not describe an account as hemorrhaging money or ask you to kill a charge.

The first transaction allegedly happened at: "an agricultural processing surplus in Stockton, CA." The second supposedly involved: "a payday lending chain in Modesto." Neither phrase identifies an actual merchant. They sound specific at first because they include industries and real California cities. However, they fall apart when you look closer. A legitimate transaction alert would usually show the merchant's name. It would not rely on vague descriptions such as "agricultural processing surplus."

The sender claims Paul's contactless spending limit has been "crushed to $0." In the same message, it says the second $8,250 transaction is pending and "will auto-approve in 35 minutes." Those claims do not fit together. If the sender had already blocked contactless activity, why would another contactless charge automatically go through? The contradiction matters because it shows the message was written to create panic rather than explain a real account problem.

The message says: "Do not ignore this." It then orders Paul: "You must call." The sender provides a case number, tells him to "verbally kill" the charge and warns that the money will be "gone forever" if he fails to respond. It also threatens to blacklist his account and calls this his "only warning." That language gives Paul one supposed solution: call the number in the text. The message never tells him to open Wallet, check his bank's official app or call the number printed on his card. That is the biggest red flag of all. Every part of the message funnels him toward a stranger waiting on the other end of the phone.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS

Apple Pay users should verify suspicious charges through Wallet, their bank’s official app or the number printed on their card — not contact information in an unexpected text. (Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How this Apple Pay callback scam likely works

The text serves as bait. The phone call allows the scammer to take control of the conversation. Once you call, the person may claim to see your account. They could ask for your name, card number or Apple Account email. Next, they may request a verification code and describe it as a way to cancel the charge.

A scammer could also ask you to install a remote-access app. That would let the person view your screen or guide you through financial transactions. Some callback scams eventually instruct people to transfer money into a "safe" account. Others claim they sent an oversized refund and demand that the extra money be returned.

The FTC warns that fake support agents may seek remote access, steal card information or convince people to move money. CyberGuy previously heard from another person whose Apple Pay scam text nearly led to a $15,000 loss. In that case, the caller used personal information and pressure to keep her on the phone while she drove to her bank.
Do not call the number in the text. Instead, check through channels you already trust:

Open the Wallet app on your iPhone.Select the credit or debit card involved.Tap the Transactions tab.Review the latest activity.Open your bank or card issuer's official app for the full account history.Call the number on the back of the physical card if anything looks wrong.
Open the Wallet app on your iPhone.
Select the credit or debit card involved.
Tap the Transactions tab.
Review the latest activity.
Open your bank or card issuer's official app for the full account history.
Call the number on the back of the physical card if anything looks wrong.

Apple notes that Wallet may not display the complete transaction history for every card. Your bank or card issuer remains the best source for questions about an Apple Pay charge. Do not rely on a phone number from a text, caller ID or sponsored search result.
How to report the fake Apple Pay text
Before deleting the message, save a screenshot that includes the sender information.
On an iPhone:

Tap Report Spam or Report Junk under the message, depending on what appears.Block the sender.Delete the conversation.Email the screenshot to reportphishing@apple.com.Forward the unwanted text to 7726, which spells SPAM.File a report with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Tap Report Spam or Report Junk under the message, depending on what appears.
Block the sender.
Delete the conversation.
Email the screenshot to reportphishing@apple.com.
Forward the unwanted text to 7726, which spells SPAM.
File a report with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Apple recommends emailing screenshots of suspicious Apple text messages to its phishing address. It also lets iPhone owners report junk directly inside Messages. For more ways to handle messages like this, see our guide on how to protect yourself from tech support scams.
What to do if you already called the number
Hang up as soon as you suspect fraud. Then take action based on what you shared:

You only called: Block the number and watch for follow-up calls or texts. Scammers may now know that your phone number reaches a real person.You provided a card or bank number: Contact the financial institution through its official app or the number on the card. Ask it to secure the account and review recent activity.You shared an Apple Account password: Change that password immediately. Confirm that two-factor authentication remains enabled and review the devices connected to your Apple Account. Apple recommends changing the password right away when information may have been entered into a scam site or given to a scammer.You gave away a verification code: Contact the affected company immediately. Never approve an unexpected login request.You installed remote-access software: Disconnect the device from the internet. Remove the remote-access software, then run a full security scan using strong antivirus software. If the scammer may have seen your financial information, contact your bank from a different trusted device.You shared your Social Security number: Place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Continue monitoring your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts.

FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA
Apple says malicious websites could exploit a Safari flaw to steal passwords or payment information from unpatched iPhones and iPads. (Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Ways to protect yourself from similar scam texts
These steps can help you check the warning safely without following the scammer's script.

A deadline can make a fake warning feel real. Give yourself time to check the account independently. A legitimate fraud department will still be there after you close the text and open the official app.

Do not call the number in the text or reply to the sender. Instead, open Wallet or your bank's official app and review recent transactions. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Never rely on contact information supplied in an unexpected message.

A security code can approve a login, password reset or payment. Never read one to a caller, even when the person claims it will cancel a fraudulent charge. Also, do not install an app or share your screen because someone says they need access to fix the problem. Apple representatives will not ask for your password, device passcode or two-factor authentication code.

The message Paul received contains no link. Therefore, antivirus software would not stop the pressure created by the text or phone call. However, scam campaigns can quickly change tactics. A later message may include a fake Apple login page or another dangerous site. Strong security software can detect malicious links and warn you about known scam pages. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

The text sent to Paul did not include his name or other private details. However, callers may use information from data brokers or past breaches to make their stories sound credible. A data removal service can reduce the amount of personal information available through people-search sites. It cannot erase every record or stop every scam. Still, less exposed data gives criminals fewer details to use against you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Consider stronger monitoring if you shared sensitive information or continue receiving targeted financial scams. Identity theft protection can alert you when someone opens a new credit account. It may also notify you when monitored information appears in known breaches. The service cannot prevent every form of identity theft. Therefore, you still need to review alerts and secure affected accounts. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

Reporting the message may help Apple and your carrier identify similar scams. On an iPhone, tap Report Spam or Report Junk beneath the message, depending on the option shown. Then block the sender and delete the conversation. You can also forward the text to 7726, which spells SPAM. Because this message impersonates Apple, take a screenshot and email it to reportphishing@apple.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

This Apple Pay scam piles on fear from the opening line. The $8,250 charge grabs your attention, while the 35-minute deadline tries to stop you from checking whether any of it is real. Even the strange phrases serve a purpose because they keep the message sounding urgent and severe. Paul made the right move by pausing instead of calling. When an unexpected fraud alert arrives, leave the message and check through Wallet, your bank's official app or the number printed on your card. Never give a caller a verification code or access to your screen.

title: Is cyberbullying hiding in your child's group chat?
summary: Cyberbullying often hides inside jokes, group chats and AI deepfakes. These 15 tips help parents and grandparents start the conversation early.
story: Child and adolescent family therapist Darby Fox explains how teens view social media. New research indicates that while some find platforms like Snapchat beneficial for friendships, most encounter online harassment or bullying on TikTok, Instagram, and other platforms. Fox advises parents to implement strict monitoring and maintain open dialogue to protect their children's mental well-being.

"It was only a joke." Those five words can stop an important conversation before it begins. Maybe your child or grandchild posted a rude comment in a group chat. Another kid added an embarrassing picture. Soon, classmates were sharing it and piling on with laughing reactions.

To the children taking part, it may feel like ordinary online drama. To the child being targeted, every notification can feel like another person joining the attack. The warning signs of cyberbullying are not always obvious. Some children hide what they are experiencing. Others take part without realizing their behavior has crossed a line.

That is why cybersecurity education needs to go beyond strong passwords, antivirus software and password managers. Those protections remain essential. However, children also need guidance about empathy, privacy and the consequences of what they post. Parents play a central role. Grandparents can also become trusted listeners, especially when a child feels nervous about telling Mom or Dad. Share this article with the adults in your family. Then use it to start a conversation before a child needs help.
