JEWISH STUDENT TARGETED WITH ANTISEMITIC ABUSE, LAPTOP CORD ATTACK AT COLORADO SCHOOL, ADL ALLEGES
Cyberbullying can spread through group chats, social media and gaming platforms, leaving children vulnerable to rumors, humiliating images and online harassment. (iStock)
Cyberbullying can hide inside ordinary online behavior

Cyberbullying rarely arrives with a warning label. It may appear as a cruel joke, an altered photo or a rumor inside a private chat. Someone might create a fake account to embarrass a classmate. A group may deliberately exclude one child and then share screenshots of the conversation.

The CDC defines bullying as unwanted aggressive behavior that involves a real or perceived power imbalance. The behavior repeats or has a strong chance of being repeated. Cyberbullying occurs when children use texting, social media or other technology to carry out that behavior. That definition can become confusing online.

One person may post something only once. However, dozens of other people can save and share it. The child who created the post may call it a single joke, while the person being targeted watches it circulate for days. Children may also believe they are only watching. Yet forwarding a humiliating image or adding a laughing reaction can make the attack feel much larger. Adults need to help children connect an online action with the real person receiving it.
What the latest cyberbullying data tells families

The latest available research shows that online harassment remains part of daily life for many young people. The CDC reports that more than one in six U.S. high school students experienced electronic bullying during the previous year. That includes bullying through texting and social media. Female students reported it more often than male students.

A World Health Organization study involving 44 countries and regions found that 15% of adolescents had experienced cyberbullying. Meanwhile, 12% admitted cyberbullying someone else. Both figures had increased compared with the organization's earlier research. A 2026 Pew Research Center study offers a closer look at the social platforms teenagers use. Roughly three-quarters of teen TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat users said harassment and bullying were problems on those platforms for people their age.

Nearly three in 10 teen Snapchat users said they had personally experienced at least one form of harassment covered by the survey. Those behaviors included offensive name-calling, rumor spreading or physical threats. The figure was about one in five among teen Instagram and TikTok users. These numbers do not mean every disagreement counts as bullying. Still, families should not wait for an online situation to become severe before discussing it.
Your child may not realize they joined the bullying
Ask a child whether they have bullied anyone and the answer will probably be no. Ask whether they have forwarded an embarrassing screenshot and you may hear a different response.

Children often picture a bully as one openly cruel person who targets someone weaker. Online harassment can look far less organized. A teenager may add an emoji without thinking. Someone else may share the post because everyone at school has already seen it. Another child may remain silent because speaking up could make them the next target.

Each action can increase the pressure on the person being humiliated. Parents and grandparents should avoid starting this conversation with an accusation. Instead, use an example your child can understand.

Ask how the person in the picture might feel. Find out whether they gave permission for the post. You could also ask what your child would want a friend to do if someone shared the same content about them. These questions help children examine their decisions without immediately feeling attacked.
Why telling a child to go offline may not solve it

I recently spoke with a high school senior and her mother, who works in education. The student explained that bullying often looks very different from the scenes adults remember from movies. Much of it happens in private chats, anonymous apps and social media accounts that hide the person posting.

Rumors can spread across a school before the person being discussed knows they exist. AI tools can also produce altered photos, fake audio and convincing videos of a classmate. When I asked whether leaving social media could provide some relief, the student explained that her phone connected her with friends and much of her school life. That response stayed with me.

Adults often see putting down a phone as a break. A teenager may see it as disappearing from their social circle. Leaving an app can also mean missing plans or school updates while everyone else continues discussing the situation.

Pew Research Center found that 74% of teens said social media helped them feel connected to what was happening in their friends' lives. At the same time, 39% said social media made them feel overwhelmed by drama. Nearly one-third said it sometimes left them feeling excluded. "Delete the app" should not be the only advice a child hears.
Parents may feel ready to talk before children feel ready to answer

Adults often assume their children know they can come to them. Children may feel differently. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 80% of parents felt highly comfortable discussing their teenager's mental health. Only 52% of teens felt equally comfortable having that conversation with a parent. That gap should get every parent's attention.

A parent may believe the door is wide open. Meanwhile, the child may worry about losing a phone or being blamed for what happened. The child may also fear that an adult will immediately call the school and make the situation more public.

Grandparents can sometimes help bridge that distance. A teenager may reveal something during a car ride or while visiting for the weekend. The conversation may begin casually instead of during a serious family meeting. Listen closely when a child suddenly asks what you would do in a "hypothetical" situation. They may be testing whether it feels safe to tell you more.
COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?
Children may contribute to cyberbullying without realizing it by forwarding embarrassing screenshots, sharing harmful posts or reacting to humiliating content. (iStock)
AI deepfakes are raising the stakes for children

Generative AI has made a painful form of online abuse much easier to create. A classmate can take an ordinary social media photo and use an AI tool to create a fake nude image. Someone can also clone a voice, produce a false video or build a convincing impersonation account. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received more than 400,000 CyberTipline reports with a generative AI connection during 2025.

NCMEC also identified more than 275 direct victims of AI-generated child sexual abuse material during 2024 and 2025. In many cases, the person responsible had direct access to the child. Those reports involve child exploitation rather than cyberbullying alone. However, NCMEC warns that classmates can use AI to create fake images and videos for bullying.

The content can circulate through schools and cause severe emotional harm. AI fakes may also be used for blackmail or sextortion. Parents should never dismiss an altered image because it is fake. The humiliation can feel painfully real. Copies may also keep circulating after the original post disappears. A child may fear that teachers, classmates or future friends will believe the image is genuine.
Tips for talking to kids about cyberbullying
One serious lecture will not prepare a child for every app, friend or group chat. Instead, return to this conversation as your child's online habits change. These steps can help you begin.

Opening with "You spend too much time on that phone" will probably lead to an argument. Ask which game they have been playing. Find out what their friends are sharing. You could also ask whether a group chat has started feeling uncomfortable or stressful.

The goal is to understand where your child spends time online. You probably know the names of their closest school friends. Try to learn about the people they interact with online too. That interest can make it easier for a child to describe a problem later.

Children need examples they can recognize. A joke becomes harmful when the person asks for it to stop and the group keeps going. Sharing someone's picture without permission can also cross a boundary.

Spreading a rumor or creating a fake account to embarrass someone can cause lasting harm. Ask your child whether they would make the same comment with the other person sitting beside them. That pause may stop an impulsive post from growing into a much bigger problem.
Many children stay silent because they fear losing access to their device. Tell your child that showing you a troubling message will not automatically lead to punishment.

You may eventually need to restrict an app or change how the device is used. However, your first response should focus on what happened and whether the child feels safe. Listen before contacting another family. When possible, explain what you plan to do next. A child is more likely to keep talking when they feel included in the response.

An angry reply can create another screenshot for people to share. Tell your child to stop responding when an exchange becomes heated. They can mute the conversation and show the device to a trusted adult. They should also avoid forwarding the content.

Even a reaction emoji can keep the post active and encourage more children to join. Federal bullying guidance advises children not to reply to or forward cyberbullying messages. It also recommends blocking threatening or questionable accounts.
The first instinct may be to erase a cruel post immediately. Take screenshots first. Capture the username, date and complete conversation.

Save emails, links and text messages. Write down when the behavior happened and whether anyone else saw it. You can use that evidence when reporting the account to the platform or school. StopBullying.gov recommends saving screenshots, emails and messages before reporting cyberbullying.

After saving the evidence, block the person responsible. Report the post through the app or platform. Choose the category that most accurately describes what happened. If students from the same school are involved, contact an administrator and ask for the school's cyberbullying policy.

Tell the school what you already reported to the platform. Share enough evidence to explain the situation without spreading the harmful content further. Direct threats or stalking may require contacting law enforcement. Seek emergency help when anyone faces immediate danger.
Make your child's social media accounts private when the platform offers that choice. Review the follower list together. Remove accounts your child does not recognize or no longer trusts.
Check whether posts reveal a school name or regular location. Look for phone numbers and home addresses too. Family members should review their own accounts.

A grandparent may proudly share a school photo without noticing the logo on a uniform. A relative might post a practice schedule or tag the child's exact location. Before sharing, ask what an angry classmate or stranger could learn from the post.
A stolen account can quickly become a cyberbullying tool. Someone may impersonate your child, publish private conversations or send cruel messages to classmates.

Use a different password for every account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so children do not reuse one login across several apps. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available.

Children should also avoid sharing passwords with friends. Friendships can change, and access given today may be abused after an argument. Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at CyberGuy.com.
STUDY FINDS MORE AI PRAISE FOR BLACK STUDENTS, SOFTER TREATMENT OF FEMALES
AI tools have raised the stakes for cyberbullying by making it easier to create fake images, cloned voices and convincing videos targeting children. (AP Photo/Kiichiro Sato, File)

Require children to ask before installing an unofficial gaming client, mod or computer program. A convincing video can promote a download that hides malware. Once installed, malicious software may steal passwords or allow someone to access private files.
Tell children never to disable security software because an online creator says a warning is harmless. They should download mods only from established communities recognized by the game's developer.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious files and block dangerous websites. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Parental controls can help manage app downloads, content access and time spent on a device. Apple's Screen Time allows parents to set app limits and restrict certain content on a child's iPhone or iPad.

Google Family Link can manage apps and set screen-time limits on supported Android devices and Chromebooks. Microsoft Family Safety includes screen-time settings and content filters across supported devices. Some web filtering features require Microsoft Edge.
Tell children which controls you use and why. Secret monitoring can damage trust. A child who understands the rules has a better chance of respecting the boundaries.
You can also review my top child monitoring programs if built-in settings do not provide enough support at CyberGuy.com.
Do not tell a child to ignore an explicit deepfake because people know it was created with AI. Save the evidence without forwarding it. Report every account distributing the content.

Contact the school when students are involved. You can also report suspected child sexual exploitation to NCMEC's CyberTipline. Its Take It Down service creates a digital fingerprint of eligible images or videos so participating platforms can detect copies without the image leaving the device.
Do not download or ask someone to send you an explicit image of a minor to make a report. NCMEC specifically warns against downloading or sharing the content for submission.
A bully may send a child their home address or the names of relatives to frighten them. That information could come from public social media posts, people-search websites or data brokers.

Limit the family details you publish publicly. Ask relatives to do the same. A data removal service may reduce the information available through people-search and broker sites. No service can erase every detail, but ongoing removal can make sensitive information harder to locate. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Contact the school when classmates are involved or the online harassment begins affecting attendance. Report credible threats to law enforcement. Seek immediate help when a child appears to be in danger.
Do not try to negotiate with someone who claims to control a child's account, camera or computer. Disconnect the device from the internet. Then run a full security scan.
Change passwords from another device that you know is safe. Most importantly, reassure the child that asking for help was the right decision.
Children notice how adults behave online. They see angry arguments on Facebook. They notice when family members share humiliating memes or attack someone in the comments.
An adult may view that behavior as blowing off steam. A child may see permission to act the same way. Before posting, ask whether you would say those words with your child sitting beside you.

Grandparents can set a powerful example too. They often have close relationships with grandchildren and may hear something a child hesitates to tell a parent. Let your grandchild know they can show you a troubling message without being blamed. Then involve the parents unless doing so could place the child in immediate danger.
Families preparing for the school year can also review my updated best back-to-school supplies and tech for students at CyberGuy.com.
You do not have to wait for a crisis. Send this article to another parent. Share it with grandparents, relatives and anyone who regularly cares for your child.
Then agree on how the adults will respond if a child reports an online problem. A child should hear the same message from every trusted adult: Tell us what happened. We will listen before reacting.
That response may stop a child from hiding something because they fear punishment or embarrassment. It may also give a bystander the confidence to speak up when someone else is being targeted.
Kurt's key takeaways

Cyberbullying may begin with a joke, rumor or altered picture. Within minutes, it can follow a child across several accounts and into the classroom. Recent research shows that many teenagers see harassment as a serious problem on the platforms they use. AI has also made humiliating fake content easier to create and harder to contain. Security tools can protect accounts and devices. Parental controls can create useful boundaries. However, children still need adults who will listen before taking over. Parents and grandparents should keep the conversation going as apps and friendships change. Share these tips with the people who care for the children in your family. Then make sure every child knows which trusted adult they can approach when something feels wrong.

title: Is your Social Security number on the dark web?
summary: A leaked Social Security number can fuel tax fraud, benefits fraud and new account openings. Key warning signs and a credit freeze can limit damage.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
If you suspect your Social Security number is on the dark web, the right move is not to panic. It is to act quickly, methodically and in the right order.

A leaked Social Security number can be used in ways that go far beyond one fraudulent credit card charge. Criminals may try to open new credit accounts, file fake tax returns, hijack benefits or combine your SSN with other stolen details to impersonate you. The good news is that you can take concrete steps to check for signs of exposure and reduce the damage if your information has already been compromised.
This guide walks through how to check whether your SSN may be exposed, what to do next and how ongoing monitoring can help you catch problems earlier.

PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS
Check account alerts, credit reports and financial activity for signs that someone may be using your personal information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Can you actually check whether your Social Security number is on the dark web?

Not directly in most cases. Rather than trying to search the dark web yourself, it is safer to rely on breach notices, account alerts, credit reports and reputable dark web monitoring tools. In real life, SSN exposure usually shows up first through warning signs like a breach notice, a strange credit inquiry or suspicious account activity.
What are the first signs your SSN may be exposed?
Some warning signs are obvious, and others are easy to dismiss until they pile up.
Watch for things like:

A data breach notice from an employer, insurer, bank, retailer, school or healthcare providerUnfamiliar credit inquiries or new accounts on your credit reportAlerts about loans, buy-now-pay-later activity, utility accounts or address changes you did not authorizeIRS, Social Security or state agency notices that do not match your recent activityCalls or messages from debt collectors about accounts you never openedA sudden spike in scam attempts using accurate personal details
A data breach notice from an employer, insurer, bank, retailer, school or healthcare provider
Unfamiliar credit inquiries or new accounts on your credit report
Alerts about loans, buy-now-pay-later activity, utility accounts or address changes you did not authorize
IRS, Social Security or state agency notices that do not match your recent activity
Calls or messages from debt collectors about accounts you never opened
A sudden spike in scam attempts using accurate personal details
None of these signs proves your SSN is being sold on the dark web. However, they may indicate identity exposure that needs immediate attention.
IS ID.ME SAFE TO USE? WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
A leaked Social Security number can be difficult to recover, so freezing your credit and monitoring for fraud are critical. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to check whether your Social Security number may be exposed
If a company says your personal information was exposed, do not ignore it. Read the notice closely to see what data may have been involved, note the dates and save a copy for your records.

A dark web monitoring or exposure scan service can help you check whether your information appears in known breach data without trying to search hidden sites yourself. Some credit monitoring services offer a free scan and include dark web monitoring.
Look across all three credit bureaus for unfamiliar hard inquiries, new accounts, wrong addresses or collections that are not yours. Fraud often appears here before you see bigger damage.

Check bank accounts, credit cards, payment apps, buy-now-pay-later services and retirement accounts for anything unusual. Turn on alerts for big purchases, password changes and profile updates if you have not already.
Review financial documents carefully and keep records of unfamiliar accounts, inquiries and transactions you may need to dispute. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What should you do next if your SSN has been leaked?
If you think your SSN is already exposed, move through these steps as quickly as possible.

A credit freeze is one of the strongest steps you can take. It makes it much harder for someone to open new credit in your name because lenders generally cannot access your credit file while it is frozen. If you are not actively applying for credit, freezing your file at all three bureaus is usually the safest default.
A fraud alert tells lenders to take extra steps to verify identity before opening new accounts. It is not as strong as a freeze, but it can still be a useful layer of protection.

Start with your primary email account, then update passwords for banking, retirement, shopping, payment and healthcare logins. Use a reputable password manager to create and securely store strong, unique passwords for every account. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever possible. This matters because many identity theft cases begin with account takeover, not only new account fraud.

If your SSN is compromised, watch for signs of tax fraud or benefits misuse. Unexpected mail, rejected tax filings or notices about claims or services you did not request should be investigated immediately.
Keep records of breach notices, account alerts, calls with banks, dispute reference numbers and dates. If fraud appears later, that paper trail can save time and reduce stress.

If someone has already used your information, report it to the relevant financial institution right away and file an identity theft report through the proper government channels. That documentation can help when disputing fraudulent accounts and charges.
Can you remove your Social Security number from the dark web?

Usually, no. Once sensitive data is leaked, copied, sold and reposted, it is rarely possible to claw it back completely. That is why the smartest response is not to focus on "getting it removed" from criminal spaces. It is to reduce how useful that information is to criminals. In practice, that means freezing credit, tightening account security, removing extra personal information from public-facing sources when possible and keeping ongoing watch for fraud signals.
How identity monitoring can help without replacing the basics

An identity monitoring service can add another layer of protection after you complete the immediate cleanup steps. Depending on the service, it may monitor dark web sources, credit reports, financial accounts and changes to your personal information.

Some services also provide restoration specialists who can guide you through disputes and recovery if identity theft occurs. These tools may help you spot warning signs sooner, but they do not replace credit freezes, strong unique passwords, multifactor authentication and regular account reviews.
Avoid these common mistakes

Waiting for obvious fraud before taking actionAssuming one password change solves the problemRelying only on your bank to catch identity misuseIgnoring small charges or account alerts because they seem minorTrying to investigate the dark web through risky sites or forumsForgetting to secure your primary email account, which can unlock many of your other accounts
Waiting for obvious fraud before taking action
Assuming one password change solves the problem
Relying only on your bank to catch identity misuse
Ignoring small charges or account alerts because they seem minor
Trying to investigate the dark web through risky sites or forums
Forgetting to secure your primary email account, which can unlock many of your other accounts
See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

If your Social Security number may be on the dark web, speed matters more than certainty. You do not need perfect proof before acting. Start with the signs you can verify: breach notices, account alerts, credit reports and unusual activity across your financial life. Lock down what you can, freeze your credit, strengthen account security and keep monitoring. And if you want ongoing help after the first round of cleanup, an identity theft protection service can add another layer through dark web monitoring, data broker removal, financial alerts and restoration support when identity issues get messy.

title: Self-destructing phone code sparks federal case
summary: Samuel Tunick faces a felony charge after a GrapheneOS duress PIN allegedly wiped his Google Pixel during a CBP phone search at Atlanta's airport.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Your phone holds a running record of your life. It can reveal private messages, photos, financial records and location history. That explains why some people turn to extreme security tools. One of them is a secret phone wipe code that erases stored data when someone enters a secondary passcode. However, using that feature during a federal inspection can create serious legal trouble.

An Atlanta man now faces a felony charge after a special passcode allegedly erased his Google Pixel while U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers were trying to inspect it. Prosecutors say he knowingly destroyed digital property that the government had lawful authority to seize. His attorneys dispute that account. They argue that agents detained him unlawfully and had no valid authority to take the phone.
The unresolved case puts personal privacy and border security on a collision course. It also shows how quickly a phone protection feature can become the center of a federal prosecution.

Join us on Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
UK SPY POWERS DRAW US SCRUTINY OVER ALLEGED APPLE ENCRYPTION BACKDOOR DEMAND
A Google Pixel displays GrapheneOS, the privacy-focused operating system at the center of the federal phone-wipe case. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How a secret phone wipe code led to a federal charge

Samuel Tunick, a U.S. citizen who lives in Atlanta, returned from a vacation in the Dominican Republic on Jan. 24, 2025. CBP officers directed him to a secondary inspection area at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. During the encounter, agents took possession of his Google Pixel and asked for its passcode.

Tunick allegedly supplied a code that did not unlock the phone. Instead, an officer entered it and triggered a complete wipe. According to court filings described in published reports, the screen went dark, flashed several times and appeared to restart. The phone remained physically intact, but its stored data was gone.

Federal authorities later allowed Tunick to enter the country. A grand jury indicted him on Nov. 13, 2025, under a rarely used federal law covering the destruction of property to prevent a government seizure. Tunick pleaded not guilty. The charge remains an allegation, and the court has not decided whether the government's seizure was lawful. The case appears to be among the first publicly reported federal prosecutions centered on a phone's duress wipe feature.
How the GrapheneOS duress passcode wipes a phone

Tunick's Pixel reportedly ran GrapheneOS, an open-source operating system designed to increase privacy and security on supported Google Pixel phones. GrapheneOS replaces the standard operating system. It does not work like a regular Android app.

One optional feature lets the phone's owner create a duress PIN or password. This credential differs from the code that normally unlocks the screen. When someone enters the duress credential, GrapheneOS immediately and irreversibly wipes the device. The process also removes installed eSIMs.

GrapheneOS says the wipe does not require a reboot and cannot be interrupted after it begins. The code works anywhere the operating system requests the device credentials, including the lock screen. The feature could help someone facing a violent thief or another coercive situation. Yet using it during a government search raises a separate legal question. Installing GrapheneOS or setting up a duress passcode is not the crime alleged in this case. Prosecutors are focusing on when Tunick allegedly used the feature and what he intended to accomplish.
Why a phone wipe during a border search may be a felony

Federal prosecutors charged Tunick under 18 U.S.C. Section 2232(a). The law applies when someone knowingly destroys, damages or takes another action against property to prevent the government from lawfully taking custody of it.

The statute can apply at any point surrounding a search or seizure. A conviction carries up to five years in federal prison and may also include a fine. The government appears to view the physical phone as a container. The stored information represents the property agents wanted to inspect and preserve.

According to the indictment, Tunick knowingly caused the contents of his Pixel to be deleted. Prosecutors allege that he acted to prevent the government from taking control of that information. The charge does not require prosecutors to prove that the phone contained evidence of a separate crime. The immediate issue involves the alleged destruction and Tunick's intent when he supplied the code.
However, the statute only applies when the government acts under lawful authority. That requirement sits at the center of the defense's challenge.
ARE APPLE DEVICES SPYING? WHAT YOUR IPHONE TRACKS
GrapheneOS lets owners create a duress password that can trigger an immediate and irreversible wipe of the device. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why the defense says the border phone search was unlawful

Tunick's attorneys argue that CBP officers violated his constitutional rights during the airport encounter. They claim agents detained him without a warrant, denied his requests to speak with an attorney and failed to advise him of his rights. The defense has asked the court to suppress statements and evidence connected to the inspection.

His attorneys also allege that agents used concerns about illegal material as a pretext to examine his connections to the movement opposing Atlanta's police and fire training facility. Opponents commonly call the facility Cop City. Tunick has participated in activism against the project, according to his defense team.

These remain defense allegations. Prosecutors dispute the claim that the airport encounter was unlawful and argue that officers acted under their border inspection authority. Magistrate Judge Christopher C. Bly held an evidentiary hearing on July 20, 2026. As of today, the court had not ruled on Tunick's motion to suppress. Therefore, Tunick remains presumed innocent unless prosecutors prove the charge beyond a reasonable doubt.
What authority CBP has to search phones at the US border

Federal officers have broader search authority at an international border than police usually have elsewhere in the country. The border-search exception allows the government to inspect travelers and their belongings as they enter the United States. International arrival areas inside airports serve as ports of entry for this purpose.

CBP says electronic-device searches can help officers investigate national security threats, child exploitation, smuggling and other violations enforced by the agency. CBP divides phone inspections into basic and advanced searches.

During a basic search, an officer manually reviews information stored on the device. An advanced search involves connecting external equipment that can copy or analyze its contents. Under CBP's current directive, an advanced search requires reasonable suspicion of an activity that violates a law enforced by CBP or a national security concern. A senior manager must also approve it.

However, federal courts have not adopted one uniform nationwide standard for every phone search at the border. The legal protection can depend on the search method and the federal jurisdiction where the inspection occurs. That uncertainty leaves travelers with fewer clear answers than they might expect.
Can you refuse to unlock your phone at the U.S. border?

A U.S. citizen cannot be denied entry solely because CBP cannot inspect a locked electronic device. Still, refusing access may extend the inspection. Officers can also detain the phone if a passcode or encryption prevents them from examining it.

CBP says a traveler must present a device in a condition that allows inspection. Its policy also states that U.S. citizens will not be denied entry solely because officers cannot inspect the device. Foreign visitors face different risks. Refusing to cooperate may affect whether CBP admits them to the United States.

Meanwhile, courts continue to wrestle with questions involving compelled passcodes and biometric unlocking. The answer may vary by jurisdiction and circumstance. Anyone carrying confidential business records or other highly sensitive material should consider speaking with a qualified attorney before international travel.
Travelers should review the sensitive information on their phones before reaching an international border inspection. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why the timing of a phone wipe changes the legal risk

Removing personal information before a trip differs from deleting data after officers have begun an inspection. You may decide at home that you do not want to carry old files or unnecessary accounts across the border. You could also use a separate travel phone that contains less personal information.

Those choices happen before government agents stop you or take possession of the device. The legal risk changes once an active inspection begins. Prosecutors may view a deliberate wipe at that point as an attempt to interfere with a search or seizure.

In Tunick's case, his intent will likely become a major issue. Prosecutors say he provided the code while knowing what it would do. His lawyers maintain that the government lacked lawful authority from the start. The court must evaluate both sides before deciding whether the case moves forward.
How to protect your phone before international travel

The safest time to review your digital privacy is before you arrive at the airport. For a broader security checklist, read our guide on how to keep your phone safe abroad. The following steps can reduce how much personal information you carry without encouraging a confrontation during an inspection.

Review the information stored on your phone before leaving home. Remove files that you will not need during the trip. A separate travel phone may make sense when your primary device contains sensitive business information or private communications. Keep only the apps and accounts you expect to use. You can find more ways to reduce exposed information in our guide on how to minimize your digital footprint when you travel.

Create an encrypted backup before your trip. Confirm that you know how to restore it. A working backup can protect your photos, documents, contacts and account records if the phone is lost or held by authorities. Also, keep essential travel information somewhere besides your phone. A printed itinerary can help if you temporarily lose access to the device.

Use a strong passcode that someone cannot easily guess, and store it in a trusted password manager if needed. Avoid birthdays and repeated numbers. Turn off notification previews on the lock screen. Otherwise, text messages and account alerts may remain visible without authentication. Before leaving, review these iPhone and Android security settings that help protect your data.

A full shutdown may place encrypted information on many modern phones into a more protected state before the first unlock. Make that decision before entering the inspection area. Suddenly powering down after an officer orders you to hand over the device could raise questions about your intent.

U.S. citizens retain the right to enter the country. However, declining to unlock a phone can lead to delays or the temporary seizure of the device. The consequences may be more serious for foreign visitors. Anyone with immigration concerns should get advice based on their specific status before traveling.

A duress passcode may be legal to install. Using it while officers are trying to inspect or seize a phone creates a different risk. Tunick's prosecution shows that the government may treat that action as an intentional effort to destroy property. Do not make an irreversible decision based only on what a privacy feature promises. Once a federal inspection begins, your actions can become evidence in a criminal case.

Ask for a receipt that identifies the device and the agency holding it. After leaving the inspection area, write down what happened while the details remain fresh. Include the time, officers' names, questions asked and any paperwork you received. Those notes could help an attorney evaluate the encounter.
Kurt's key takeaways

A secret phone wipe code can protect sensitive information during a dangerous encounter. The same code can lead to a federal charge when it erases data during an active government inspection. Federal officers have a legitimate responsibility to secure the border and preserve potential evidence. At the same time, your phone can expose deeply personal details about your life. The court must now decide whether agents acted within their lawful authority. It must also consider what Tunick intended when he provided the code. Until that happens, the case remains unresolved and Tunick remains presumed innocent. For travelers, preparation offers the safest path. Review your phone before leaving home and understand what may happen if you refuse a device search. A privacy choice made before a trip gives you time to consider the consequences. A wipe code activated during an airport inspection could turn a difficult encounter into a federal criminal case.

Should border officers need a warrant before searching the private contents of your phone, or should protecting the country give them broader access when you return from overseas? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Smart toilet seat could detect AFib in 30 seconds
summary: The HARO EKG-seat by Hamberger Medical records a six-lead EKG in 30 seconds while you sit, scanning for atrial fibrillation and irregular heartbeat.
story: Eko Health co-founder and CEO Connor Landgraf discusses how their AI-powered stethoscope is revolutionizing cardiac care and improving patient outcomes. This innovative device amplifies heart and lung sounds, analyzes them in real-time and detects early signs of heart disease and arrhythmias in just 15 seconds. The technology offers physicians consistent, reliable insights, enhancing early diagnosis and intervention.

Your next bathroom break could come with an unexpected bonus: a check of your heart rhythm. German medical technology company Hamberger Medical has developed the HARO EKG-seat. It looks like a regular toilet seat, but built-in sensors record an electrocardiogram, also called an EKG or ECG, while you sit.

After about 30 seconds, a connected smartphone app analyzes the reading for signs of an irregular heart rhythm, including possible atrial fibrillation. AFib is the most common type of irregular heartbeat, and millions of people may have it without realizing anything feels wrong. It sounds like the kind of idea someone dreamed up during a very long bathroom break.

However, the possibility of catching a silent heart condition during something you already do every day deserves attention. Here's what the early research reveals about how well the seat works and where its limits begin.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?
A smart toilet seat developed in Germany could help detect irregular heart rhythms in about 30 seconds without electrodes or a wearable. (iStock)
How the smart toilet seat checks your heart

A conventional medical EKG usually requires you to lie down while a medical professional places electrodes on your chest and other parts of your body. The HARO EKG-seat takes a different approach. Its sensors collect electrical signals from your body while you sit normally. The seat records a six-lead resting EKG and sends the information to its companion app through Bluetooth.

You do not need to attach sticky pads or remember to put on a wearable. You sit for about 30 seconds and let the seat do the work. Hamberger Medical says participants in its usability testing could operate the system without special instructions. The oldest participants in one reported study were in their 90s, according to published reports about the device. That simplicity may become one of its biggest strengths. Many health devices end up forgotten in a drawer after the novelty fades. A toilet seat is harder to forget.
Smart toilet seat study shows promising AFib results

The company tested the seat through what it calls the Hamberger Heart Study. Researchers compared the seat's six-lead EKG with a standard 12-lead medical EKG. Hamberger Medical reported a high level of agreement between the two systems when checking for AFib and other rhythm abnormalities.

That sounds encouraging, but there is an important limitation. The complete results have not been published in an independently peer-reviewed medical journal. Public reports also do not provide enough detail about the study's size, false alerts or performance across different groups.

Without those numbers, we cannot tell how often the seat might miss AFib or mistakenly warn someone whose heart rhythm is normal. For now, the results should be viewed as promising company-reported findings. They do not prove that the seat can replace a hospital EKG or a doctor's diagnosis.
Why AFib can be difficult to catch

AFib causes the heart's upper chambers to beat irregularly. Blood may then pool inside the heart, which can allow clots to form. A clot can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. The American Heart Association says AFib is linked to about five times the risk of stroke. Some people feel a racing heartbeat or fluttering in their chest. Others notice fatigue, dizziness or shortness of breath.

However, AFib can also arrive without obvious warning signs. A person may feel fine while the irregular rhythm comes and goes. That creates a detection problem. A brief EKG at a doctor's office may look normal if the AFib episode ended before the appointment. Doctors sometimes use longer-term monitors when they suspect an intermittent rhythm problem. A toilet seat that records readings regularly could provide more chances to capture an episode.
WEARABLE PATCH VIBRATES WHEN DANGER IS NEARBY
The HARO EKG-seat records a six-lead EKG during a routine bathroom visit and analyzes the reading for possible atrial fibrillation. (Hamberger Medical)
Early AFib detection could help prevent serious problems

The American Heart Association estimates that about 5 million Americans currently live with AFib. It projects that more than 12 million could have the condition by 2030. Early detection can help doctors decide whether someone needs medication, additional monitoring or treatment to restore a normal rhythm.

Dr. Paari Dominic, a cardiac electrophysiologist, told the American Medical Association that earlier intervention can significantly improve outcomes. He noted that research supports pursuing normal rhythm within a year of detecting AFib in appropriate patients. However, a notification from a toilet seat should begin a medical conversation. It should never end one.
Who faces a higher risk of AFib?

Age raises the likelihood of developing AFib. High blood pressure also plays a major role. Diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and certain heart conditions can increase the risk. Smoking and excessive alcohol use may contribute as well.

Heavy drinking can sometimes trigger an irregular heartbeat even in people without a known heart condition. Doctors often call this "holiday heart syndrome" because cases can rise during celebrations involving heavier alcohol use. People who already face a higher risk could benefit most from convenient monitoring. That decision should involve a cardiologist or another qualified medical professional.
How the smart toilet seat handles health data

A heart-monitoring toilet seat collects highly sensitive information, so its privacy protections deserve a close look. According to Hamberger Medical's app privacy policy, EKG processing happens locally on the connected phone or tablet. The company says readings are not sent to its servers. The app also lets you export a PDF report. Hamberger Medical recommends protecting the file with a password before sending it to someone else. However, your phone's backup settings may still upload app information to iCloud or Google Backup. The company notes that this depends on how you configured your device.

Before using any connected health product, check its backup settings and sharing options. You should also protect your phone with a strong passcode. For additional steps, see our guide on how to stop health and fitness apps from using your private data.
HEART CONDITION TIED TO LINDSEY GRAHAM'S DEATH CAN STRIKE WITHOUT WARNING — WHAT TO KNOW
Built-in sensors allow the HARO EKG-seat to monitor a user’s heart rhythm and send the results to a connected smartphone app. (iStock)
Is the HARO EKG-seat available to buy?

The HARO EKG-seat does not currently appear to be available for purchase. Hamberger Medical previously said the device was sold exclusively through its official German online shop at approximately $2,870. CyberGuy reached out to Hamberger Medical to confirm current availability, pricing and whether the company plans to sell the EKG-seat in the United States, but did not hear back before our deadline.
What this means to you

The HARO EKG-seat shows how health monitoring could blend into your normal routine. That part is genuinely promising. The clinical report suggests the seat can record EKGs that cardiologists interpret with strong accuracy. However, the current app results do not support relying on its automated AFib classification alone.

A normal app reading should not convince you to ignore symptoms. An abnormal warning should lead to a conversation with a medical professional. Contact your doctor if you notice a racing or irregular heartbeat, recurring dizziness or unexplained shortness of breath. Chest pain or pressure may signal a medical emergency, so call 911 right away. Never start or stop heart medication because of a consumer device result. Your doctor may order a clinical EKG or longer-term monitoring before making a diagnosis.
Kurt's key takeaways

There is something undeniably clever about turning an ordinary toilet seat into a heart monitor. It fits health screening into a routine that people already follow without reminders. The company-reported results sound encouraging, especially for a condition that may hide between doctor visits. Smart health technology works best when it helps you notice a concern sooner and gives your doctor useful information. It becomes dangerous when a gadget creates false confidence or replaces professional care.
Would you trust a smart toilet seat with your heart data if it could uncover a silent problem before your next doctor visit? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

- OpenAI to pay $3.2 million to settle DOJ allegations it favored foreign workers over Americans
- AI kill-switch bill could shut down rogue models
- Battlefield robots open new front in innovation war with major US adversary

STACKED DECK: OpenAI and one of its subsidiaries will pay $3.2 million to settle allegations that they discriminated against U.S. workers by favoring foreign workers with temporary employment visas, the Justice Department announced Tuesday.

title: Russian hackers can steal emails without a click
summary: Laundry Bear exploits security flaw in unpatched Zimbra servers, stealing 90 days of emails and authentication data without victims clicking a link.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Opening an unexpected email can feel relatively harmless when you avoid its links and attachments. However, a Russian hacking campaign has turned that familiar safety advice on its head.

CISA says the Russian state-sponsored group Laundry Bear can compromise certain email accounts when someone simply opens or previews a malicious message. The attack targets organizations running unpatched versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.
Once the email appears, hidden code can collect passwords, authentication data and as much as 90 days of messages. You may never see a warning or realize that anything happened.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued the warning with the National Security Agency, FBI and cyber authorities from several allied countries. The agencies say the group has successfully targeted more than 10 Western organizations since July 2025.
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT

Russian state-sponsored hackers can steal passwords, two-factor authentication tokens and up to 90 days of email when users view malicious messages in unpatched Zimbra accounts. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
Russian hackers can steal emails without a normal click

Laundry Bear, which Microsoft tracks as Void Blizzard, exploits a security flaw known as CVE-2025-66376. The cross-site scripting vulnerability affects the Classic user interface in certain versions of the Zimbra Collaboration Suite.

Zimbra is an email and collaboration platform used by some governments, schools, businesses and other organizations as an alternative to services such as Microsoft Exchange or Google Workspace. Attackers can place malicious JavaScript inside a specially crafted HTML email. That code runs automatically when a vulnerable Zimbra webmail client displays the message.

The person reading the email does not need to open an attachment. The attack also avoids the usual request to enter a password on an obvious phishing page. However, the email still needs to appear on the screen. CISA describes the technique as a zero-click exploit. Proofpoint calls it a "half-click" attack because someone must open the email or allow it to appear in a preview pane. Either description leads to the same concern. A message can look harmless while code hidden inside it quietly attacks the email account.
The email security flaw was patched in 2025

Laundry Bear reportedly used the flaw as a zero-day before Zimbra released a patch in November 2025. A zero-day attack exploits a security weakness before the software maker provides a fix. CISA later added the vulnerability to its list of flaws that hackers actively exploit.

The available patch closes the known security hole. Yet Laundry Bear continues to target organizations that have not installed the update. That makes delayed patching especially dangerous. An organization may have strong passwords and trained employees, but an exposed email server can still give attackers another way inside.

The campaign has reached organizations connected to the defense industrial base and government. Attackers have also targeted education, energy, law enforcement, media, nonprofit groups and technology companies.
One email can expose 90 days of messages

According to CISA, the malicious code attempts to collect the target's last 90 days of email. That could include private conversations with coworkers, contract discussions or information about upcoming meetings. An inbox may also contain password reset notices, invoices and documents that reveal how an organization operates.

Laundry Bear also collects the person's email address and password. The attack can copy the organization's Global Address List, which acts as a directory of employees and contacts. The hackers may then gain enough information to impersonate a trusted coworker or identify more valuable accounts.

CISA says the exploit also targets two-factor authentication tokens. Those tokens help prove that someone has already completed an authentication step. A stolen token or session cookie can let an attacker enter an account without completing the normal login process again.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Malicious code hidden inside an email can run when a vulnerable Zimbra webmail client displays the message, giving hackers access to sensitive account data. (Getty Images)
Hackers can create a hidden way back into an account

Stealing information provides immediate value, but Laundry Bear also tries to preserve its access. The attack creates a new Zimbra application passcode and sends it back to the hackers. Legacy email programs use these passcodes when they connect through services such as IMAP or ActiveSync and cannot support modern time-based authentication.

An unauthorized passcode can give the hackers another entrance to the mailbox. That access may continue even after someone changes the main account password. CISA has urged administrators to look for suspicious application passcodes, particularly passcodes labeled "ZimbraWeb."
Organizations should treat an unknown passcode as a sign that someone may have entered the account. Simply installing the patch after a compromise may leave the attacker's access in place.
How the stolen email data leaves the network

Laundry Bear sends the stolen information to servers controlled by the group. CISA says the attackers use a collection framework called Flowerbed. The system moves smaller pieces of data through Domain Name System requests. DNS normally helps computers find websites and online services.

Attackers can hide encoded information inside those requests. Because organizations generate large amounts of legitimate DNS traffic, the malicious activity may blend into the background. Laundry Bear sends larger collections through encrypted HTTPS connections. That can include compressed archives containing mailbox data. Security teams may need to inspect network logs, authentication records and mailbox activity to understand what left the organization.
Fake email login pages provide another route

Laundry Bear also uses adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits. These tools create login pages that closely resemble legitimate email portals. When someone enters a username and password, the phishing system captures those credentials. It can also intercept session cookies created during the login process. That means an attacker may gain access even when the account uses conventional multifactor authentication.

CISA's indicators of compromise include domains that impersonated Zimbra infrastructure. Examples include mailnalysis.com, zimbrastat.com, zimbra-metadata.com and zmailanalytics.com. The presence of one of these domains in network logs could point to phishing or unauthorized account activity. However, organizations should review CISA's complete list because attackers can change their infrastructure.

Proofpoint found that Laundry Bear sent messages from attacker-controlled Proton Mail accounts and email addresses the group had already compromised. In one example, the sender claimed to represent a Belgian media-verification organization. The email proposed cooperation between European institutions fighting disinformation. It included a legitimate-looking link to a European Union events calendar. However, the malicious code sat inside the email rather than the linked website.
Laundry Bear has targeted governments and Ukraine

Dutch intelligence agencies publicly identified Laundry Bear in May 2025. Their investigation linked the group to a 2024 breach of the Dutch National Police. That incident exposed personal information belonging to police personnel. Investigators said the attack helped them identify a previously unknown Russian cyberespionage group.
Since at least 2024, Laundry Bear has focused on organizations connected to Russian strategic interests. Its targets have included NATO member states and groups supporting Ukraine.

Microsoft has documented compromises involving defense organizations as well as entities in transportation and aviation.A separate campaign targeted members of Ukraine's military with charity-themed phishing emails. Those messages disguised malware as requests for donations.
These campaigns suggest the group cares more about long-term intelligence collection than a quick financial payout. Access to email can reveal relationships, future plans and internal decisions.
PAIDWORK BREACH EXPOSES 23M USER RECORDS
CISA warns that Laundry Bear can compromise vulnerable Zimbra accounts without requiring users to click a link or open an attachment. (shapecharge/Getty Images)
Ways to stay safe from the email attack

The strongest protection starts with the organization running the email server because employees cannot personally patch a vulnerable installation. However, you can still take steps to spot suspicious activity and protect your other accounts.

Administrators should update Zimbra Collaboration Suite to a currently supported version and install all available security fixes. Organizations should confirm that the patch reached every server. An overlooked system may remain exposed even when the primary mail server has received the update.

Installing the patch blocks the known flaw, but it cannot undo a previous intrusion. Security teams should review CISA's published indicators of compromise. They should also search network records for connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Authentication logs may reveal unusual locations, unexpected devices or activity outside normal working hours.

Review every Zimbra application passcode connected to an account. Pay close attention to unfamiliar entries and anything labeled "ZimbraWeb." Revoke any passcode that the account owner or IT department cannot verify. Because application passcodes can survive a regular password change, this review plays an important role in removing persistent access.

Administrators should examine mailbox access records and forwarding settings. They should also look for unfamiliar filters, deleted messages or sent emails that the account owner does not recognize. A compromised account may send convincing phishing messages to coworkers because the email comes from a trusted internal address.

Contact your IT or security team if you notice unfamiliar sent messages, unexpected password resets or login alerts you cannot explain. Do not rely only on changing your password. Laundry Bear can create an application passcode that may continue providing mailbox access after the main password changes. Your IT team should revoke unauthorized passcodes, end active sessions and check the account for suspicious activity.

Wait until your IT department has patched the server and removed unauthorized access. Then change your email password and any other password you reused. Create a unique password for every account. A password manager can generate strong credentials and store them securely. Hackers may test stolen email credentials on banking, shopping or social media accounts. Reused passwords can turn one compromised inbox into several compromised accounts.

CISA recommends phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where organizations can support it. Security keys and passkeys provide stronger protection than methods that rely on temporary codes. However, organizations still need to patch the underlying email software. Authentication controls cannot fully protect an account when malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail interface.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads, fake login pages and follow-up malware connected to a broader phishing campaign. However, antivirus software may not stop this email exploit because the malicious code runs inside a vulnerable webmail session. Your organization still needs to update Zimbra and investigate the account for unauthorized access. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

An email login page can look convincing and still belong to an attacker. Instead of following a link inside an email, open your organization's known webmail address directly. Report unfamiliar authentication requests or repeated sign-in prompts to your security team. A sudden request to log in again could signal a phishing attempt or unauthorized account activity.
Kurt's key takeaways

For years, we have warned you to avoid suspicious links and unexpected attachments. That advice still helps, but Laundry Bear shows why your organization also needs to keep the software behind your inbox updated. In this campaign, viewing an email can trigger malicious code on an unpatched server. The attackers can then reach into the mailbox, collect months of messages and steal authentication data. The hidden application passcode adds another concern. Changing a password may provide a false sense of security when an attacker has already created a separate route back into the account. Organizations using Zimbra should patch immediately and then investigate for signs of earlier access. Employees should remain cautious around unexpected login pages, even when the page carries familiar company branding.

title: Police rescue 60 cats and kittens from abandoned sailboat off Washington beach after 6-day operation
summary: Tacoma police spent six days rescuing 60 cats from an abandoned 40-foot sailboat off Owens Beach, with many animals found frightened and malnourished.
story: Bodycam video shows Lee County deputies arresting a Fort Myers father accused of killing two family kittens and injuring a third as a form of punishment against his teenage daughter, according to authorities.
An abandoned sailboat off a Washington beach was home to an unexpected crew: 60 cats and kittens, many of them some frightened and malnourished.
The Tacoma Police Department said the unusual rescue began Aug. 6 when its Marine Services Unit responded to reports of an abandoned 40-foot sailboat in the waters off Owen Beach.

Officers initially discovered more than 30 cats and kittens living in unsafe conditions aboard the vessel, with many appearing frightened and malnourished. Marine Services began coordinating with Animal Control and the department's Forensics Unit to safely remove the animals.
What initially appeared to be a rescue involving more than 30 cats eventually grew to 60 over the course of a rescue effort spanning six days.
FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS
Tacoma police rescued 60 cats and kittens from a 40-foot sailboat located off Owen Beach after a six-day rescue effort. (Tacoma Police Department)
"That's a wrap! The final cat is off the boat. Fur real this time!" police wrote. "Final cat count: 60!"
Police said Animal Control was "as certain as they can be that all cats have officially disembarked."
"That's all for meow!" the department joked online.
Despite believing all 60 cats had been rescued, police said they would continue making trips to the boat this week as a precaution.
HERO SHEEPDOG BECOMES UNLIKELY RESCUE PARTNER AFTER UNEXPECTED MOVE AIDS FIRST RESPONDERS
Tacoma Animal Control and Marine Services worked to safely remove 60 cats and kittens from a sailboat anchored off Owen Beach. (Tacoma Police Department)

"While we believe we have safely removed all of the cats from the boat, as any cat owner knows, cats are exceptionally good at hiding," police said. "Because there is always a possibility that a cat may remain onboard, our work isn't quite finished."
The department said the additional searches would be conducted under the authority of a search warrant.
Police said Marine Services has also begun the process of having the legally registered vessel moved.

Authorities asked people visiting Owen Beach or boating nearby to notify Animal Control if they spot another cat aboard the vessel, while warning members of the public not to attempt their own rescues.
FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE
Tacoma police rescued 60 cats and kittens from a 40-foot sailboat anchored off Owen Beach in Washington after a six-day operation. (Tacoma Police Department)

"We know many animal lovers in our community want to help, and we appreciate the concern for these cats," police said. "However, this remains an active criminal case. Our teams are working hard to protect the animals while also protecting the integrity of the investigation."
"PLEASE DO NOT BOARD THE VESSEL unless you are the legal owner," police added.
The warning followed an incident in which private cat rescue trapper Camille Sutherland told KING 5 she boarded the vessel overnight and captured two cats, which she took to the Humane Society.
Some of the cats and kittens discovered aboard the sailboat were frightened and malnourished, Tacoma police said. (Tacoma Police Department)
Sutherland told the outlet she was trying to help and believed authorities were taking too long to rescue the animals.
Police told KING 5 that the unauthorized boarding complicated their investigation into the vessel's owner.
Police have not announced any arrests or charges in connection with the case.

Tacoma Police Marine Services responded to reports of an abandoned sailboat off Owen Beach before discovering dozens of cats and kittens aboard. (Tacoma Police Department)
More than 40 of the 60 rescued cats were taken to the Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County, while the remaining animals were placed in foster homes in the area, according to KING 5.

title: Convicted rapist who preyed on women at America's top party school faces reckoning after courthouse dash
summary: Arian Eteghaei received 30 years to life for forcible rape and sexual assault of multiple victims while a student at UC Santa Barbara, then fled custody.
story: Emily Compagno, Kayleigh McEnany, Harris Faulkner, and Steve Doocy discuss the arrest of Israel Christopher Flores-Ortiz (19), an illegal immigrant from El Salvador, accused of groping 12 female high school classmates in Fairfax County, Virginia. The Outnumbered panel slams the school district for allegedly covering up the assaults for weeks, violating state law. They also criticize the Biden administration's immigration policies, which allowed him to enter illegally in 2024.

A former UC Santa Barbara student convicted of raping and sexually assaulting multiple women will spend at least three decades behind bars, capping a yearslong prosecution involving disturbing allegations of sexual violence at one of America's top party schools.

Arian Eteghaei, 24, was sentenced to 30 years to life in California state prison after a jury found him guilty of forcible rape and forcible sexual penetration, but not before authorities say he made a brazen run for freedom, bolting from courthouse custody moments after his conviction.
His sentencing comes amid renewed scrutiny over sexual violence at UC Santa Barbara, which has been ranked the nation's top party school by Niche for the past two years.

Eteghaei's case adds to those concerns. He was also convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence, while jurors found true a special allegation that the sexual offenses were committed against more than one victim.
AMERICA'S TOP PARTY COLLEGE HIT BY ANOTHER SEX ATTACK WEEKS AFTER BRUTAL CAMPUS RAPE CASE

"This case would not have been possible without the extraordinary courage of the victims who came forward and participated in a long and difficult legal process," Santa Barbara County District Attorney John T. Savrnoch said. "Their strength and willingness to testify allowed the truth to be heard and ultimately allowed the defendant to be held accountable for the serious harm he caused."
Authorities say Eteghaei escaped by force while in custody on Jan. 16, the same day the jury returned its verdict.
The alleged escape landed Eteghaei another felony case, with prosecutors charging him in March with one count of escape by force.
STUDENTS AT TOP PARTY COLLEGE ON EDGE AFTER RAPE, STRANGULATION REPORTED IN CAMPUS HOUSING
Students walk on the University of California, Santa Barbara campus in Santa Barbara, Calif. (Kevin Koeppen Photography / Getty Images, File)
Eteghaei's sexual assault prosecution stretched back years and centered on crimes committed while he was a student at UC Santa Barbara.

"This case required years of persistence, careful investigation, and tremendous support for the victims," Savrnoch said. "The collective work of this team exemplifies the commitment of law enforcement, prosecutors, investigators, and victim advocates to seeking justice for survivors of sexual violence."

Campus crime data previously reviewed by Fox News Digital show more than 100 reported rapes between 2022 and 2024, while two separate sexual assault reports this spring and summer prompted campus-wide warnings and heightened concerns about student safety.
In June, UC Santa Barbara police issued a campus-wide Timely Warning after a woman reported being stalked and groped in broad daylight near Tierra De Fortuna Park.
RIDESHARE DRIVER ARRESTED IN ALLEGED SCHEME TARGETING IVY LEAGUE STUDENTS FOR SEX: PROSECUTORS

Police said the woman was walking along a paved access road on UCSB's West Campus around 11:30 a.m. June 24, when a man riding a bicycle passed her before circling back multiple times over the next 15 minutes.

During the first two encounters, police said the man stopped to ask her questions. On the third pass, investigators said he approached the woman from behind, groped her and fled toward nearby Tierra De Fortuna Park.
The incident marked the second Timely Warning issued by UCSB police in under two months.
In May, an 18-year-old freshman reported she was raped and strangled after meeting a man at a fraternity party before returning to her dorm at Tropicana Gardens in Isla Vista.
FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL

UC Santa Barbara freshman Elizabeth "Liz" Hamel died after a fall from a campus residence hall in February 2025; police ruled it an accident, but the district attorney’s office says the case remains under review. (Marli Miller/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Days after the attack, the survivor's family, through attorney Tyrone Maho, publicly appealed for witnesses to come forward, saying anyone who attended the fraternity party or was near Tropicana Gardens on the night of May 9 could hold critical information.

The family also urged the university's chancellor to ask the Santa Barbara County Sheriff's Office to take over the investigation, arguing that the unidentified attacker remained "a potential threat to our community," while expressing gratitude for the work already done by UC Santa Barbara police.
The attack prompted a candlelight vigil where students gathered to support the survivor and raise concerns about campus safety.
UC Santa Barbara has been ranked the nation's top party school by Niche for the past two years.
TEACHER WHO SERVED AS GOP STATE LAWMAKER ALLEGEDLY USED ROBLOX TO LURE STUDENT INTO SEXUAL RELATIONSHIP
Walkway and Storke Tower are shown on the University of California at Santa Barbara campus. (Marli Miller/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Campus crime data previously reviewed by Fox News Digital showed the university recorded more than 100 reported rapes between 2022 and 2024, according to its Annual Security and Fire Safety Reports.
The reports also showed increases in other reported crimes in recent years, including weapons arrests and burglaries.

In a statement previously provided to Fox News Digital following the May attack, UC Santa Barbara police said federal law limits what officials can disclose about active investigations, but emphasized that reports of crimes on university property are fully investigated by sworn officers.
The department said it remained in direct contact with the survivor's family and works closely with the Santa Barbara County Sheriff's Office and District Attorney's Office when appropriate.
