title: Texas judge accused of 'doxxing' political critic faces federal lawsuit, growing push to oust him from office
summary: West Texas judge Terry Johnson allegedly posted a critic's Social Security and driver's license numbers on Facebook, sparking a federal lawsuit.
story: Attorney James "Trey" Trainor discusses the federal civil rights lawsuit accusing Midland County Judge Terry Johnson of retaliating against Christino "Nino America" Rodriquez by allegedly exposing his sensitive personal information online.

What began as a controversial Facebook post has spiraled into a legal firestorm for a West Texas judge, who now faces a federal civil rights lawsuit and an unprecedented effort by his own district attorney to remove him from office.

Midland County Judge Terry Johnson is accused of posting a political critic’s Social Security number, driver’s license number and date of birth on Facebook less than 24 hours after the man published federal court records involving Midland County.

Christino Rodriquez, who goes by "Nino America" online, alleges in a 26-page federal lawsuit that Johnson retaliated against him for criticizing local government by using his position to obtain confidential information and publishing it online.
BABYLON BEE SUES NEW MEXICO OFFICIALS OVER LAW REQUIRING AI DISCLAIMERS ON POLITICAL SATIRE
Midland County Judge Terry Johnson faces a federal civil rights lawsuit and a separate effort seeking his removal from office. (Re-Elect Terry Johnson for Midland County Judge Facebook)

According to the lawsuit, Johnson posted a 2015 arrest warrant on his personal Facebook page with the caption, "Convicted felon trying to be a player." The complaint alleges the charges connected to the warrant were later dismissed and Rodriquez was not convicted in the case.
The filing also points to what was redacted — and what wasn’t.

Rodriquez’s home address and telephone number appeared blacked out, while his Social Security and driver’s license numbers remained visible. The lawsuit argues the selective redactions support its allegation that the disclosure was intentional.
James "Trey" Trainor, an attorney representing Rodriquez, told Fox News Digital the case goes beyond one Facebook post.

"The lawsuit is really about retaliation and abuse of power," Trainor said. "It’s kind of secondarily about First Amendment rights and the ability of people to actually criticize government without having government being used as a weapon against them."
Trainor said Rodriquez is active in the Midland community, attends public events and speaks out about local government.
"At the end of the day, he did that and he upset the county judge, and the county judge thought it was time to retaliate against him," Trainor alleged.
Trainor said Johnson had an employee access a criminal justice information system to obtain information about Rodriquez.
The federal complaint alleges Johnson obtained the unredacted warrant either through his own official access or through county personnel acting at his request or direction.
Trainor said the disclosure has left Rodriquez and his wife worried about identity theft and where the information could end up.
IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?
"This is probably the highest form of doxxing that you could ever engage in by putting this type of personal information out there," Trainor said.

"We don’t know how many pictures were taken, how many screenshots were saved, all of those types of things," he added. "So we really don’t have an overall understanding yet of how broad the damage is."
Trainor said his team has begun discussions with the Social Security Administration about potentially changing Rodriquez’s Social Security number.
The lawsuit seeks compensatory and punitive damages and other relief, including lifetime identity-theft protection and credit monitoring. No dollar amount has been attached to the case.

Christino "Nino America" Rodriquez is suing Midland County Judge Terry Johnson in federal court, alleging Johnson retaliated against him by posting sensitive personal information online after Rodriquez published records involving Midland County. (Nino America Facebook)
"We’re still looking into how much it’s actually going to cost and talking to experts on what the overall negative effect on Nino’s life is going to be," Trainor said.
For Trainor, the case also raises a broader question about what happens when citizens criticize those in power.

"We need that information to be available to law enforcement to track down the bad guys," Trainor said of criminal justice information. "The only difference here is that my client wasn’t a bad guy. He was just somebody who decided to speak out about a local issue."
Meanwhile, the separate effort to remove Johnson from office is also evolving.
Midland County District Attorney Glenn Harwood filed a petition Aug. 6 seeking Johnson’s removal, the first step under Texas law in attempting to oust a county-level elected official.
"There’s a lot of gates that it has to go through before it actually gets to a removal action," Harwood told Fox News Digital.

Harwood said the petition goes to the region’s administrative judge, who can dismiss it or assign it to another judge. An outside prosecutor would also have to decide whether to pursue the civil action.

Now, Midland ISD Trustee Brandon Hodges has moved to intervene in the case, arguing his involvement could keep the removal effort alive if a legal challenge arises over Harwood’s dual role as district attorney and the resident who initiated the proceeding.

Hodges’ filing says he is not seeking to replace Harwood or add new allegations against Johnson. Instead, he is asking to join as an independently qualified Midland County resident and adopt the same grounds for removal already alleged by Harwood.
UTAH SUPREME COURT JUSTICE RESIGNS AMID PROBE INTO ALLEGED RELATIONSHIP WITH REDISTRICTING ATTORNEY

Midland County Judge Terry Johnson is facing a petition seeking his removal from office amid allegations involving the disclosure of a resident’s personal information. (Midland County, TX — Government Facebook)

"I intervened so this removal case does not die on a procedural technicality tied to Glenn Harwood’s dual role," Hodges said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "If the court rules against him on that issue, the case still needs to move."
"Midland County deserves a real decision, not delay, excuses, or a quiet escape hatch for insiders," Hodges added. "I filed to help make sure that happens."

The 16-page filing argues Harwood occupies an unusual position because he initiated the removal proceeding as a Midland County resident while also serving as district attorney and swearing that the factual allegations in his petition are within his personal knowledge.

Hodges does not allege Harwood acted improperly and is not asking the court to remove him from the case. His filing instead describes the intervention as a way to prevent a potential dispute unique to Harwood from derailing the removal proceeding.
Steven Villela, a candidate for Midland County Commissioner Precinct 3, also joined those calls in a Facebook post, saying he agreed with Harwood that Johnson should resign.
"No elected official is above the law, and every public servant has a duty to protect the rights and confidential information of the people they serve," Villela wrote.
"Accountability isn’t about politics, it’s about doing what’s right," he added.
PROSECUTOR OUSTED AFTER ALLEGED ROMANCE WITH ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SEX-CRIME SUSPECT: 'PATTERN OF MISCONDUCT'
The Midland County Courthouse in Midland, Texas, where a growing legal battle involving County Judge Terry Johnson has unfolded. (Midland County, TX — Government Facebook)
Harwood emphasized that the removal effort is separate from Rodriquez’s federal lawsuit, saying he has "no role" in that case.
He also acknowledged what he described as a "potential criminal case," but declined to comment further because "nothing has happened on that front publicly yet."
Trainor separately told Fox News Digital that he and Rodriquez were interviewed by a Texas Ranger.
Trainor said the Ranger asked questions to verify whether the information shown online, including the Social Security and driver’s license numbers, belonged to Rodriquez.
Christino "Nino America" Rodriquez alleges Midland County Judge Terry Johnson exposed his personal identifying information in a Facebook post. (Nino America Facebook)
Trainor also said subpoenas had been issued to Meta seeking confirmation of when and where the information was posted and potentially viewed.
The controversy has also generated public calls for Johnson to leave office.
Midland County resident Shandi Williams called for Johnson’s resignation during a Commissioners Court meeting, according to the Midland Reporter-Telegram.

Johnson lost his reelection bid after failing to advance from the March 3 primary. If he remains in office, his term is expected to end in early 2027, when election winner Jay Marquez is set to take office, according to the Reporter-Telegram.
Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson and his attorney for comment.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: ICE eyes $20M purchase of electric shock gloves as Hochul warns of legal consequences
summary: New York Democratic leaders Kathy Hochul and Letitia James warn ICE could face legal action over electric shock gloves DHS plans to acquire.
story: A federal judge blocked New York state regulations attempting to force federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to wear identification, marking a significant legal victory for the agency. Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on the ruling, which halts state-level efforts to unmask federal officers.

New York's Democratic leaders are threatening potential legal action against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers over a new piece of equipment ICE could soon add to its arsenal: gloves capable of delivering an electric shock.
Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James said Wednesday that recently enacted state protections could expose ICE officers to legal consequences if the devices are used in New York.

The warning comes as the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moves toward acquiring thousands of devices described in federal procurement records as "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices."
ICE could spend up to $20 million on the equipment.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY
Federal agents  (John Moore/Getty Images)
The new devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., short for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and they are designed to deliver an electrical charge through contact with a person.

"You cannot trample on someone’s constitutional rights, and you cannot cause them undo harm. You will be held accountable," Hochul said when asked about the electric shock gloves. "[The protections] should be in effect here."
James said her office is reviewing the DHS proposal and examining whether use of the technology would violate New York law.
The proposal "appears to be in violation of a number of laws," James said, including the State Administrative Procedure Act.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks at a news conference in Manhattan in New York City Feb. 20, 2025. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)
James also indicated that her office would pursue legal action against DHS if a person in New York were injured by the devices.
"You can best be assured of that," James said.

ICE defended its process for evaluating equipment in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying the agency considers officers' safety and existing law enforcement standards when assessing new technology.

"ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country," a DHS spokesperson wrote.
"Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.
NEW YORK SHERIFFS 'MAD AS HELL' AS HOCHUL PUSHES TO BAN KEY LAW ENFORCEMENT PARTNERSHIP
New York Attorney General Letitia James holds a news conference in the Manhattan borough of New York City Feb. 16, 2024. (David Dee Delgado/Reuters)
"Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training. The latest ICE use of force policy is available here."

The gloves are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, a company based in Lexington, Kentucky. Demonstration videos released by the company show the devices being used on test subjects who fall to the ground after physical contact with a person wearing the gloves.
Compliant Technologies founder and CEO Jeff Niklaus declined to discuss the potential federal purchase when contacted by The Associated Press.
"Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject," Niklaus wrote in an email to The Associated Press.
The clash over ICE equipment comes as Hochul and James are also seeking to curtail cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.
New York law enforcement agencies have until Aug. 24 to end civil immigration enforcement agreements with ICE or potentially face legal consequences.
James said a dozen law enforcement agencies in the state maintained such agreements as of July, including Nassau County.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's office and Compliant Technologies for comment.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Kansas convicted felon, sex offender allegedly kills fellow family members before taking his own life: police
summary: Ronald Williams Sr., a registered sex offender, allegedly killed Kelly George and their four children in Winfield, Kansas, before a 911 call.
story: A wealthy restaurateur is accused of killing his pregnant wife and their two children in a Texas murder-suicide. (KRIV)
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A registered sex offender with a lengthy criminal history allegedly slaughtered the mother of his children and their four young kids inside their Kansas home, weeks after police had encounters with him over what the chief described as "erratic behavior."

Ronald H. Williams Sr., 53, allegedly killed Kelly L. George, 44, and their four children, Carol A. Williams, 9; Ronald H. Williams Jr., 7; Sarah K. Williams, 5; and Kelly M. Magee-Williams, 3, before making a chilling 911 call Tuesday morning, according to authorities.
Williams allegedly told the dispatcher that he had killed his entire family and was preparing to kill himself.
FLORIDA DEPUTY KILLED EX-GIRLFRIEND OVER A TV, THEN HIMSELF, SHERIFF SAYS
Ronald Williams allegedly killed a woman and four children inside a Winfield, Kan., home before taking his own life, authorities said. (Google Maps/Kansas Bureau of Investigation)
Officers happened to be working a traffic crash roughly two blocks away and raced to the Winfield home almost immediately, Police Chief Robbie DeLong said during a news conference.
As the first officer approached the house, a single gunshot rang out from inside.
With officers initially unable to determine what had happened inside, police backed away, established a perimeter and treated the home as a barricaded situation.
Nearly two hours later, officers breached the front door.
Inside, they discovered a devastating scene, with Williams, George and all four children dead from gunshot wounds.
Investigators also believe the final gunshot heard by the arriving officer was Williams taking his own life.
MICHIGAN DAD SHOT WIFE, SIX KIDS THEN SET FAMILY HOME ABLAZE IN MURDER-SUICIDE, SHERIFF SAYS
Residential neighborhood in Winfield, Kan., where authorities investigated the deaths of five family members. (Google Maps)
But the news conference also revealed that Tuesday's massacre was not law enforcement's first encounter with Williams.
DeLong said officers had dealt with Williams over "erratic behavior," including contact as recently as within the previous few weeks.
Police had also received calls involving aggressive behavior in public and reports of gunfire, although DeLong said investigators had been unable to determine the source of the reported shots.
Williams’ behavior had raised enough concern to put him on law enforcement's radar, but DeLong said nothing officers encountered suggested he was on the verge of killing his family.

The disturbing killings came after decades of brushes with the law for Williams, who operated under a long list of aliases and whose criminal history included a felony sex offense and a requirement to register as a sex offender in Kansas.
MARCELLUS WILEY'S WIFE CLAIMS EX-NFL STAR THREATENED TO KILL HER BEFORE FOURTH OF JULY DOMESTIC BATTERY ARREST

Kansas law enforcement officials provide an update on the investigation into the Winfield family killings that left a woman, four children and the suspected shooter dead. (Kansas Bureau of Investigation)
Williams appeared on the Kansas Bureau of Investigation's sex offender registry under the name Freddie Lu'Carl's Williams, with "Ronald Williams" among numerous aliases listed by the state.
His encounters with the criminal justice system stretched for nearly three decades.

Court records reviewed by KCTV showed Williams faced felony charges involving drugs, battery, assault on a law enforcement officer, burglary, attempted rape and kidnapping, among other alleged crimes, in cases dating from 1995 through 2024.
The charges spanned multiple jurisdictions, including Wyandotte, Johnson and Franklin counties, according to KCTV.
For those who lived just steps from the family, the killings left behind shock, heartbreak and haunting questions about whether something had been missed.
Ann Stofferan, who lives only a couple of houses from the scene, told KWCH that learning children were among the dead made her "stomach churn."
"I just felt so sad and heartbroken for that family," Stofferan told the outlet. "Because I just can't imagine what that man was thinking to do that. I just can't."
DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE
Another neighbor offered an especially haunting recollection, telling KWCH she remembered hearing Williams make an ominous statement to his wife before the killings.
"I remember him telling his wife, 'I'm going to do it, I'm going to do it, I'm going to call the cops, and I'm going to do it,'" the woman told the outlet.
She said she did not know at the time what Williams allegedly meant.
"How do you kill your own family? How do you do that? I just don't get it," she said.
Tonya Asbury, who lives about a block away, told KWCH the killings left her wondering whether something could have been done before five lives were lost.
"I hate to say it, but somebody failed," Asbury said. "Somebody in this community failed that family. Failed him and that family."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Investigators have not publicly identified a motive for the killings.
The scene had a profound impact on the officers and investigators who responded, with peer-support teams and mental health professionals called in to help them process what they encountered.
For DeLong, the scale of the killings was unprecedented during his career in the community.
"In my 20-plus years here, no, I can't remember anything remotely close to this," DeLong said.
The KBI and Winfield Police Department are continuing to investigate.

title: Deadly military helicopter crash in Texas kills 2, sparks wildfire and forces evacuations: officials
summary: A military helicopter crashed near Salado, Texas, sparking a vegetation fire as Bell County authorities work an active scene with details still emerging.
story: Two people were killed when an Apache helicopter crashed south of Salado, Texas, sparking a wildfire and prompting evacuations, according to authorities.

Two people were killed Wednesday when a Fort Hood AH-64 Apache attack helicopter violently crashed into a field in Central Texas, sparking a wildfire that forced evacuations and sent emergency crews racing to the scene, authorities said.
Bell County Sheriff's Office spokesman Cliff Coleman said authorities received the call about the crash at approximately 1:34 p.m.
The helicopter went down in a field south of Salado, roughly 30 minutes from Fort Hood. KWTX reported the crash occurred off Dove Hollow Lane.
PILOT EJECTS AS F-35 CRASHES AT MCAS MIRAMAR, SPARKING FIRE
A firefighting helicopter responds to a wildfire sparked by a deadly military helicopter crash near Salado, Texas. (KDTX)
Coleman described the crash as violent and confirmed two people were killed. No one else was injured.
Coleman identified the aircraft as an Apache helicopter and initially said it was believed to be from Fort Hood, but deferred to military officials for confirmation.
Fort Hood later confirmed the aircraft was an AH-64 Apache attack helicopter based at the installation. The identities of the two people killed have not been released.
Local emergency services, military responders and law enforcement were actively responding to the scene, Fort Hood said in a statement.
COAST GUARD HELICOPTER CRASHES DURING ALASKA TRAINING MISSION, INJURING FOUR CREW MEMBERS
A firefighting helicopter responds near the scene of a deadly Apache military helicopter crash south of Salado, Texas. (KDTX)

"Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts," Brigadier General Ethan Diven, First Cavalry Division Acting Commanding General, said. "Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information."
Fort Hood called the crash an ongoing and developing situation and said additional information would be released as it becomes available.
The crash sparked a wildfire, prompting a large emergency response, road closures and evacuations.

Coleman said the fire remained uncontrolled as of 4 p.m. ET and that some residents had been evacuated because of the flames. KWTX reported that Farm to Market Road 2843 was shut down near the crash site.
TEXAS CESSNA PLANE CRASH KILLS 5; NTSB INVESTIGATING
A police vehicle sits near a burned field after a military helicopter crash sparked a wildfire south of Salado, Texas. (KDTX)
Salado Fire/Bell County ESD #1 said crews were battling a "major grass fire" along FM 2843 and warned the public that the roadway was impassable in the affected area.
"Please avoid the roadway and choose an alternate route," the department said in a public safety alert. "This will help keep traffic clear for responding fire and emergency personnel."
The department also urged drivers not to attempt to travel through the area or around emergency vehicles.
Coleman said Fort Hood is leading the investigation into the crash. The cause has not been released.
Abhiram Garapati, a Republican congressional candidate in Texas, offered prayers for those involved in the crash and the first responders at the scene.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"My prayers are with those aboard, the first responders responding to the scene, and any individuals affected by the fire that began as a result of the crash," Garapati wrote on Facebook.
Fort Hood has not yet released the identities of the crew or additional details about the circumstances leading up to the crash.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Bystander shot dead after intervening in Florida man, woman's roadside fight; murder suspect was out on bond
summary: Raul Lionel Vazquez allegedly shot a man who was running away after intervening in a roadside fight following a car crash in Apopka.
story: The Orange County Sheriff's Department said Vazquez, 26, fatally shot 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill on Tuesday after Hill intervened in a roadside argument between Vazquez and a woman. (Credit: Orange County Sheriff's Department)

A Florida man was shot dead after intervening in a roadside fight between a man and woman following a car crash — allegedly at the hands of a suspect who was already out on bond in a separate aggravated assault case involving a deadly weapon.
Raul Lionel Vazquez, 26, has been charged with the second-degree murder of 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill, the Orange County Sheriff's Office said on social media.

At 8:27 a.m. on Tuesday, sheriff's deputies responded to an intersection in Apopka, a town northwest of Orlando, and found Hill lying face down with a gunshot wound, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by Fox News Digital.
Hill, who leaves behind a wife and a 10-year-old daughter, was rushed to the hospital but was pronounced dead at 9:20 a.m., the affidavit said.

The booking photo of Raul Lionel Vazquez, 26, who was charged with second-degree murder on Tuesday. The Orange County Sheriff's Office say he shot 56-year-old Daryl Alexander Hill in Apopka, Fla. (Orange County Sheriff's Office)

Hill was described as someone with a "a contagious personality, an incredible sense of humor, and a way of bringing laughter and joy to the people around him," according to a GoFundMe set up by a friend of Hill's wife, Suzy Hill.

Before Hill was shot, Vazquez and a woman, Kaidy Honaker, were seen by multiple witnesses fighting inside their white Chevy Silverado pickup truck when it crashed into a black Lexus, according to the affidavit. The two continued their heated altercation on the sidewalk.
Vazquez, who was seen shirtless and wearing no shoes, got in Honaker's face and appeared to be yelling and pointing at her, the affidavit said.

Two witnesses said they saw Hill riding a bicycle nearby and told authorities that he got involved in the argument, which led to Vazquez and Hill tackling each other into the bushes, per the affidavit.
An undated photo of Daryl Alexander Hill and his wife, Suzy Hill. He also leaves behind a 10-year-old daughter. (GoFundMe)
BOY, 12, KILLED AFTER SUSPECT OPENED FIRE DURING BRAWL NEAR THEATER DISTRICT, POLICE SAY
According to the affidavit, Honaker joined the fight as well, later saying she did so to pull Hill off Vazquez.
After the fight in the bushes, Hill began running away from Vazquez and Honaker, yelling "help" with his hands in the air, the affidavit said.
Vazquez retrieved what was later determined to be a shotgun from his pickup truck and fired one round, hitting Hill and causing him to fall to the ground, according to the affidavit.
In an interview with investigators, Vazquez offered "many different accounts" of what happened but said that Hill "was fighting him and getting the better of him," according to the affidavit.
Vazquez did not have an attorney on record. Fox News Digital reached out to the public defender's office for the Ninth Judicial Circuit, which serves Orange and Osceola counties.
Vazquez is escorted by Orange County Sheriff's deputies on Tuesday. (Orange County Sheriff's Office)
At the time of the shooting, Vazquez was out on bond for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

The Apopka Police Department investigated that case, which involved Vazquez and an accomplice allegedly threatening two people with a gun on Nov. 13, 2025, according to court records obtained by Fox News Digital.
In February, Vazquez pleaded not guilty to the charges and was granted a surety bond of $5,000.

The State Attorney's Office for the Ninth Judicial Circuit told Fox News Digital that the conditions of the bond included "no contact with the co-defendant, victims, or witnesses, as well as a requirement that he surrender any firearms within 24 hours of release."
The trial for that case is scheduled for Sept. 22, the state attorney's office said.
Vazquez is loaded into a police vehicle on Tuesday. (Orange County Sheriff's Office)
State Attorney Monique Worrell said in a statement to Fox News Digital that it recognizes "questions surrounding [Vasquez's] prior arrests."

"An arrest is not a conviction, and every case must be evaluated based on the evidence available, the participation of witnesses and victims, and the law," Worrell said. "Where the evidence supports prosecution, our office prosecutes. Where the evidence does not legally or ethically support moving forward, prosecutors cannot pursue a case simply because an arrest was made.
"The public deserves accurate information about how those prior cases were handled, and we will provide that information to the extent we can without compromising this active prosecution."

Vazquez was also arrested in March 2025 for a domestic violence incident that allegedly involved strangling someone, per court records.
He pleaded not guilty, and his bond was later discharged.
The state attorney's office told Fox News Digital that prosecutors could not proceed with the case because the alleged victim "was unavailable or unwilling to cooperate."

When the victim tried to call 911, Savetz took her phone. That’s when she told her two children to go inside.

The children were "extremely brave," calling 911 and giving dispatchers everything needed to identify the suspect, Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco told reporters.

Legend Storer, 20, has been charged with second-degree murder, first-degree burglary involving a dangerous instrument and indecent exposure in connection with the Aug. 5 death of Michael "Mike" Dyer, 63, according to court records obtained by Fox News Digital.

The Maui Police Department said the bizarre chain of events began around 1:45 a.m., when surveillance footage captured an unclothed man approaching Dyer’s office at a condominium resort on Lower Honoapiʻilani Road in Lahaina.

Just over an hour later, at about 3:02 a.m., dispatchers received a report of a nude man wandering through a neighborhood in nearby Kahana.
Officers tracked down the unclothed 20-year-old around 3:35 a.m. and found that he had suffered numerous abrasions, police said. He was taken to Maui Memorial Medical Center for evaluation.
Then, at 5:31 a.m., police were called to the resort after Dyer was found unresponsive. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Investigators reviewing surveillance footage later determined that the man found wandering naked in Kahana was the same person seen in the footage from the resort, police said.

Maui Police Department did not publicly identify the suspect by name, citing a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruling and its policy against routinely releasing identifying information about people who have been arrested.

title: Accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson asks judge to take potential death penalty off table
summary: Tyler Robinson's defense argues prosecutors failed to prove the sole aggravating factor that could make Charlie Kirk's killing a death penalty case.
story: Criminal defense attorney Donna Rotunno analyzes the latest court developments in two high-profile cases on 'Fox & Friends First'. Rotunno examines the newly released messages from Lindsey Clancy regarding her medication dependency and the defense arguments in the Tyler Robinson case in Utah.
Lawyers for accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson are arguing that prosecutors haven't established a case for the potential death penalty in a new court filing made public Tuesday night.
"The facts and the law require this Court to strike the sole aggravating factor," defense attorneys Kathy Nester, Michael Burt, Richard Novak and Staci Visser wrote in a 41-page brief.

After a weeklong preliminary hearing in early July, Judge Tony Graf Jr. gave both sides in the case time to file briefs before he makes a decision on whether there is enough probable cause to send the case to trial — which he is expected to announce on Sept. 1.
CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking during his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

Robinson, 23, is accused of shooting the 31-year-old Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, during a Turning Point USA event. Kirk had founded the group to promote conservatism on campuses around the country and was speaking in front of a crowd of more than 2,000 in the courtyard when he was struck and killed by a single bullet.

Robinson's defense argued in Tuesday's filing that prosecutors didn't establish probable cause concerning the aggravating factor — that the shooting created a high probability of death to someone other than Kirk and that Robinson knew of that "high probability."
SEND US A TIP
Tyler Robinson, accused of the murder of Charlie Kirk, appears during a hearing in Fourth District Court in Provo, Utah, Thursday, December, 11, 2025. (Rick Egan/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)
Without the aggravator, the potential death penalty would be taken off the table.

"The State had over ten months to investigate the shooting death of Charlie Kirk and to develop legally sufficient evidence that Mr. Robinson 'knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk and the defendant,' the sole aggravator alleged in the Information which in theory exposes Mr. Robinson to the potential punishment of death," Robinson's attorneys wrote. "The State’s presentation of its evidence as to this alleged circumstance in aggravation at the preliminary hearing in July 2026 wholly fails to carry its burden of proof."
FRIEND OF CHARLIE KIRK LABELS COURTROOM EVIDENCE 'DEVASTATING' AFTER CHILLING SURVEILLANCE FOOTAGE SHOWN
Robinson's lawyers noted that there was only one shot fired and that it struck Kirk. No one else was hit.

People run after shots were fired during an appearance by Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking during his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
They also argued that no one else was in the line of fire — noting that the bullet came from the rooftop, following a downward trajectory before striking Kirk.
"The only evidence presented supports that the bullet travelled above, not through, the crowd," they wrote.
TYLER ROBINSON'S AND LANCE TWIGGS' DNA BOTH ALLEGEDLY FOUND ON KEY EVIDENCE IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION
When the suspected murder weapon was recovered, a .30-06 bolt-action Mauser rifle, there was a spent casing in the chamber and three unfired rounds.
A crowd watches as Charlie Kirk appears at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)
And the evidence introduced by Utah County prosecutors indicates Kirk was the lone target, according to the defense filing.
TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE SUFFERS DUAL SETBACKS AS JUDGE HOLDS OFF ON DEATH PENALTY DECISION

"The communications the State admitted between Mr. Robinson and Mr. Twiggs indicate Mr. Robinson’s intention to kill Charlie Kirk," the defense wrote, citing an alleged message from Robinson: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and I took it."

Lance Twiggs, Tyler Robinson's roommate and reported romantic partner, is shown during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)
"There is no mention of any threat or intended harm to any other individual(s)."
Prosecutors have a deadline next week to reply to the brief. Graf's decision is expected at the Sept. 1 hearing.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Donna Rotunno, a Chicago-based lawyer and Fox News contributor, said Robinson's argument is a long-shot, especially at the probable cause stage of the case.

"The evidence in the preliminary hearing has already proven that there were many people there," she told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "The evidence has shown where the shooter was vs. where Charlie was and where the shot was taken from, the amount of people who were in the line of fire. They can argue those facts from other pieces of evidence that they've introduced. They didn’t need somebody specifically to get on the witness stand and say there were all these people in danger."
People run after shots were fired during an appearance by Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)

Prosecutors have alleged that Robinson is the man who appears on surveillance video approaching a sniper's perch. According to investigators, the killer opened fire from a rooftop on the far side of the packed courtyard, which was full of spectators.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"If you drive a car into a crowd, that whole crowd is in danger," Rotunno added. "I don’t think that argument is a stretch."
TYLER ROBINSON ASKS FOR MORE SECRET HEARINGS AFTER LOSING FIGHT OVER CAMERAS IN COURT
TPUSA founder Charlie Kirk appears at a Utah Valley University speaking event in Orem, Utah, on September 10, 2025. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune via REUTERS)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Robinson's lawyers also renewed their attempt to throw out hearsay evidence from the preliminary hearing, arguing that prosecutors haven't established its reliability.
Similar objections failed in July, and Rotunno said she expects them to fail again.
"They're relitigating many issues that the judge has already ruled on, and they're going nowhere," she said.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

An approximation of the suspected movements of Tyler Robinson, Charlie Kirk's alleged assassin, based on court documents, video from the scene and conversations with law enforcement. (Google Maps, Fox News Digital)

The defense is also asking Graf to strike two lesser charges — witness tampering and committing a violent offense in the presence of a child — arguing that Robinson was advising his roommate Lance Twiggs to exercise his constitutional rights and that prosecutors failed to show Robinson knew children were present at the time of the shooting.
UTAH VALLEY UNIVERSITY SCRAPS CONTROVERSIAL COMMENCEMENT SPEAKER WHO CRITICIZED CHARLIE KIRK AFTER HIS MURDER

And they argue that the enhancement that Kirk was targeted for his political expression should also be dropped, disputing an alleged text from Robinson to Twiggs stating, "I had enough of his hatred."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It is the State that argues that because Mr. Robinson and Mr. Twiggs are two men who love each other and/or, it speculates, because Mr. Twiggs (and not Mr. Robinson) was at least intermittently identifying as a female to his close friends, it is Mr. Kirk’s views on these topics which are the 'hatred' Mr. Robinson was referring to," the defense wrote. "These circumstances are not sufficient to establish, even by probable cause which if any political expression of Mr. Kirk motivated Mr. Robinson to select Mr. Kirk for an act of violence."
Robinson has not yet entered a plea.

title: Trump's DC crime crackdown 'working' as city sees homicides plummet 43% since 2025: slain intern's mom
summary: Tamara Jachym says Trump's National Guard deployment in Washington, D.C., is working after her son Eric Tarpinian-Jachym was fatally shot in 2025.
story: Tamara Jachym, the mother of a Capitol Hill intern killed in Washington last summer, says the National Guard deployment is "working" as D.C. homicides fall sharply.
The mother of a Congressional intern who was killed in 2025 says President Donald Trump's crime crackdown in Washington, D.C., is working as homicides have plummeted by over 40% over the past year.

New data from the Major Cities Chiefs Association shows that homicides in Washington, D.C., have dropped by 43.9% in the first half of 2026 compared to the previous year. In total, there were 46 homicides during that time period in 2026 compared to 82 in 2025.

The drop in Washington, D.C., homicides came after Trump deployed the National Guard and took control of its police force in early August 2025 to "rescue our nation's capital from crime, bloodshed, bedlam and squalor and worse."

title: WATCH: Neighbor’s double take helped police identify accused wildfire arsonist as flames raced nearby
summary: Paul Child spotted a stranger near railroad tracks twice before smoke rose, leading to a field showup that helped police ID accused arsonist Farinacci.
story: An eyewitness says he saw Aaron Farinacci near the site of Spokane’s Old Trails fire before smoke rose, then later helped deputies identify the alleged arsonist.

Paul Child drove past a stranger twice near railroad tracks outside his Washington home, then watched smoke rise about 10 minutes after the man crouched in nearby bushes – setting off a chain of events that helped police identify an accused wildfire arsonist.
Newly obtained bodycam footage shows officers evacuating Child’s family and taking him, his grandson and the boy’s friend to a field showup after detaining a man who matched their description.
While Child and the other witnesses waited near the showup scene, bodycam footage captured an officer saying the detained man had "a whole fanny pack full of matches."
The video does not show the alleged matches or establish how they were recovered.
MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE
Aaron F. Farinacci was arrested on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire in eastern Washington. (Arizona Department of Corrections)
Child said he and the other witnesses — his grandson and his grandson’s friend — were not told about the alleged matches or other items before they were asked to view the detained man.
"We thought he had a backpack," Child told Fox News Digital. "They didn’t say anything to us anyway about the fanny pack with matches, cigarettes [and] I guess lighter in it."
CANADIAN WILDFIRE SMOKE IGNITES CROSS-BORDER FEUD OVER OTTAWA'S 'WILLFUL NEGLIGENCE'

Child told Fox News Digital that he, his grandson and the grandson’s friend spotted a man twice near railroad tracks close to the apparent fire origin. The second time, Child said, the man’s behavior appeared unusual.
Wildfire witness Paul Child speaks with an Airway Heights officer near his pickup truck as authorities respond to the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 1, 2026. (Airway Heights Police Department)
"He was kind of bent over and looked like he was doing something in the bushes," Child said. "He got up, saw us. When he saw us, he turned to face us and kind of was pacing back and forth nervously."
Child said there was no smoke when the group last saw the man. Within about 10 minutes of returning home, however, he said smoke began rising about a half-mile away.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Bodycam footage from the Airway Heights Police Department shows smoke billowing in the distance as Officer Pace speaks with Child’s family about evacuating. The officer later tells them police may have detained "your guy" and that they could be asked to take part in a showup.
Airway Heights police body-camera footage shows smoke from the Old Trails Fire near a rural property on Aug. 1, 2026. (Airway Heights Police Department)
A field showup is an in-person identification procedure in which witnesses view a person detained shortly after an incident.
While the footage does not show the identification, Child said Pace escorted him and the two boys to a location about a mile and a half from his home.

"We pulled off to the side of the road, and they got an individual out from the back of the … Spokane County deputy car," Child said. "We looked at him, and all three of us gave them [a] positive, 100% positive ID that’s who we’d seen in the area just before the fire started."
Child said he and the two teen witnesses positively identified the detained man during the field showup. Authorities later identified the man as Aaron Forrest Farinacci.
SPOKANE FIRE SURVIVOR FINDS 'JOY' THROUGH JESUS AFTER ALLEGED ARSON DESTROYS HOME AND BELONGINGS
Smoke billows near a rural property outside Airway Heights, Washington, as an officer responds to the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 1, 2026. (Airway Heights Police Department)
The Aug. 1 field showup did not immediately lead to charges. Farinacci was released after witnesses identified the detained man, then was arrested on charges two days later, on Aug. 3.
Child said he did not initially realize Farinacci had been released.

Paul Child, a witness who reported the arson suspect arrested for the Old Trails Fire, looks out near a wooded area sprayed with fire retardant at his home in Spokane, Wash., Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. (Lindsey Wasson / AP Images)

"I was like, well, thank God, because … I thought they had him detained the whole time. I didn’t realize they didn’t have probable cause to hold him for a couple days. … He could walk right back up that road," Child said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Heavy smoke blankets the Spokane area as firefighters battle several fast-moving wildfires that have forced thousands of evacuations and prompted a massive emergency response. (Spokane Valley Fire Department)

Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails Fire, one of three blazes that have burned across Spokane and Stevens counties since Aug. 1. The Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane fires had burned a combined 10,002 acres and damaged or destroyed more than 920 structures, Spokane fire officials reported Monday.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

title: Heroic Florida K-9 returns to sheriff's office days after being shot protecting 3 deputies, losing leg
summary: K-9 Ace, the Polk County German shepherd who lost a leg shielding three deputies, made an emotional return to the sheriff's office after recovering ahead of retirement.
story: K-9 Ace returned to the Polk County Sheriff's Office for the first time since surviving a line-of-duty shooting and losing his left front leg as the longtime police dog prepares for retirement. (Polk County Sheriff's Office via Facebook)
Less than a week after being shot and losing a leg while protecting three deputies, heroic Florida K-9 Ace was back on his feet Tuesday for an emotional return to the sheriff's office.
Ace, a 7-year-old German shepherd who has served with the Polk County Sheriff's Office since March 2020, was wounded as deputies attempted to arrest 27-year-old Angel Bowers.
Authorities said Bowers allegedly fired at least four rounds at three deputies who were attempting to arrest him after he failed to appear in court. Bowers was killed by deputies at the scene.
DEPUTY US MARSHAL FATALLY SHOT WHILE SERVING ARREST WARRANT IN LOUISIANA

Polk County Sheriff's Office K-9 Ace returned to the agency less than a week after being shot while protecting three deputies and undergoing surgery to amputate his left front leg. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said Ace protected the three deputies from Bowers but was shot in his left front leg, shattering the bone and tearing an artery that caused massive blood loss.
Ace's partner and handler, Deputy Natalie Oestreich, treated his wounds and carried him to safety, according to the sheriff's office.

Ace was rushed to Parkway Veterinary Emergency Clinic in Lakeland, where he was stabilized before a Tampa General Hospital Aeromed helicopter transported him to the Veterinary Medical Center at Lakewood Ranch. Veterinarians there performed a several-hour surgery to amputate his left front leg.
On Sunday, the sheriff's office posted video showing deputies arriving at the veterinary medical center to greet an energetic Ace as he prepared to return home.
AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND

"Upon waking from the anesthesia, Ace attempted to walk out of there," the sheriff's office wrote. "He has not been deterred since. In fact he outran the camera attempting to film his release this afternoon!"
Video shows Ace interacting with deputies before walking out of the medical center under his own power to thunderous applause while wearing a shirt that read "ride or die."
Two days later, Ace made his first trip back to the sheriff's office since being shot in the line of duty.

"Look at Ace. He's happy; he's eating; he bit my finger," Judd said. "We are so proud of Natalie and Ace. They stood in the gap between good and evil, and they saved three deputies' lives. That's why we're so proud of him. He did so good."
MAN WANTED IN DEPUTY AMBUSH CAUGHT AFTER WILDLIFE CAMERA SIGHTING AND MAJOR MANHUNT
K-9 Ace was back on his feet days after suffering a gunshot wound that resulted in the amputation of his left front leg. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)
Judd said Oestreich will spend time with Ace as he continues to recover before she returns to work. Ace, however, will retire from law enforcement.
"Chill out and enjoy your retirement Ace," Judd said.
The sheriff's office also honored Ace in a social media post, writing, "His days of chasing bad guys may be over, but Ace will always be one of our heroes!"

K-9 Ace will retire after being critically wounded while protecting three Polk County deputies during an attempted arrest. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)

Polk Sheriff's Charities Inc. has established a K-9 fund to help support Ace's care. The sheriff's office said those interested in helping can donate directly to the fund through the organization's website.

title: Five teen friends killed after vehicle plunges down Colorado cliff, leaving community shattered
summary: Five 17-year-old boys from Grand Junction, Colorado, died when their vehicle plunged off a cliff along Lookout Lane, with speed being investigated as a possible factor.
story: Gwinnett County Police dashcam footage shows a horrific three-vehicle collision on May 23, where a 7-year-old boy was miraculously ejected from a truck onto a police cruiser. Officer Arianna James, who witnessed the crash, describes rushing to the child's aid, comforting him as he feared being left by his father. This terrifying event highlights the importance of child safety in vehicles.

Five 17-year-old friends were killed when their vehicle plunged off a cliff and down a steep Colorado hillside, leaving their families and community grappling with an unimaginable loss just as a new school year begins.
The five boys, all from Grand Junction, were traveling along Lookout Lane late Saturday when their vehicle veered off the roadway and went down the steep incline, according to authorities.

Three of the teenagers, including the driver and front-seat passenger, were wearing seat belts, while the other two were not buckled in and were ejected from the vehicle, the Mesa County Coroner's Office said.

Authorities were not alerted to the wreck until approximately 7:45 a.m. Sunday, when 911 dispatchers received a report that a vehicle may have gone over the edge of a cliff, according to the Grand Junction Police Department.
Police and firefighters responding to the area discovered the wrecked vehicle along the hillside.
Speed is being investigated as a possible factor, police said. Authorities have not publicly identified the driver or said what caused the vehicle to leave the roadway.

One of the victims was Braden Taylor, 17, whose grandfather, Calvin Wilken, confirmed his death in an emotional Facebook post obtained by Fox News Digital.
"Very sad news our youngest grandson Braden 17 died in a car rollover down 5 ledges of a very steep drop off over looking the railroad tracks and the Gunnison River," Wilken wrote.

Wilken said the crash occurred just blocks from the family's former home in a ridge-top development above the area.
A GoFundMe established for Braden's parents said the teenager was their youngest son and that the family is now confronting unexpected funeral expenses while trying to process his death.

"Her involvement in this case came about after one of the prosecutors — I don't recall which — made it out on direct examination that McLean is some kind of a five-star institution where the doctors, the psychiatrists, the psychotherapists, and the counselors were all banging into each other in the hallway trying to interview Miss Clancy, who was just blithely refusing care and treatment, which is not the case," Reddington said.

title: Ukraine pounds Black Sea Fleet’s ‘last major stronghold’ while Putin flexes naval power in Pacific
summary: Putin threatened to seize European vessels from the Russian Black Sea to the Pacific after Ukraine's drone attack crippled Novorossiysk grain terminals.
story: More than 13,000 troops and dozens of ships, submarines and aircraft take part in Russian naval drills across the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Northwest Pacific. (Credit: East2West)

Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened Wednesday to seize European vessels in retaliation if European countries begin seizing Russian merchant ships after Ukraine launched a major overnight attack on a key Russian Black Sea naval and commercial hub and Moscow staged large-scale war games in the Pacific.

The developments underscore a growing battle at sea: Ukraine is hitting one of Russia’s most important Black Sea naval and export hubs, while Moscow is warning it could seize European vessels and flexing its naval power in the Pacific. Though the events are not directly linked, they show how the war is increasingly extending beyond the front lines into strategic ports and international shipping routes.

Ukraine hammered the port city of Novorossiysk in a massive overnight drone attack that put two major grain terminals out of operation, according to Russian industry sources cited by Reuters Aug. 12. Novorossiysk is a major Black Sea export hub and also serves as a base for Russian warships that Moscow relocated there after repeated Ukrainian attacks on its Black Sea Fleet in Crimea.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed responsibility Wednesday morning for an operation targeting the Novorossiysk naval base, calling it "the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea." In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used Palianytsia jet-powered drones, Neptune missiles and unmanned naval systems and claimed hits on air-defense positions, piers and port infrastructure.
UKRAINE LAUNCHES WHAT APPEARS TO BE ONE OF ITS LARGEST DRONE ATTACKS AGAINST RUSSIA: REPORT

Russian President Vladimir Putin is welcomed on board the missile cruiser Varyag as he observes a military drill of Pacific fleet, in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin Region, Russia, Aug. 12, 2026. (Sputnik/Gavriil Grigorov/Pool via Reuters)
"The occupation fleet and all the infrastructure supporting it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues," Zelenskyy wrote.

The governor of Russia’s Krasnodar region said at least two people, including an 8-year-old child, were killed in the wider wave of attacks. Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said more than two dozen residential buildings, four businesses and educational facilities were damaged, and the city’s water supply was suspended. Reuters reported that Chicago wheat futures rose roughly 3% amid concerns over potential disruptions to Russian grain exports.

Separately Wednesday, thousands of miles to the east, Putin appeared aboard the Russian missile cruiser Varyag near Sakhalin while observing Pacific Fleet exercises and issued a warning to European governments increasingly targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet.

The European Union has expanded sanctions against hundreds of vessels and detained some ships and their crews for checks, while some European governments are considering tougher maritime enforcement against vessels suspected of sanctions evasion, Reuters reported Wednesday.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

A damaged private house after an overnight attack, what local authorities called a Ukrainian drone strike, in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Novorossiysk, Russia, in this still image taken from video released Aug. 12, 2026. (Operations Headquarters of Krasnodar Region/Handout via Reuters)

Quoting Putin, Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X, "Attempts to seize Russian vessels & sell off our property are outright piracy. If such plans are implemented, Russia will respond in kind – wherever we deem necessary, including within the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility."

The warning came against the backdrop of sweeping Russian naval exercises. The drills stretched across the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Northwest Pacific and involved more than 13,000 personnel and around 60 ships, submarines and support vessels. Russian Defense Ministry figures reported separately put the number of participating aircraft, helicopters and unmanned systems at around 30.

Video supplied by East2West showed Russian forces firing anti-ship missiles during the drills. Bastion coastal missile systems launched Oniks cruise missiles at simulated enemy ships from Kamchatka and the Kuril Islands, while the corvette Smerch fired a Uran anti-ship cruise missile, according to East2West.

Putin also used his Pacific appearance to accuse NATO of expanding its presence in the Asia-Pacific and Arctic regions, pointing to new military alliances and planned weapons deployments that he said were increasing the potential for conflict.
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS
A firefighter extinguishes a fire that appeared after Russian drone strikes amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region, Ukraine, Aug. 12, 2026. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)

The developments unfolded as attacks continued on both sides. Reuters reported that Russia struck the Ukrainian port of Odesa and that a separate Russian attack set fire to a shopping mall in Zaporizhzhia, underscoring the continuing pressure on ports and logistics infrastructure as the war approaches four and a half years.
Separately, Romania said its naval forces destroyed two suspected Russian Gerbera drones over the Black Sea, roughly 90 nautical miles from Constanta, according to East2West.
Romanian naval forces destroy two suspected Russian Gerbera drones over the Black Sea, roughly 90 nautical miles off Constanta, according to East2West. (East2West)

NATO said its North Atlantic Council met Wednesday to discuss Russian airspace violations in Poland and Romania and recent drone incidents. A NATO spokesperson said allies "condemned Russia for actions, expressed solidarity with allies affected [and] reaffirmed support to Ukraine."
